这个受轻视的单音节字后面跟什么词，全不要紧——这个前缀之后无论来什么酒，都受欢迎。
芒西虽算不得最爱吐露心曲，却是我所知的最可与之交谈的人。社交的原则与他这个人不可分。他若无话可说，便举杯祝您健康；他说话又快又含糊，你没听清，也同样满有把握地应一声——你知道他意思总是好的。他的口头禅是：“咱们人人身上都有几分花花公子气”；他自己却一丝也没有。同芒西交谈不上六句，我便发现他认得我几位旧识（这本身就是一封现成的引荐信，因为议论共同朋友的为人与小癖，是友谊的大甜味剂与黏合剂）——而且近二十年来，城里大多数才子名士他都过从甚密。托宾、华兹华斯、波尔森、威尔逊、佩利、厄斯金，还有许多别的，他都认识。他谈起佩利的谐趣与谦和，又活灵活现地描摹当年苹果酒窖里的波尔森，怎样长饮连着长引。不过，对那一类学问，他心存疑虑。我说起只见过那位希腊语教授一面，是在伦敦学会的图书馆里：他穿一件锈旧的黑色外衣，衣摆上挂着蛛网，鼻梁上从上到下贴着一大块粗布朗纸，活脱一个喝醉的木匠，正用一种近乎屈尊的和蔼口气同一位馆主说话——芒西听了，忍不住为古典文学的体面略表不安。“恕我直言，先生，常识难道不是头等要紧的东西？天才与学问若于立身处世毫无用处，又有什么可贵？”—芒西是爱那曙色将临的时辰的人：这时只剩下三三两两的几个知己，像破晓前的星辰；这时谈吐与麦酒“越品越好”。某晚只剩下威尔斯、芒西和我。我们同坐了几个钟头，彼此都不生厌。

===Original===

The conversation turned on the Beauties of Charles the Second’s Court at Windsor, and from thence to Count Grammont, their gallant and gay historian. We took our favourite passages in turn﻿—one preferring that of Killigrew’s country cousin, who, having been resolutely refused by Miss Warminster (one of the Maids of Honour), when he found she had been unexpectedly brought to bed, fell on his knees and thanked God that now she might take compassion on him﻿—another insisting that the Chevalier Hamilton’s assignation with Lady Chesterfield, when she kept him all night shivering in an old outhouse, was better. Jacob Hall’s prowess was not forgotten, nor the story of Miss Stuart’s garters. I was getting on in my way with that delicate *endroit* in which Miss Churchill is first introduced at court and is besieged (as a matter of course) by the Duke of York, who was gallant as well as bigoted on system. His assiduities, however, soon slackened, owing (it is said) to her having a pale, thin face: till one day, as they were riding out hunting together, she fell from her horse, and was taken up almost lifeless. The whole assembled court was thrown by this event into admiration that such a body should belong to such a face63 (so transcendent a pattern was she of the female form), and the Duke was fixed. This, I contended, was striking, affecting, and grand, the sublime of amorous biography, and said I could conceive of nothing finer than the idea of a young person in her situation, who was the object of indifference or scorn from outward appearance, with the proud suppressed consciousness of a Goddess-like symmetry, locked up by “fear and niceness, the handmaids of all women,” from the wonder and worship of mankind. I said so then, and I think so now: my tongue grew wanton in the praise of this passage, and I believe it bore the bell from its competitors. Wells then spoke of Lucius Apuleius and his *Golden Ass*, which contains the story of Cupid and Psyche, with other matter rich and rare, and went on to the romance of Heliodorus, Theagenes and Chariclea and in it the presiding deities of Love and Wine appear in all their pristine strength, youth, and grace, crowned and worshipped as of yore. The night waned, but our glasses brightened, enriched with the pearls of Grecian story.

===Chinese===

话头转到查理二世的温莎宫廷诸美，再从那里转到她们的风流而快活的信史编纂者格拉蒙伯爵。我们轮流献上各自心爱的段落——一位偏爱基利格鲁的乡下表兄那一段：他被沃明斯特小姐（宫廷侍女之一）斩钉截铁地拒绝了，待到发现她竟意外地生了孩子，扑通跪倒，感谢上帝，这下她或许肯可怜他了——另一位坚称汉密尔顿骑士与切斯特菲尔德夫人的幽会更好：夫人让他在一间旧外屋里发着抖等了一整夜。雅各布·霍尔的本事没有被人忘记，斯图尔特小姐吊袜带的故事也没有。我则照我的路子，正讲到那处精妙的*段落*（*endroit*）：丘吉尔小姐初入宫廷，便（理所当然地）遭到约克公爵的围攻——公爵既是成见上的、也是风流上的按部就班者。然而他的殷勤不久便松懈了，据说是因为她脸色苍白清瘦：直到有一天，两人一同出猎，她从马上跌下，抬起来时几乎没了气息。这一下，满朝上下都惊呆了：这样的身段竟配着这样一张脸63（她是女性形体无与伦比的范本）；公爵的心也定了。我力主，这一段惊人、动人而堂皇，是情爱传记的崇高极致；我说，再想不出比这更妙的意念了：一个处境如此的少女，因外貌而遭人冷淡与轻视，却怀着女神般匀称的身段那骄人而自抑的自觉，被“畏惧与羞怯——一切女子的侍女”锁闭着，不令世人惊叹与膜拜。我当时这样讲，如今仍这样想：我的舌头在赞这一段时放肆起来；我相信它压倒了同场的竞争者。随后威尔斯谈起卢基乌斯·阿普列尤斯和他的《金驴记》（*Golden Ass*），里面藏着丘比特与普赛克的故事，还有别的富丽而珍罕的材料；又谈到赫利奥多罗斯的传奇《忒阿革涅斯与卡里克勒亚》：在其中，爱与酒的主宰之神以其太初的力量、青春与优雅现身，一如既往地受着加冕与礼拜。夜阑了，我们的杯子却愈加明澈，盛满了希腊故事的珠玑。

===Original===

Our cupbearer slept in a corner of the room, like another Endymion, in the pale ray of a half-extinguished lamp, and starting up at a fresh summons for a further supply, he swore it was too late, and was inexorable to entreaty. Mounsey sat with his hat on and with a hectic flush in his face while any hope remained, but as soon as we rose to go, he darted out of the room as quick as lightning, determined not to be the last that went.﻿—I said some time after to the waiter, that “Mr. Mounsey was no flincher.”
“Oh! sir,” says he, “you should have known him formerly, when Mr. Hume and Mr. Ayrton used to be here. Now he is quite another man: he seldom stays later than one or two.”
“Why, did they keep it up much then?”
“Oh! yes; and used to sing catches and all sorts.”
“What, did Mr. Mounsey sing catches?”
“He joined chorus, sir, and was as merry as the best of them. He was always a pleasant gentleman!”
This Hume and Ayrton succumbed in the fight. Ayrton was a dry Scotchman, Hume a good-natured, hearty Englishman. I do not mean that the same character applies to all Scotchmen or to all Englishmen. Hume was of the Pipe-Office (not unfitly appointed), and in his cheerfuller cups would delight to speak of a widow and a bowling-green, that ran in his head to the last. “What is the good of talking of those things now?” said the man of utility. “I don’t know,” replied the other, quaffing another glass of sparkling ale, and with a lambent fire playing in his eye and round his bald forehead﻿—(he had a head that Sir Joshua would have made something bland and genial of)﻿—“I don’t know, but they were delightful to me at the time, and are still pleasant to talk and think of.”﻿—*Such a one*, in Touchstone’s phrase, *is a natural philosopher*; and in nine cases out of ten that sort of philosophy is the best! I could enlarge this sketch, such as it is; but to prose on to the end of the chapter might prove less profitable than tedious.
I like very well to sit in a room where there are people talking on subjects I know nothing of, if I am only allowed to sit silent and as a spectator; but I do not much like to join in the conversation, except with people and on subjects to my taste. Sympathy is necessary to society. To look on, a variety of faces, humours, and opinions is sufficient; to mix with others, agreement as well as variety is indispensable. What makes good society?

===Chinese===

我们的司酒童睡在屋角，像又一个恩底弥翁，睡在一盏半灭的灯的苍白光线里；新的添酒声把他惊起，他赌咒说太晚了，任凭央告也不为所动。只要还有一线指望，芒西便戴着帽子坐在那里，脸上带着酒后的红晕；可我们一站起身要走，他立刻闪电般冲出房间，打定主意不做最后一个走的。——过了一阵子，我对侍者说：“芒西先生可不是临阵脱逃的人。”
“哦！先生，”他说，“您该见见从前的他，那时休姆先生和艾尔顿先生常来。如今他完全换了个人：很少坐到一两点以后。”
“怎么，那时他们喝得很凶吗？”
“哦！是的；还常唱轮唱曲，什么都唱。”
“什么，芒西先生也唱轮唱曲？”
“他跟着唱副歌，先生，同他们中间最快活的一样快活。他一向是位可亲的先生！”
休姆与艾尔顿后来都在这场战斗里倒下了。艾尔顿是个干巴巴的苏格兰人，休姆是位和善、热肠的英格兰人。我并不是说同样的性格适用于全体苏格兰人或全体英格兰人。休姆在烟草税署供职（任命得不算不称职），酒至欢处，最爱谈起一位寡妇和一片滚球场——这念头在他脑中萦绕到最后。“如今还谈这些有什么用？”那位讲实效的人说。“我不知道，”他答道，一面又干了一杯腾沫的麦酒，眼里、秃顶四周闪着一层柔光——（他那颗头，落在雷诺兹爵士手里准能画出一幅温厚可亲的什么）——“我不知道，只是那些事当时使我快乐，如今谈谈想想，也还是愉快。”——用试金石的话说，*这样的人，是一位天生的哲人*；十有八九，这种哲学才是最好的！
这幅速写，尽管如此，本还可以铺展；但若絮叨到章末，恐怕得不偿失，徒增冗闷。
我很乐意坐在一间屋里，听人们谈论我一窍不通的题目，只要容我默默旁观；但加入交谈，我就不大乐意了，除非其人其题都合我的口味。交往离不开同情。做旁观者，形形色色的面孔、脾气与见解尽够了；要与人相接，除多样之外，投契也必不可少。什么造就好的社交圈？

===Original===

I answer, in one word, real fellowship. Without a similitude of tastes, acquirements, and pursuits (whatever may be the difference of tempers and characters) there can be no intimacy or even casual intercourse worth the having. What makes the most agreeable party? A number of people with a number of ideas in common, “yet so as with a difference”; that is, who can put one or more subjects which they have all studied in the greatest variety of entertaining or useful lights. Or, in other words, a succession of good things said with good-humour, and addressed to the understandings of those who hear them, make the most desirable conversation. Ladies, lovers, beaux, wits, philosophers, the fashionable or the vulgar, are the fittest company for one another. The discourse at Randal’s is the best for boxers; that at Long’s for lords and loungers. I prefer Hunt’s conversation almost to any other person’s, because, with a familiar range of subjects, he colours with a totally new and sparkling light, reflected from his own character. Elia, the grave and witty, says things not to be surpassed in essence; but the manner is more painful and less a relief to my own thoughts. Someone conceived he could not be an excellent companion, because he was seen walking down the side of the Thames, *passibus iniquis*, after dining at Richmond. The objection was not valid. I will, however, admit that the said Elia is the worst company in the world in bad company, if it be granted me that in good company he is nearly the best that can be. He is one of those of whom it may be said, “Tell me your company, and I’ll tell you your manners.” He is the creature of sympathy, and makes good whatever opinion you seem to entertain of him. He cannot outgo the apprehensions of the circle, and invariably acts up or down to the point of refinement or vulgarity at which they pitch him. He appears to take a pleasure in exaggerating the prejudice of strangers against him; a pride in confirming the prepossessions of friends. In whatever scale of intellect he is placed, he is as lively or as stupid as the rest can be for their lives. If you think him odd and ridiculous, he becomes more and more so every minute, *à la folie*, till he is a wonder gazed by all﻿—set him against a good wit and a ready apprehension, and he brightens more and more﻿—

我答曰，一句话：真正的情谊。趣味、造诣与追求若不相类（脾气性格尽可千差万别），便没有亲密可言，连值得拥有的寻常往来也没有。什么使一个聚会最为融洽？一群人，抱着一群共同的见解，“却又同中有异”；也就是说，他们能就人人都研习过的一两个题目，从最五花八门的有趣或有益的角度加以阐发。或者换一种说法：一连串怀着好性情说出、又说到听者心坎里的妙语，构成最可欲的谈话。淑女与淑女、情郎与情郎、纨绔与纨绔、才子与才子、哲人与哲人、时髦人与时髦人、俗人与俗人，各与其同类，才是最相宜的伴侣。兰德尔府上的言谈，最适合拳师；朗格斯府上的，最适合勋爵与闲人。亨特的谈话我几乎爱胜过任何人，因为题目尽管家常，他涂上去的光色却全然新奇而闪耀，是从他自己性格里映出来的。伊利亚（Elia），庄重而谈谐的那位，说出的话本质无可超越；只是那方式更费力，对我自己的思想也少些松快。有人认定他做不成极佳的游伴，因为在里士满赴宴之后，有人见他沿泰晤士河岸走，*passibus iniquis*（脚步歪斜）。这一条反对不成立。不过我可以承认：这位伊利亚在糟糕的伙伴中间是天底下最糟的伴，只要容我说：在好的伙伴中间，他几乎是绝顶好的伴。他属于那样一类人：“告诉我你同谁作伴，我就能说出你的举止。”他是同情的造物，你对他似乎抱有什么看法，他便把那看法坐实。他超不出这个圈子所预期的高度，总是就着人家给他标定的雅或俗的刻度，向上或向下演。他仿佛以夸张生人对自己的偏见为乐，以坐实朋友的先入之见为荣。无论把他放进哪个智识层级，他都能同其余的人一样活泼、或一样愚蠢，不遗余力。你若觉得他古怪可笑，他便一分钟比一分钟更古怪可笑，*直至癫狂*，直到成为万众围观的奇观——把他放到一位好的才智与敏捷的悟性面前，他便一分比一分更亮——

> “或像一道钢门

===Original===

Fronting the sun, receives and renders back

Its figure and its heat.”

We had a pleasant party one evening at Procter’s. A young literary bookseller who was present went away delighted with the elegance of the repast, and spoke in raptures of a servant in green livery and a patent lamp. I thought myself that the charm of the evening consisted in some talk about Beaumont and Fletcher and the old poets, in which everyone took part or interest, and in a consciousness that we could not pay our host a better compliment than in thus alluding to studies in which he excelled, and in praising authors whom he had imitated with feeling and sweetness!﻿—I should think it may also be laid down as a rule on this subject, that to constitute good company a certain proportion of hearers and speakers is requisite. Coleridge makes good company for this reason. He immediately establishes the principle of the division of labour in this respect wherever he comes. He takes his cue as speaker, and the rest of the party theirs as listeners﻿—a “Circa herd”﻿—without any previous arrangement having been gone through. I will just add that there can be no good society without perfect freedom from affectation and constraint. If the unreserved communication of feeling or opinion leads to offensive familiarity, it is not well; but it is no better where the absence of offensive remarks arises only from formality and an assumed respectfulness of manner.
I do not think there is anything deserving the name of society to be found out of London; and that for the two following reasons. First, there is *neighbourhood* elsewhere, accidental or unavoidable acquaintance: people are thrown together by chance or grow together like trees; but you can pick your society nowhere but in London. The very persons that of all others you would wish to associate with in almost every line of life (or at least of intellectual pursuit) are to be met with there. It is hard if out of a million of people you cannot find half a dozen to your liking. Individuals may seem lost and hid in the size of the place; but in fact, from this very circumstance, you are within two or three miles’ reach of persons that, without it, you would be some hundreds apart from. Secondly, London is the only place in which each individual in company is treated according to his value in company, and to that only.

迎着太阳，把太阳的形与热接过来，又送回去。”

一天晚上，我们在普罗克特家有一场愉快的聚会。在座的一位年轻的文人书商走时对那晚宴席的雅致心醉神迷，眉飞色舞地夸起那穿绿色号衣的仆人和那盏专利油灯。我自己倒觉得，那晚的魅力在于一番关于博蒙特与弗莱彻和老诗人的谈论，人人参与、人人关切；还在于一种默契：向他所长于的学问致意、盛赞他以深情与甜美摹习过的作家，便是对主人最好的恭维！——我想，在这个题目上还可以立一条规则：要构成好的社交，听者与说者须有一定比例。柯尔律治之所以是好伴，正因如此。他一到场，便立刻确立起这一方面的分工原则。他领了说的差事，其余人领了听的差事——“一圈听众”——事先无须任何安排。再补一句：没有彻底摆脱做作与拘束，便没有好的社交。情感与见解的毫无保留，若流于冒犯的亲昵，固然不好；但若免于冒犯之言只是出于客套与装出来的恭敬，也好不到哪里。
我认为，伦敦之外再没有配称“社交”的东西；理由有二。其一，别处只有*街坊*，偶然的或躲不开的相识：人们被机缘抛在一处，或像树一样长在一处；而只有在伦敦，社交才挑得拣得。几乎每一行当（或至少每一种智识追求）里，你最愿结交的那些人，在那里都遇得到。百万人之中找不出六七个合意的，未免说不过去。个人在这座城的体量里似乎湮没无闻；可恰恰因为这体量，那些否则与你相隔数百里的人，都近在你两三英里之内。其二，只有在伦敦，席间每个人得到的对待，才只按他在席间的分量，且仅按这一种分量。

===Original===

In every other part of the kingdom he carries another character about with him, which supersedes the intellectual or social one. It is known in Manchester or Liverpool what every man in the room is worth in land or money; what are his connections and prospects in life﻿—and this gives a character of servility or arrogance, of mercenaries or impertinence to the whole of provincial intercourse. You laugh not in proportion to a man’s wit, but his wealth; you have to consider not what, but whom you contradict. You speak by the pound, and are heard by the rood. In the metropolis there is neither time nor inclination for these remote calculations. Every man depends on the quantity of sense, wit, or good manners he brings into society for the reception he meets with in it. A Member of Parliament soon finds his level as a commoner: the merchant and manufacturer cannot bring his goods to market here: the great landed proprietor shrinks from being the lord of acres into a pleasant companion or a dull fellow. When a visitor enters or leaves a room, it is not inquired whether he is rich or poor, whether he lives in a garret or a palace, or comes in his own or a hackney coach, but whether he has a good expression of countenance, with an unaffected manner, and whether he is a man of understanding or a blockhead. These are the circumstances by which you make a favourable impression on the company, and by which they estimate you in the abstract. In the country, they consider whether you have a vote at the next election or a place in your gift, and measure the capacity of others to instruct or entertain them by the strength of their pockets and their credit with their banker. Personal merit is at a prodigious discount in the provinces. I like the country very well if I want to enjoy my own company; but London is the only place for equal society, or where a man can say a good thing or express an honest opinion without subjecting himself to being insulted, unless he first lays his purse on the table to back his pretensions to talent or independence of spirit. I speak from experience.64

在王国的其他任何地方，他都随身带着另一个身份，把智识的身份、社交的身份盖了过去。在曼彻斯特或利物浦，屋里每个人有多少地产或钱财、有什么姻亲与前程，人人皆知——这就给整个外省交往烙上了奴颜或倨傲、逐利或无礼的印记。你的笑不随人的机智走，而随他的财富走；你须掂量的不是你在反驳什么，而是你在反驳谁。你以镑为单位说话，人家以英亩为单位听你。在都会，人们既无工夫、也无心思作这些迂远的盘算。每个人在社交中受到怎样的接待，全看他带进社交的见识、机智与教养有多少。议员很快就被放平成一个平民：商人与厂主在这里没法把货抬到市场上来：大地主也从千顷之主的身份里缩出来，变成一个可亲的伴或一个乏味的人。客人进门或离席，没人打听他富或穷、住阁楼还是住宫殿、坐自备车还是雇的马车；只看他面容是否舒朗、举止是否自然，看他是明白人还是木头。这些才是你给席间众人留下好感的凭据，才是他们据以给你“抽象定价”的凭据。在乡间，人们掂量的是你在下届选举有没有一张票、手里有没有可赠的职位，衡量旁人能否教益或娱乐自己的尺度，是对方钱袋的鼓瘪与在银行里的信用。在外省，个人的才德折价惊人。若想享受自己的陪伴，乡间甚好；但要平等的社交，要能说一句妙语、发一通诚实之见而不受辱——除非先把钱袋押在桌上来撑自己才具与独立精神的身价——那就只有伦敦。这是我亲历之言。64

### On Corporate Bodies / 论法人团体
===Original===

> “Corporate bodies have no soul.”

===Chinese===

> “法人团体没有灵魂。”

===Original===

Corporate bodies are more corrupt and profligate than individuals, because they have more power to do mischief, and are less amenable to disgrace or punishment. They feel neither shame, remorse, gratitude, nor goodwill. The principle of private or natural conscience is extinguished in each individual (we have no moral sense in the breasts of others), and nothing is considered but how the united efforts of the whole (released from idle scruples) may be best directed to the obtaining of political advantages and privileges to be shared as common spoil. Each member reaps the benefit, and lays the blame, if there is any, upon the rest. The *esprit de corps* becomes the ruling passion of every corporate body, compared with which the motives of delicacy or decorum towards others are looked upon as being both impertinent and improper. If any person sets up a plea of this sort in opposition to the rest, he is overruled, he gets ill-blood, and does no good: he is regarded as an interloper, a black sheep in the flock, and is either “sent to Coventry” or obliged to acquiesce in the notions and wishes of those he associates and is expected to cooperate with. The refinements of private judgment are referred to and negatived in a committee of the whole body, while the projects and interests of the Corporation meet with a secret but powerful support in the self-love of the different members. Remonstrance, opposition, is fruitless, troublesome, invidious; it answers no one end; and a conformity to the sense of the company is found to be no less necessary to a reputation for good-fellowship than to a quiet life. Self-love and social here look like the same; and in consulting the interests of a particular class, which are also your own, there is even a show of public virtue. He who is a captious, impracticable, dissatisfied member of his little club or coterie is immediately set down as a bad member of the community in general, as no friend to regularity and order, as “a pestilent fellow,” and one who is incapable of sympathy, attachment, or cordial cooperation in any department or undertaking. Thus the most refractory novice in such matters becomes weaned from his obligations to the larger society, which only breed him inconvenience without any adequate recompense, and wedded to a nearer and dearer one, where he finds every kind of comfort and consolation.

===Chinese===

法人团体比个人更腐败、更放荡，因为它们为害的力量更大，也更不受耻辱与惩罚的约束。它们既不知羞耻，不知悔恨，也不知感恩与善意。私人的或天然良心的原则，在每个成员身上都熄灭了（在别人的胸中，我们并没有道德感）；大家考虑的只有一件事：如何把整个团体（既已摆脱了无谓的顾忌）的合力，最妥善地导向政治利益与特权的攝取，以便当作共同的赃物来分。利益各人各得，罪名——若有罪名——则推给其余的人。团体精神（*esprit de corps*）成了每个法人团体的主宰激情；同它一比，对他人细腻或体面的动机，都被视为既不相宜又不合体统。谁若提出这类异议与众人作对，就会被否决，结下怨仇，还落不到好：他被当作闯入者、羊群里的黑羊，不是被“集体抵制”，就是不得不默许同伙们的见解与愿望——大家原指望他合作的。私人判断的精微之处，被提交全体委员会讨论后否决；而法人团体的图谋与利益，却在各成员的自爱里得到一种秘密而有力的支持。规劝与反对，徒劳、招嫌、惹怨，一个目的也达不成；而随和众人的意见，既是安宁日子之所必需，也是好交情的名声之所必需。在这里，自爱与社交之爱看起来是一回事；在为一己之私的特定阶层的利益谋划时（那利益也是你自己的），甚至还能摆出一副公益之德的样子。谁若在他的小俱乐部或小圈子里是个挑剔、难处、不满足的成员，立刻被认定为整个社会的坏成员、规章与秩序之敌、“一个惹是生非的家伙”，一个在任何部门、任何事业上都不能同情、不能亲附、不能衷心合作的人。就这样，这类事情里最不服帖的新手，也渐渐断了奶——不再对更大的社会尽什么义务（那义务只给他带来麻烦而无相当的补偿），而同更亲近、更贴心的小社会结了婚——在那里他找到各式各样的慰藉与温暖。

===Original===

He contracts the vague and unmeaning character of Man into the more emphatic title of Freeman and Alderman. The claims of an undefined humanity sit looser and looser upon him, at the same time that he draws the bands of his new engagements closer and tighter about him. He loses sight, by degrees, of all common sense and feeling in the petty squabbles, intrigues, feuds, and airs of affected importance to which he has made himself an accessory. He is quite an altered man. “Really the society were under considerable obligations to him in that last business”; that is to say, in some paltry job or underhand attempt to encroach upon the rights or dictate to the understandings of the neighbourhood. In the meantime they eat, drink, and carouse together. They wash down all minor animosities and unavoidable differences of opinion in pint bumpers; and the complaints of the multitude are lost in the clatter of plates and the roaring of loyal catches at every quarter’s meeting or mayor’s feast. The town-hall reels with an unwieldy sense of self-importance; “the very stones prate” of processions; the common pump creaks in concert with the uncorking of bottles and tapping of beer-barrels: the market-cross looks big with authority. Everything has an ambiguous, upstart, repulsive air. Circle within circle is formed, an *imperium in imperio*: and the business is to exclude from the first circle all the notions, opinions, ideas, interests, and pretensions of the second. Hence there arises not only an antipathy to common sense and decency in those things where there is a real opposition of interest or clashing of prejudice, but it becomes a habit and a favourite amusement in those who are “dressed in a little brief authority,” to thwart, annoy, insult, and harass others on all occasions where the least opportunity or pretext for it occurs. Spite, bickerings, backbiting, insinuations, lies, jealousies, nicknames are the order of the day, and nobody knows what it’s all about. One would think that the mayor, aldermen, and liverymen were a higher and more select species of animals than their townsmen; though there is no difference whatever but in their gowns and staff of office! This is the essence of the *esprit de corps*. It is certainly not a very delectable source of contemplation or subject to treat of.

===Chinese===

他把“人”这个空泛而无谓的身份，收束成更响亮的头衔：自由民与市参事。那种未曾界定的博爱的要求，在他身上越来越松；与此同时，他把新交情的一圈圈带子越勒越紧。在那些他甘愿从旁出力的口角、密谋、宿怨与做作的威风中，他渐渐把一切常识与感情都看丢了。他整个人都变了。“上一桩事里，会社实在多亏了他”；也就是说，在某种卑鄙的勾当或偷偷摸摸侵夺乡邻权利、教训乡邻头脑的企图里。与此同时，他们一道大吃大喝，喧饮作乐。小小的嫌隙与免不了的分歧，都拿大品脱杯的酒冲了下去；民众的怨声，则淹没在季度会议或市长宴会上杯盘的铿锵与忠君轮唱曲的吼叫里。市政厅带着一股臃肿的自重感摇摇晃晃；“连石头都唠叨着”巡游；公用水井的吱呀声与开瓶、开桶的声响此唱彼和：市场的十字架端足了权威的架子。一切都带着一种含混、暴发、拒人的气息。圈里又套圈，形成*国中之国*：而头等要务，就是把第二个圈子的一切观念、意见、想法、利益与抱负，从第一个圈子里排除出去。于是，凡利益真正相抵、偏见真正相撞之处，他们不但厌恶常识与体面；对那些“裹着一层浮浅的威权”的人，遇事刁难、搅扰、侮辱、纠缠他人，还成了一种习惯、一种最爱的消遣——只要稍有机会或口实。恶意、口角、背毁、影射、谎言、嫉妒、诨名，是每日的通例，而谁也说不清这一切为的是什么。人们会以为市长、参事与同业公会成员是比同城人更高一等、更精选的动物；其实除了礼袍与官杖，毫无分别！这便是团体精神的本质。它实在算不上一个可供静观或论述的雅趣之源。

===Original===

Public bodies are so far worse than the individuals composing them, because the *official* takes place of the *moral sense*. The nerves that in themselves were soft and pliable enough, and responded naturally to the touch of pity, when fastened into a machine of that sort become callous and rigid, and throw off every extraneous application that can be made to them with perfect apathy. An appeal is made to the ties of individual friendship: the body in general know nothing of them. A case has occurred which strongly called forth the compassion of the person who was witness of it; but the body (or any special deputation of them) were not present when it happened. These little weaknesses and “compunctious visitings of nature” are effectually guarded against, indeed, by the very rules and regulations of the society, as well as by its spirit. The individual is the creature of his feelings of all sorts, the sport of his vices and his virtues﻿—like the fool in Shakespeare, “motley’s his proper wear”:﻿—corporate bodies are dressed in a moral uniform; mixed motives do not operate there, frailty is made into a system, “diseases are turned into commodities.” Only so much of anyone’s natural or genuine impulses can influence him in his artificial capacity as formally comes home to the aggregate conscience of those with whom he acts, or bears upon the interests (real or pretended), the importance, respectability, and professed objects of the society. Beyond that point the nerve is bound up, the conscience is seared, and the torpedo-touch of so much inert matter operates to deaden the best feelings and harden the heart. Laughter and tears are said to be the characteristic signs of humanity. Laughter is common enough in such places as a set-off to the mock-gravity; but who ever saw a public body in tears? Nothing but a job or some knavery can keep them serious for ten minutes together.80
Such are the qualifications and the apprenticeship necessary to make a man tolerated, to enable him to pass as a cipher, or be admitted as a mere numerical unit, in any corporate body: to be a leader and dictator he must be diplomatic in impertinence, and officious in every dirty work. He must not merely conform to established prejudices; he must flatter them. He must not merely be insensible to the demands of moderation and equity; he must be loud against them.

===Chinese===

公共团体之所以更坏于组成它们的个人，是因为*官能*取代了*道德感*。那些神经本身原够柔软灵活，天然会应怜悯之触而颤动；一旦被固定进这样一部机器，便变得麻木僵硬，以全然的冷漠弹开一切外加的触动。有人呼吁私人的友谊之情：团体对此一概无知。某一件事发生了，曾强烈唤起目击者的怜悯；但团体（或它的任何特别代表团）事发时不在场。这些小小的软弱、这些“天性的良心发现”，确实已被会社的章程与规则——连同它的精神——有效地防范住了。个人是他种种情感的造物，是他恶德与美德的玩偶——像莎士比亚笔下的弄人，“彩衣是他的本装”：——法人团体则穿一身道德的制服；混杂的动机在那里不起作用，软弱被制成了体系，“疾病被做成了商品”。一个人的天然或本真的冲动，唯有那能够正式抵达同僚们的总合良心、或触及会社的利益（真的或装的）、威望、体面与标榜的目标的部分，才能在他的人造身份里起作用。超过这一点，神经便被捆扎起来，良心便被烙平；这一大团惰性物质的电鳗之触，只教最好的情感迟钝、心肠变硬。据说笑与泪是人性的特有表征。笑，在这种地方倒是常闻，用来调剂那假正经；可谁见过一个公共团体流泪？只有一桩肥缺或一件无赖勾当，才能让他们连着严肃十分钟。80
这便是一个人在任何法人团体里求容身、充个数、被当作一个数字单位所需的资格与学徒期：若要做领袖与独裁者，他还须在无礼上有机变，在每件脏活上都卖力。他不能仅仅顺从既定的偏见；他必须奉承它们。他不能仅仅对节制与公道的要求无动于衷；他必须高声反对它们。

===Original===

He must not simply fall in with all sorts of contemptible cabals and intrigues; he must be indefatigable in fomenting them, and setting everybody together by the ears. He must not only repeat, but invent lies. He must make speeches and write handbills; he must be devoted to the wishes and objects of the society, its creature, its jackal, its busybody, its mouthpiece, its prompter; he must deal in law cases, in demurrers, in charters, in traditions, in commonplaces, in logic and rhetoric﻿—in everything but common sense and honesty. He must (in Mr. Burke’s phrase) “disembowel himself of his natural entrails, and be stuffed with paltry, blurred sheets of parchment about the rights” of the privileged few. He must be a concentrated essence, a varnished, powdered representative of the vices, absurdities, hypocrisy, jealousy, pride, and pragmaticalness of his party. Such a one, by bustle and self-importance and puffing, by flattering one to his face and abusing another behind his back, by lending himself to the weaknesses of some, and pampering the mischievous propensities of others, will pass for a great man in a little society.
Age does not improve the morality of public bodies. They grow more and more tenacious of their idle privileges and senseless self-consequence. They get weak and obstinate at the same time. Those who belong to them have all the upstart pride and pettifogging spirit of their present character ingrafted on the venerableness and superstitious sanctity of ancient institutions. They are naturally at issue, first with their neighbours, and next with their contemporaries, on all matters of common propriety and judgment. They become more attached to forms, the more obsolete they are; and the defence of every absurd and invidious distinction is a debt which (by implication) they owe to the dead as well as the living. What might once have been of serious practical utility they turn to farce, by retaining the letter when the spirit is gone: and they do this the more, the more glaring the inconsistency and want of sound reasoning; for they think they thus give proof of their zeal and attachment to the abstract principle on which old establishments exist, the ground of prescription and authority. *The greater the wrong, the greater the right*, in all such cases.

===Chinese===

他不能仅仅凑合进各种可鄙的阴谋与勾当；他必须孜孜不倦地煽动它们，挑得人人相斗。他不但要复述谎言，还要发明谎言。他必须发表演说、印发传单；必须把自己献给会社的愿望与目标，做它的造物、它的豺狼、它的包打听、它的喉舌、它的提词人；他必须经营讼案、抗辩、特许状、老例、套话、逻辑与修辞——经营一切，除了常识与诚实。他必须（用伯克先生的话说）“把自己天生的脏腑掏空，塞满关于特权少数之权利的破烂污皱的羊皮纸”。他必须是一瓶浓缩精华，是他那一党的恶德、荒唐、伪善、嫉妒、骄矜与自以为是上过漆、扑过粉的代表。这样一个人，凭着奔忙、自重与吹嘘，当面奉承这个、背后糟践那个，迁就某些人的弱点、纵容另一些人的害人倾向，便能在一个小社会里博得大人物之名。
年岁并不能改善公共团体的道德。他们对那些无聊的特权与没头脑的自负，越老抓得越紧。他们同时变得又虚弱又顽固。属于他们的人，把现下身份里那种暴发户的骄傲与讼棍气，嫁接到古老建制令人敬畏的尊严与迷信的圣洁上。在一切关乎通行礼俗与判断的事上，他们天然先与乡邻龃龉，继而与同时代人格格不入。形式越是陈旧，他们越是依恋；每一项荒谬招怨的差等的辩护，都是他们（不言而喻地）欠死者、也欠生者的一笔债。曾经或有切实功用的东西，他们靠留其形而弃其神，把它变成闹剧；而其中的矛盾与推理之荒疏越刺眼，他们越要这么干；因为他们以为，这样就证明了自己对旧建制赖以存在的抽象原则、对惯例与权威之根基的热忱与忠贞。在这一切事例中，*错得越大，对得越大*。

===Original===

The *esprit de corps* does not take much merit to itself for upholding what is justifiable in any system, or the proceedings of any party, but for adhering to what is palpably injurious. You may exact the first from an enemy: the last is the province of a friend. It has been made a subject of complaint, that the champions of the Church, for example, who are advanced to dignities and honours, are hardly ever those who defend the common principles of Christianity, but those who volunteer to man the outworks, and set up ingenious excuses for the questionable points, the ticklish places in the established form of worship, that is, for those which are attacked from without, and are supposed in danger of being undermined by stratagem, or carried by assault!
The great resorts and seats of learning often outlive in this way the intention of the founders as the world outgrows them. They may be said to resemble antiquated coquettes of the last age, who think everything ridiculous and intolerable but what was in fashion when they were young, and yet are standing proofs of the progress of taste and the vanity of human pretensions. Our universities are, in a great measure, become cisterns to hold, not conduits to disperse knowledge. The age has the start of them; that is, other sources of knowledge have been opened since their formation, to which the world have had access, and have drunk plentifully at those living fountains, but from which they are debarred by the tenor of their charter, and as a matter of dignity and privilege. They have grown poor, like the old grandees in some countries, by subsisting on the inheritance of learning, while the people have grown rich by trade. They are too much in the nature of *fixtures* in intellect: they stop the way in the road to truth; or at any rate (for they do not themselves advance) they can only be of service as a check-weight on the too hasty and rapid career of innovation. All that has been invented or thought in the last two hundred years they take no cognizance of, or as little as possible; they are above it; they stand upon the ancient landmarks, and will not budge; whatever was not known when they were first endowed, they are still in profound and lofty ignorance of.

===Chinese===

团体精神并不以坚持任何制度或任何党派行为中站得住脚的部分为荣；它引以为荣的，是死守那明明白白有害的部分。前者，你可以要求敌人做到：后者，才是朋友的专职。有人抱怨说，比方教会那些擢升高位与尊荣的卫道士，几乎从来不是捍卫基督教共同原理的人，而是自告奋勇守外围工事的人，为那些可疑之点、既定崇拜形式里的敏感处所巧设托词——也就是为那些遭受外来攻击、被认定有被计谋挖倒或强攻拿下之虞的地方辩护！
那些学问的大本营与渊薮，也常常这样在世界越过了它们之后，仍比创立者的初衷活得长久。可以说，她们像上个时代过气的风骚老妇，以为除自己年轻时流行的东西之外，一切皆可笑、皆难忍；而她们自己，恰恰是趣味之进步与人类自负之虚妄的活的证明。我们的大学在很大程度上，已成了蓄水的池沼，而不再是输水的渠道——蓄的是知识，却不再输送知识。时代跑到了它们前头；这就是说，自它们创立以来，又开通了别处的知识源泉，世人得以趋近，并在那些活泉边痛饮；而大学自身，却被自己的章程、被体面与特权的考量，挡在了泉边。它们像某些国家的老贵族，靠坐食学问的祖产而变穷；人民却靠贸易富了起来。它们在智识上太像一种*固定装置*：它们堵在通往真理的路上；或者至少（因为它们自己并不前进）只能当作一个砝码，压一压创新那过于急躁迅疾的势头。近二百年间发明与思考的一切，它们一概不认，或尽量少认；它们超乎其上；它们踩着古老的界石，寸步不移；当初受封时无人知晓的东西，它们至今仍以一种深沉而高贵的无知一无所知。

===Original===

Yet in that period how much has been done in literature, arts, and science, of which (with the exception of mathematical knowledge, the hardest to gainsay or subject to the trammels of prejudice and barbarous *ipse dixits*) scarce any trace is to be found in the authentic modes of study and legitimate inquiry which prevail at either of our Universities! The unavoidable aim of all corporate bodies of learning is not to grow wise, or teach others wisdom, but to prevent anyone else from being or seeming wiser than themselves; in other words, their infallible tendency is in the end to suppress inquiry and darken knowledge, by setting limits to the mind of man, and saying to his proud spirit, *Hitherto shalt thou come, and no farther!* It would not be an unedifying experiment to make a collection of the titles of works published in the course of the year by Members of the Universities. If any attempt is to be made to patch up an idle system in policy or legislation, or church government, it is by a member of the University: if any hashed-up speculation on an old exploded argument is to be brought forward “in spite of *shame*, in erring reason’s spite,” it is by a Member of the University: if a paltry project is ushered into the world for combining ancient prejudices with modern timeserving, it is by a Member of the University. Thus we get at a stated supply of the annual Defences of the Sinking Fund, Thoughts on the Evils of Education, Treatises on Predestination, and Eulogies on Mr. Malthus, all from the same source, and through the same vent. If they came from any other quarter nobody would look at them; but they have an imprimatur from dullness and authority: we know that there is no offence in them; and they are stuck in the shop windows, and read (in the intervals of Lord Byron’s works, or the Scotch novels) in cathedral towns and close boroughs!
It is, I understand and believe, pretty much the same in more modern institutions for the encouragement of the Fine Arts. The end is lost in the means: rules take place of nature and genius; cabal and bustle, and struggle for rank and precedence, supersede the study and the love of art.

===Chinese===

然而在那两百年里，文学、艺术与科学有多少成就——其中（除去数学，它最难抵赖、最难套进偏见与野蛮的*武断*的枷锁）在我们的两所大学通行的正宗治学方式与合法探究里，几乎寻不出半点踪影！一切学术法人团体不可避免的目标，不是使自己变智，或教人智慧，而是不让别人比他们更智、或显得更智；换言之，他们万无一失的趋向，终归是压制探究、弄暗知识——给人心立界，对他的骄魂说：*你到此为止，不得再往！*把大学成员一年之内刊行的著作题目收集成一册，倒不失为一桩有益的实验。凡要缝补政治、立法或教会治理中一套无聊的制度的，是大学成员；凡要把一个早已破产的老论点回锅热炒、“不顾*羞耻*、不顾迷误的理性之怨”端出来的，是大学成员；凡要向世界推出一项把古老偏见同现代趋时缝合起来的可怜计划的，也是大学成员。于是我们定期得到年度供应：《偿债基金辩护词》、《论教育之弊》、《论预定论》与《马牧斯先生颂》，皆出同一源头，走同一出口。若出自别处，无人理会；但它们盖着迟钝与权威的出版许可：我们知道其中没有冒犯；于是它们插在书铺橱窗里，在大教堂城镇与封闭选邑，（在拜伦勋爵或苏格兰小说的间隙里）被人捧读！
据我所知所信，较晚近的那些美术奖励机构，情形也大同小异。目的淹没在手段里：规则取代了自然与天才；阴谋与奔忙、对名位与班次的争抢，盖过了研习与热爱艺术。

===Original===

A Royal Academy is a kind of hospital and infirmary for the obliquities of taste and ingenuity﻿—a receptacle where enthusiasm and originality stop and stagnate, and spread their influence no farther, instead of being a school founded for genius, or a temple built to fame. The generality of those who wriggle, or fawn, or beg their way to a seat there, live on their certificate of merit to a good old age, and are seldom heard of afterwards. If a man of sterling capacity gets among them, and minds his own business he is nobody; he makes no figure in council, in voting, in resolutions or speeches. If he comes forward with plans and views for the good of the Academy and the advancement of art, he is immediately set upon as a visionary, a fanatic, with notions hostile to the interest and credit of the existing members of the society. If he directs the ambition of the scholars to the study of History, this strikes at once at the emoluments of the profession, who are most of them (by God’s will) portrait painters. If he eulogises the Antique, and speaks highly of the Old Masters, he is supposed to be actuated by envy to living painters and native talent. If, again, he insists on a knowledge of anatomy as essential to correct drawing, this would seem to imply a want of it in our most eminent designers. Every plan, suggestion, argument, that has the general purposes and principles of art for its object, is thwarted, scouted, ridiculed, slandered, as having a malignant aspect towards the profits and pretensions of the great mass of flourishing and respectable artists in the country. This leads to irritation and ill-will on all sides. The obstinacy of the constituted authorities keeps pace with the violence and extravagance opposed to it; and they lay all the blame on the folly and mistakes they have themselves occasioned or increased. It is considered as a personal quarrel, not a public question; by which means the dignity of the body is implicated in resenting the slips and inadvertencies of its members, not in promoting their common and declared objects. In this sort of wretched *tracasserie* the Barrys and H﻿—﻿—﻿s stand no chance with the Catons, the Tubbs, and F﻿—﻿—﻿s. Sir Joshua even was obliged to hold himself aloof from them, and Fuseli passes as a kind of nondescript, or one of his own grotesques.

===Chinese===

皇家美术学院，是趣味与才智之乖僻的一座医院与疗养院——一个让热忱与独创停滞不前、再也不能扩大影响的收容所；而不是为天才设的学校，或为声名筑的庙宇。那些靠钻营、谄媚或哀告挤进一个席位的人，多半凭着那纸功劳证书活到高寿，此后再无音讯。倘若一个真正有分量的人落到他们中间，只管自己的本业，那他就是无名之辈；在院务会议里、在表决里、在决议或演说里，都不见踪影。他若站出来为学院的好处、为艺术的进步献计献策，立刻被围攻为空想家、狂热分子，说他的主张跟会社现有成员的利益与体面作对。他若引导学生志于历史画，这立刻打击到这一行的进项——他们中间大多数人（承上帝之旨）是肖像画家。他若称颂古物、盛赞古代大师，就被认为是对在世画家与本土天才心怀嫉妒。他若再坚持解剖学知识乃正确素描之本，这又似乎是在影射我们最显赫的设计师们欠缺这一课。凡以艺术的总目的与总原则为旨归的计划、建议、论证，无不遭挫、遭嗤、遭讥、遭谤，被指为对全国那一大批兴旺而体面的艺术家们的利润与声望怀有歹意。于是四面八方都起了恼怒与恶意。在任当局的顽固，同比它对抗的暴烈与过激齐头并进；而他们把全部罪责，都推到那由他们自己惹起或加剧的愚蠢与过失上。这被当作私斗，而非公共问题；如此一来，这个团体的尊严便被拖去为成员们的闪失与疏漏记仇，而不是用于推进他们共同宣称的目标。在这一类龌龊的*烦扰*里，巴里们与 H———们斗不过卡顿们、塔布们和 F———们。连雷诺兹爵士也不得不同他们保持距离，而富塞利则被当成一种难以名状之物，或他自己笔下的一幅怪相。

===Original===

The air of an academy, in short, is not the air of genius and immortality; it is too close and heated, and impregnated with the notions of the common sort. A man steeped in a corrupt atmosphere of this description is no longer open to the genial impulses of nature and truth, nor sees visions of ideal beauty, nor dreams of antique grace and grandeur, nor has the finest works of art continually hovering and floating through his uplifted fancy; but the images that haunt it are rules of the academy, charters, inaugural speeches, resolutions passed or rescinded, cards of invitation to a council-meeting, or the annual dinner, prize medals, and the king’s diploma, constituting him a gentleman and esquire. He “wipes out all trivial, fond records”; all romantic aspirations; “the Raphael grace, the Guido air”; and the commands of the academy alone “must live within the book and volume of his brain, unmixed with baser matter.” It may be doubted whether any work of lasting reputation and universal interest can spring up in this soil, or ever has done in that of any academy. The last question is a matter of fact and history, not of mere opinion or prejudice; and may be ascertained as such accordingly. The mighty names of former times rose before the existence of academies; and the three greatest painters, undoubtedly, that this country has produced, Reynolds, Wilson, and Hogarth, were not “dandled and swaddled” into artists in any institution for the fine arts. I do not apprehend that the names of Chantrey or Wilkie (great as one, and considerable as the other of them is) can be made use of in any way to impugn the jet of this argument. We may find a considerable improvement in some of our artists, when they get out of the vortex for a time. Sir Thomas Lawrence is all the better for having been abstracted for a year or two from Somerset House; and Mr. Dawe, they say, has been doing wonders in the North. When will he return, and once more “bid Britannia rival Greece”?
Mr. Canning somewhere lays it down as a rule, that corporate bodies are necessarily correct and pure in their conduct, from the knowledge which the individuals composing them have of one another, and the jealous vigilance they exercise over each other’s motives and characters; whereas people collected into mobs are disorderly and unprincipled from being utterly unknown and unaccountable to each other.

===Chinese===

总之，学院的空气不是天才与不朽的空气；它太浊、太热，浸透着凡庸之辈的念头。浸在这样一种腐败气氛里的人，再不能对自然与真理的和煦冲动敞开，再见不到理想之美的幻象，再梦不见古典的优雅与雄伟，再没有最精美的艺术品不断在他高扬的想象里盘旋浮荡；萦绕他的意象，是学院的章程、特许状、就职演说、通过或撤销的决议、院务会议或年宴的请柬、奖章，以及封他为绅士与先生的那纸国王敕状。他“抹去一切琐碎痴愚的记录”；抹去一切浪漫的抱负；抹去“拉斐尔的优雅、圭多的风致”；惟独学院的院规，“必须活在他的脑之书册与卷帙里，不掺半点卑杂质料”。这片土壤里能否长出享有恒久声名与普遍兴味的作品，或任何学院的土壤里可曾长出过，是可疑的。后一个问题属事实与历史，不单是意见或偏见；也就可以据实查证。往昔的伟大名字，都崛起于学院出现之前；而本国产出的三位最伟大画家——雷诺兹、威尔逊与贺加斯——无疑都不曾在任何美术机构里被“娇养襁褓”成艺术家。我并不担心钱特里或威尔基的名字（一位伟大，一位可观）能被拿来推翻这一论证的势头。我们会发现，有些艺术家暂时脱出这漩涡之后，长进相当可观。托马斯·劳伦斯爵士被从萨默塞特府抽离一两年，反倒更好了；还有多先生，据说在北方创造了奇迹。他何时归来，再来“叫不列颠与希腊争辉”？
坎宁先生在某处立下一条规则：法人团体在行为上必然端正纯洁，因为组成它们的个人彼此相知，彼此以猜忌的警觉盯着对方的动机与品行；而聚成民众的人们，因彼此全然陌生、互不负责，便混乱而无原则。

===Original===

This is a curious *pass* of wit. I differ with him in both parts of the dilemma. To begin with the first, and to handle it somewhat cavalierly, according to the model before us; we know, for instance, there is said to be honour among thieves, but very little honesty towards others. Their honour consists in the division of the booty, not in the mode of acquiring it: they do not (often) betray one another, but they will waylay a stranger, or knock out a traveller’s brains: they may be depended on in giving the alarm when any of their posts are in danger of being surprised; and they will stand together for their ill-gotten gains to the last drop of their blood. Yet they form a distinct society, and are strictly responsible for their behaviour to one another and to their leader. They are not a mob, but a *gang*, completely in one another’s power and secrets. Their familiarity, however, with the proceedings of the corps does not lead them to expect or to exact from it a very high standard of moral honesty; that is out of the question; but they are sure to gain the good opinion of their fellows by committing all sorts of depredations, fraud, and violence against the community at large. So (not to speak it profanely) some of Mr. Croker’s friends may be very respectable people in their way﻿—“all honourable men”﻿—but their respectability is confined within party limits; everyone does not sympathise in the integrity of their views; the understanding between them and the public is not well defined or reciprocal. Or, suppose a gang of pickpockets hustle a passenger in the street, and the mob set upon them, and proceed to execute summary justice upon such as they can lay hands on, am I to conclude that the rogues are in the right, because theirs is a system of well-organised knavery, which they settled in the morning, with their eyes one upon the other, and which they regularly review at night, with a due estimate of each other’s motives, character, and conduct in the business; and that the honest men are in the wrong, because they are a casual collection of unprejudiced, disinterested individuals, taken at a venture from the mass of the people, acting without concert or responsibility, on the spur of the occasion, and giving way to their instantaneous impulses and honest anger?

===Chinese===

这真是一段奇巧的机锋。这个两难推理的两半，我都不能同意。先说前一半，并照着眼前这个榜样，来它一点轻慢的处置：比如说，我们都知道，据说盗贼之间也讲道义，但对旁人却几乎没有诚实可言。他们的道义在于分赃，而不在于取财的手段：他们（通常）不出卖同伙，却会拦劫生人、敲碎旅客的脑袋：哪个哨位有被端掉之虞时，报警靠得住他们；为不义之财，他们会血战到最后一滴血。然而他们构成一个界限分明的社会，彼此之间、对他们的头领，都严格负责。他们不是乌合之众，而是一个*帮*，彼此完全握有对方的把柄与秘密。然而，他们虽对帮内的行事了如指掌，却并不因此指望它、也并不因此要求它有很高的道德诚实；那谈不上；倒是靠对社会大众犯下种种劫掠、欺诈与暴行，他们稳赚同伙的好评。同样（恕我出言不敬），克罗克先生的某些朋友，按他们的路数或许都是体面人——“个个可敬”——但他们的体面只限于党派之内；并非人人都认同他们用心之正；他们与公众之间的谅解，既不明晰，也不对等。再或者：设有一伙扒手在街上挤撞一位过客，民众扑向他们，对抓到手的就地正法——难道我该断定无赖们有理，因为他们那一套是组织完好的无赖体系，早上定下时人人互相盯视，夜里还照例复查，对彼此在这桩买卖里的动机、品行与作为各有公允的估量；而诚实的人们反倒无理，因为他们不过是一群偶然凑合的、无偏见、无私心的个人，从民众中信手拈来，临事而起，不谋而合也互不担责，只凭一时的冲动与义愤行事？

===Original===

Mobs, in fact, then, are almost always right in their feelings, and often in their judgments, on this very account﻿—that being utterly unknown to and disconnected with each other, they have no point of union or principle of cooperation between them, but the natural sense of justice recognised by all persons in common. They appeal, at the first meeting, not to certain symbols and watchwords privately agreed upon, like Freemasons, but to the maxims and instincts proper to all the world. They have no other clue to guide them to their object but either the dictates of the heart or the universally understood sentiments of society, neither of which are likely to be in the wrong. The flame which bursts out and blazes from popular sympathy is made of honest but homely materials. It is not kindled by sparks of wit or sophistry, nor damped by the cold calculations of self-interest. The multitude may be wantonly set on by others, as is too often the case, or be carried too far in the impulse of rage and disappointment; but their resentment, when they are left to themselves, is almost uniformly, in the first instance, excited by some evident abuse and wrong; and the excesses into which they run arise from that very want of foresight and regular system which is a pledge of the uprightness and heartiness of their intentions. In short, the only class of persons to sinister and corrupt motives is not applicable is that body of individuals which usually goes by the name of the *People*!

===Chinese===

可见，民众在情感上几乎永远是对的，在判断上也常常是对的，恰恰因为这一点——他们彼此全然陌生、互不相干，彼此之间除了人人共认的天然正义感，再无别的联结点与合作原则。他们一聚拢，诉诸的不是共济会那种私相约定的暗号口令，而是普天之下共通的准则与本能。指引他们奔向目标的线索，不是心灵的指令，就是社会人人了然的情绪——这两样都不大可能是错的。从民众的同情里迸发、燃烧起来的火焰，是由诚实而朴素的材料构成的。它不靠机锋或诡辩的火星点燃，也不被私利的冷算浇灭。民众固然可能被人肆意煽动（这也太常见了），或在愤怒与失望的冲动里走得太远；但只要听其自然，他们的怨愤几乎无一例外，最初都是被某种昭然的滥用与冤屈激起的；他们所犯的过火，恰恰源于那种缺乏预见与成规的状态——而这缺乏，恰是他们用心之正、之诚的保证。总之，唯一不能以居心叵测、居心腐败论的一类人，就是通常以*人民*之名行走于世的那个群体！

### On Criticism / 论批评
===Original===

Criticism is an art that undergoes a great variety of changes, and aims at different objects at different times.
At first, it is generally satisfied to give an opinion whether a work is good or bad, and to quote a passage or two in support of this opinion: afterwards, it is bound to assign the reasons of its decision and to analyse supposed beauties or defects with microscopic minuteness. A critic does nothing nowadays who does not try to torture the most obvious expression into a thousand meanings, and enter into a circuitous explanation of all that can be urged for or against its being in the best or worst style possible. His object indeed is not to do justice to his author, whom he treats with very little ceremony, but to do himself homage, and to show his acquaintance with all the topics and resources of criticism. If he recurs to the stipulated subject in the end, it is not till after he has exhausted his budget of general knowledge; and he establishes his own claims first in an elaborate inaugural dissertation *de omni scibile et quibusdam aliis*, before he deigns to bring forward the pretensions of the original candidate for praise, who is only the second figure in the piece. We may sometimes see articles of this sort, in which no allusion whatever is made to the work under sentence of death, after the first announcement of the title-page; and I apprehend it would be a clear improvement on this species of nominal criticism to give stated periodical accounts of works that had never appeared at all, which would save the hapless author the mortification of writing, and his reviewer the trouble of reading them. If the real author is made of so little account by the modern critic, he is scarcely more an object of regard to the modern reader; and it must be confessed that after a dozen close-packed pages of subtle metaphysical distinction or solemn didactic declamation, in which the disembodied principles of all arts and sciences float before the imagination in undefined profusion, the eye turns with impatience and indifference to the imperfect embryo specimens of them, and the hopeless attempts to realise this splendid jargon in one poor work by one poor author, which is given up to summary execution with as little justice as pity. “As when a well-graced actor leaves the stage, men’s eyes are idly bent on him that enters next”﻿—so it is here.

===Chinese===

批评是一门历经诸多变化的艺术，不同的时代瞄准不同的对象。
起初，它大都满足于就一部作品的好坏发表意见，引一两段文字佐证；后来，它就必须为裁决说明理由，以显微镜般的精细剖析那假想的美或缺陷。如今，批评家若不把最浅白的表达拷问出一千种意思、不就其风格之至佳或至劣迂回地正反论证一番，便算无所作为。他的目的其实不是公平对待作者（他对作者可没多少礼数），而是向自己致敬，是炫耀他熟悉批评的一切题目与家底。倘若他最后还算回到约定的题目上来，那也须等到他倾空了通识的行囊之后；他要先在一篇精心制作的就任演说里确立自己的种种权利主张——*论一切可知之事及其他*——然后才肯屈尊提出那位原初的候赏者——在这出戏里不过是第二号人物——的资格。我们有时会读到这样的文章：自扉页上的题目宣布过后，对那部被判死刑的作品便再无一字提及；我以为，对这种有名无实的批评，一个明白的改进办法，是定期评论从未出版过的作品——这既免了不幸的作者动笔之辱，也免了他的评论家拜读之劳。既然现代批评家如此不把真正的作者当回事，现代读者也就几乎同样不把他放在眼里；而且必须承认，十几页密不透风的玄学辨析或庄严的布道式宏论读罢——一切艺术与科学的脱窍之理在其中以漫无际涯的繁富浮游于想象之前——再转向那些残缺的胚胎样本、转向某个可怜作者在某个可怜作品里化这套堂皇呓语为实的无望尝试时，眼睛便只有不耐与冷淡了：那作品随即被交付即决处决，既无公正，也无怜悯。“好比一位风姿绰约的演员下场，观众的眼睛懒懒地盯着下一个出场的”——此间正是如此。

===Original===

Whether this state of the press is not a serious abuse and a violent encroachment in the republic of letters, is more than I shall pretend to determine. The truth is, that in the quantity of works that issue from the press, it is utterly impossible they should all be read by all sorts of people. There must be *tasters* for the public, who must have a discretionary power vested in them, for which it is difficult to make them properly accountable. Authors in proportion to their numbers become not formidable, but despicable. They would not be heard of or severed from the crowd without the critic’s aid, and all complaints of ill-treatment are vain. He considers them as pensioners on his bounty for any pittance or praise, and in general sets them up as butts for his wit and spleen, or uses them as a stalking-horse to convey his own favourite notions and opinions, which he can do by this means without the possibility of censure or appeal. He looks upon his literary protégé (much as Peter Pounce looked upon Parson Adams) as a kind of humble companion or unnecessary interloper in the vehicle of fame, whom he has taken up purely to oblige him, and whom he may treat with neglect or insult, or set down in the common footpath, whenever it suits his humour or convenience. He naturally grows arbitrary with the exercise of power. He by degrees wants to have a clear stage to himself, and would be thought to have purchased a monopoly of wit, learning, and wisdom﻿—

> “Assumes the rod, affects the God,

And seems to shake the spheres.”

===Chinese===

出版界的这种状况是不是文教共和国里一桩严重的滥用与粗暴的僭越，我不敢妄断。实情是：出版物的数量如此之大，要让各色人等尽数读过，全无可能。必须有人替公众*尝味*；尝味者必须被授予裁量之权，而这权力又很难叫他们妥当地为之负责。作家随其人数而论，非但不再可畏，反而可鄙。没有批评家的援手，他们无从传名，也无从从人堆里挑出来；一切对苛待的抱怨都是徒然。他把他们看作仰自己恩泽领一份残羹或赞语的食客，通常立他们做自己的机锋与脾气的靶子，或拿他们作掩护的假猎物，好递送自己钟情的观念与意见——借这个办法，他既不会遭非难，也无从被上诉。他看待自己文学上的被保护人（很像彼得·庞斯看待亚当斯牧师那样），当作名誉之车上一个卑贱的同伴、一个多余的闯入者：捎带上他纯粹是行个好，兴之所至或方便所至，尽可以冷落他、羞辱他，或把他撂在便道上。权力的行使自然使他日益专断。他渐渐要独占一方清场，巴望人们认为他买下了机智、学问与智慧的专卖权——

> “抓起权杖，摆出神谱，

仿佛摇撼着诸天。”

===Original===

Besides, something of this overbearing manner goes a great way with the public. They cannot exactly tell whether you are right or wrong; and if you state your difficulties or pay much deference to the sentiments of others, they will think you a very silly fellow or a mere pretender. A sweeping, unqualified assertion ends all controversy, and sets opinion at rest. A sharp, sententious, cavalier, dogmatical tone is therefore necessary, even in self-defence, to the office of a reviewer. If you do not deliver your oracles without hesitation, how are the world to receive them on trust and without inquiry? People read to have something to talk about, and “to seem to know that which they do not.” Consequently, there cannot be too much dialectics and debatable matter, too much pomp and paradox, in a review. *To elevate and surprise* is the great rule for producing a dramatic or critical effect. The more you startle the reader, the more he will be able to startle others with a succession of smart intellectual shocks. The most admired of our Reviews is saturated with this sort of electrical matter, which is regularly played off so as to produce a good deal of astonishment and a strong sensation in the public mind. The intrinsic merits of an author are a question of very subordinate consideration to the keeping up the character of the work and supplying the town with a sufficient number of grave or brilliant topics for the consumption of the next three months!
This decided and paramount tone in criticism is the growth of the present century, and was not at all the fashion in that calm, peaceable period when the *Monthly Review* bore “sole sovereign sway and masterdom” over all literary productions. Though nothing can be said against the respectability or usefulness of that publication during its long and almost exclusive enjoyment of the public favour, yet the style of criticism adopted in it is such as to appear slight and unsatisfactory to a modern reader. The writers, instead of “outdoing termagant or out-Heroding Herod,” were somewhat precise and prudish, gentle almost to a fault, full of candour and modesty,

> “And of their port as meek as is a maid!”66

===Chinese===

再者，这种盛气凌人的派头，在公众那里竟很吃得开。他们说不准你是对是错；你若陈述自己的疑难、或对他人的见解过分恭谨，他们便当你是个大傻瓜或纯粹的冒牌货。一记一揽子的、不留余地的断语，便了结一切争论，叫舆论安枕。因此，评论员这一职务，哪怕只为自卫，也须有一种尖利、警句式、倨傲、武断的腔调。你的神谕若非毫不犹豫地颁发，世人如何能不加查究、径相信托？人们读书是为了有话可谈，为了“显得知道自己其实并不知道的东西”。因此，一份评论里的机锋与可议之材、铺张与悖论，多多益善。*把人捧起来、再把人吓一跳*，是制造戏剧效果或批评效果的大法。你愈能使读者惊跳，他便愈能拿一连串漂亮的智识电击去惊跳旁人。我们最受赞叹的那家评论杂志，浸透了这种电质，定期施放，在公众心里激出相当的惊诧与强烈的震动。作者固有的价值，同维持刊物的品格、给城里人供应够三个月消费的或庄或炫的谈资相比，只是一个非常次要的考虑！
批评中这种斩截而霸道的调门，是本世纪的产物；在《每月评论》（*Monthly Review*）对一切文字产品“独揽主宰之权”的那个平静温和的年代，全然不是这个风尚。那家刊物长期几乎独享公众恩宠，其体面与用处无可指摘；只是它所采的批评文体，在现代读者看来未免单薄、难餍人意。撰述诸君非但不“赛过悍妇、盖过希律”，反而有点拘谨古板，温良得近乎过错，满纸坦诚与谦抑，

> “而他们的气派，娴静如处子！”66

===Original===

There was none of that Drawcansir work going on then that there is now; no scalping of authors, no hacking and hewing of their lives and opinions, except that they used those of Tristram Shandy, Gentleman, rather scurvily; which was to be expected. All, however, had a show of courtesy and good manners. The satire was covert and artfully insinuated; the praise was short and sweet. We meet with no oracular theories; no profound analysis of principles; no unsparing exposure of the least discernible deviation from them. It was deemed sufficient to recommend the work in general terms, “This is an agreeable volume,” or “This is a work of great learning and research,” to set forth the title and table of contents, and proceed without farther preface to some appropriate extracts, for the most part concurring in opinion with the author’s text, but now and then interposing an objection to maintain appearances and assert the jurisdiction of the court. This cursory manner of hinting approbation or dissent would make but a lame figure at present. We must have not only an announcement that “This is an agreeable or able work”; but we must have it explained at full length, and so as to silence all cavillers, in what the agreeableness or ability of the work consists: the author must be reduced to a class, all the living or defunct examples of which must be characteristically and pointedly *differenced* from one another; the value of this class of writing must be developed and ascertained in comparison with others; the principles of taste, the elements of our sensations, the structure of the human faculties, all must undergo a strict scrutiny and revision. The modern or metaphysical system of criticism, in short, supposes the question, *Why?* to be repeated at the end of every decision; and the answer gives birth to interminable arguments and discussion. The former laconic mode was well adapted to guide those who merely wanted to be informed of the character and subject of a work in order to read it: the present is more useful to those whose object is less to read the work than to dispute upon its merits, and go into company clad in the whole defensive and offensive armour of criticism.

===Chinese===

那时没有如今这般的“德拉坎瑟”式砍杀；不剥作家的头皮，不对他们的生平与见解乱刀剁砍——只除了对《绅士项狄传》的作者下过些狠手；这也是意料中事。不过，一切都还讲究几分客气与礼数。讥讽是含蓄的、巧于暗示的；赞语则简短而甜美。我们遇不到神谕式的理论；遇不到对原理的深刻剖析；也遇不到对最细微的偏离毫不留情的揭发。大家认为，用泛泛之语推荐一部作品——“这是一卷可喜之书”，或“这是一部学识渊深、考据勤劬之作”——摆出书名与目录，然后不再多作开场白，径直摘录几段相宜的文字，大体上与作者正文所见略同，偶尔插进一条异议以维持体面、宣示法庭的管辖权，便已足够。这种顺笔点一点可否的方式，如今可就蹩脚了。我们不但要宣布“这是一部可喜或有才力的作品”；还必须不厌其详地解释清楚，这“可喜”或“才力”究竟何在，且要解释得叫一切吹毛求疵者哑口无言：必须把作者归入一个门类，而该门类一切在世的与已故的样本，都须各具面目地、一针见血地彼此*判别*；这一类写作的价值，必须放在同其他门类的比较中展开、确定；趣味的原理、我们感觉的要素、人类官能的构造，都必须经过一番严格的审查与修订。总之，现代的或形而上学的批评体系，是在每一条裁决之后都要追问一个*为什么*；而对这个问题的回答，又生出无穷无尽的论证与讨论。前者那种言简意赅的路数，很适合指引那些只想先摸清作品的性质与题目、以便去读它的人：如今这一套，则更适合那些目的与其说是读作品、不如说是争论其优劣的人——他们披挂着批评的全套攻防甲胄出入社交场。

===Original===

Neither are we less removed at present from the dry and meagre mode of dissecting the skeletons of works, instead of transfusing their living principles, which prevailed in Dryden’s Prefaces,67 and in the criticisms written on the model of the French school about a century ago. A genuine criticism should, as I take it, reflect the colours, the light and shade, the soul and body of a work: here we have nothing but its superficial plan and elevation, as if a poem were a piece of formal architecture. We are told something of the plot or fable, of the moral, and of the observance or violation of the three unities of time, place, and action; and perhaps a word or two is added on the dignity of the persons or the baldness of the style; but we no more know, after reading one of these complacent tirades, what the essence of the work is, what passion has been touched, or how skilfully, what tone and movement the author’s mind imparts to his subject or receives from it, than if we had been reading a homily or a gazette. That is, we are left quite in the dark as to the feelings of pleasure or pain to be derived from the genius of the performance or the manner in which it appeals to the imagination: we know to a nicety how it squares with the threadbare rules of composition, not in the least how it affects the principles of taste. We know everything about the work, and nothing of it. The critic takes good care not to baulk the reader’s fancy by anticipating the effect which the author has aimed at producing. To be sure, the works so handled were often worthy of their commentators; they had the form of imagination without the life or power; and when anyone had gone regularly through the number of acts into which they were divided, the measure in which they were written, or the story on which they were founded, there was little else to be said about them. It is curious to observe the effect which the *Paradise Lost* had on this class of critics, like throwing a tub to a whale: they could make nothing of it. “It was out of all plumb﻿—not one of the angles at the four corners was a right angle!” They did not seek for, nor would they much relish, the marrow of poetry it contained. Like polemics in religion, they had discarded the essentials of fine writing for the outward form and points of controversy.

===Chinese===

如今我们同样远离了另一种干瘪而贫乏的套路——解剖作品的骨架而不输其活的精神；那套路盛行于德莱顿的各篇序言67，也盛行于约一百年前照法国学派模式写下的那些批评。
依我看，真正的批评应当映现一部作品的色彩、光影、灵魂与肉体：而这里我们只得到它表面的平面图与立面图，仿佛一首诗是一座刻板的建筑。我们听到的，无非情节或故事如何、寓意如何、时间地点动作三一律守没守；或许再添一两句人物是否尊贵、文笔是否光秃；可是读完这一类自鸣得意的长论，我们对作品的本质、它触动了何种激情、触动得如何高明、作者的心智给题材注入、又从题材领受了何种音调与律动，依然一无所知——同读了一篇布道文或一份公报没有两样。这就是说，对于这件表演的天才可能带来的苦乐之感、它诉诸想象的方式，我们全然蒙在鼓里：它与那些磨破了的作文规则如何吻合，我们知之毫厘；它如何作用于趣味的原理，我们丝毫不晓。关于这部作品，我们无所不知；对这部作品，我们一无所知。批评家自然小心翼翼，绝不抢先说出作者刻意追求的效果，搅了读者的期待。当然，被这样摆弄的作品，往往也配得上它们的评注者：它们有想象的形式而无想象的生命或力量；谁若按部就班数完它们分作几幕、写成了什么格律、依据的是什么故事，关于它们也就再没什么可说的了。有趣的是看《失乐园》（*Paradise Lost*）对这类批评家的效果——好比朝鲸鱼抛一只木桶：他们拿它毫无办法。“它全然不合铅垂线——四角的角没一个是直角！”他们不去寻找、也未必领略其中所含的诗之精髓。像宗教里的论战家，他们为外在的形式与争辩的锋头，舍弃了佳文的命脉。

===Original===

They were at issue with Genius and Nature by what route and in what garb they should enter the Temple of the Muses. Accordingly we find that Dryden had no other way of satisfying himself of the pretensions of Milton in the epic style but by translating his anomalous work into rhyme and dramatic dialogue.68 So there are connoisseurs who give you the subject, the grouping, the perspective, and all the mechanical circumstances of a picture; but they never say a word about the expression. The reason is, they see the former, but not the latter. There are persons, however, who cannot employ themselves better than in taking an inventory of works of art (they want a faculty for higher studies), as there are works of art, so called, which seemed to have been composed expressly with an eye to such a class of connoisseurs. In them are to be found no recondite nameless beauties thrown away upon the stupid vulgar gaze; no “graces snatched beyond the reach of art”; nothing but what the merest pretender may note down in good set terms in his commonplace book, just as it is before him. Place one of these half-informed, imperfectly organised spectators before a tall canvas with groups on groups of figures, of the size of life, and engaged in a complicated action, of which they know the name and all the particulars, and there are no bounds to their burst of involuntary enthusiasm. They mount on the stilts of the subject and ascend the highest Heaven of Invention, from whence they see sights and hear revelations which they communicate with all the fervour of plenary explanation to those who may be disposed to attend to their raptures. They float with wings expanded in lofty circles, they stalk over the canvas at large strides, never condescending to pause at anything of less magnitude than a group or a colossal figure. The face forms no part of their collective inquiries; or so that it occupies only a sixth or an eighth proportion to the whole body, all is according to the received rules of composition. Point to a divine portrait of Titian, to an angelic head of Guido, close by﻿—they see and heed it not. What are the “looks commercing with the skies,” the soul speaking in the face, to them? It asks another and an inner sense to comprehend them; but for the trigonometry of painting, nature has constituted them indifferently well.

天才与自然该由哪条路、穿什么衣装进缪斯的神殿，他们同天才与自然争执不休。于是我们看到，德莱顿要认可弥尔顿在史诗体裁上的资格，唯一的办法竟是把他那部不合体例的著作译成韵文与戏剧对白。68同样，有些鉴赏家能给你讲一幅画的主题、群像的布局、透视，以及一切机械性的情况；对表情却一字不提。原因是：前者他们看得见，后者看不见。不过，也有些人，最擅长的莫过于给艺术品开清单（更高深的研习他们缺一份官能）；同样，也有号称艺术品的东西，仿佛正是专为一类鉴赏家量身裁制的。这里面找不到深藏而无名的美，不致白白抛掷给愚蠢庸众的目光；没有“艺术之力所不及而天趣夺得的神韵”；有的只是随便哪个冒牌货都能照着眼前的样子，用堂而皇之的套语记进摘录本里的东西。把这样一位一知半解、官能不全的观者，带到一幅高大的画布前——画上群像叠着群像，与真人等大，正忙于一桩复杂的行动，而行动的名目与细底他无所不知——他那不由自主的热情的迸发便没有了边。他们踩着题材的高跷，登上发明之天的绝顶，从那里看见异象、听见启示，再带着圆满解说的一切热忱，转告给肯听他们狂喜的人。他们张开双翼在高天盘旋，跨着大步巡视画布，绝不屑于在任何小于一个群像或一个巨人形象的东西前停步。面孔不在他们综合考察之列；只要头与全身的比例不过六分之一或八分之一，一切便都合乎公认的构图规则。指一指近旁提香的一幅神妙肖像、圭多的一张天使之头——他们视而不见。那“与上天交通的容颜”、那在脸上说话的灵魂，于他们何有？领会这些需要另一种、更深一层的官能；至于绘画的三角学，天公造他们时倒不偏不倚地装备齐全。

They take a stand on the distinction between portrait and history, and there they are spellbound. Tell them that there can be no fine history without portraiture, that the painter must proceed from that ground to the one above it, and that a hundred bad heads cannot make one good historical picture, and they will not believe you, though the thing is obvious to any gross capacity. Their ideas always fly to the circumference, and never fix at the centre. Art must be on a grand scale; according to them, the whole is greater than a part, and the greater necessarily implies the less. The outline is, in this view of the matter, the same thing as the filling-up, and “the limbs and flourishes of a discourse” the substance. Again, the same persons make an absolute distinction, without knowing why, between high and low subjects. Say that you would as soon have Murillo’s *Two Beggar Boys* at the Dulwich Gallery as almost any picture in the world, that is, that it would be one you would choose out of ten (had you the choice), and they reiterate upon you that surely a low subject cannot be of equal value with a high one. It is in vain that you turn to the picture: they keep to the class. They have eyes, but see not; and, upon their principles of refined taste, would be just as good judges of the merit of the picture without seeing it as with that supposed advantage. They know what the subject is *from the catalogue*!﻿—Yet it is not true, as Lord Byron asserts, that execution is everything, and the class or subject nothing. The highest subjects, equally well executed (which, however, rarely happens), are the best. But the power of execution, the manner of seeing nature, is one thing, and may be so superlative (if you are only able to judge of it) as to countervail every disadvantage of subject. Raphael’s storks in the *Miraculous Draught of Fishes*, exulting in the event, are finer than the head of Christ would have been in almost any other hands.

===Chinese===

他们站在肖像与历史画的分界上，一立定便中了定身法。你告诉他们：没有肖像便没有好的历史画，画家必须从这块地基走向上面那层；一百颗坏头颅拼不出一幅好的历史画——他们不信，虽然这道理在再迟钝的头脑也一目了然。他们的念头总往圆周上飞，从不落在圆心。艺术必须大尺度；照他们说，整体大于部分，而大的必然涵盖小的。照这种看法，轮廓同填彩是一回事，“文章的枝蔓与花饰”就是实质。再者，同样这批人，又不知所以然地在崇高题材与低微题材之间划下绝对界线。你说，德威画廊里牟利罗那幅《两个乞儿》（*Two Beggar Boys*），你几乎肯拿它换世上任何一幅画；也就是说，倘若让你十选一，它会在你选中之列——他们却向你一再重申：低微的题材，价值断不能同崇高的题材相等。你转向那幅画，也是徒然：他们抱住门类不放。他们有眼而看不见；按他们那套高雅趣味的原理，没见过那画，同样能做那画优劣的高明裁判。他们知道画的是什么——*从目录上知道的*！——不过拜伦勋爵说表现即一切、门类与题材等于零，这也不对。崇高的题材若表现得同样出色（这当然少见），才是最好的。但表现之力、观看自然的方式是另一回事，它可以高超到（只要你有眼力判断）抵偿题材的一切不利。拉斐尔《捕鱼的奇迹》（*Miraculous Draught of Fishes*）里那为这奇迹欢欣的鹳鸟，比基督的头颅落在几乎任何旁人手里画出来都要精妙。

The cant of criticism is on the other side of the question; because execution depends on various degrees of power in the artist, and a knowledge of it on various degrees of feeling and discrimination in you; but to commence artist or connoisseur in the grand style at once, without any distinction of qualifications whatever, it is only necessary for the first to choose his subject and for the last to pin his faith on the sublimity of the performance, for both to look down with ineffable contempt on the painters and admirers of subjects of low life. I remember a young Scotchman once trying to prove to me that Mrs. Dickons was a superior singer to Miss Stephens, because the former excelled in sacred music and the latter did not. At that rate, that is, if it is the singing sacred music that gives the preference, Miss Stephens would only have to sing sacred music to surpass herself and vie with her pretended rival; for this theory implies that all sacred music is equally good, and, therefore, better than any other. I grant that Madame Catalani’s singing of sacred music is superior to Miss Stephens’s ballad-strains, because her singing is better altogether, and an ocean of sound more wonderful than a simple stream of dulcet harmonies. In singing the last verse of “God Save the King” not long ago her voice towered above the whole confused noise of the orchestra like an eagle piercing the clouds, and poured “such sweet thunder” through the ear as excited equal astonishment and rapture!
Some kinds of criticism are as much too insipid as others are too pragmatical. It is not easy to combine point with solidity, spirit with moderation and candour. Many persons see nothing but beauties in a work, others nothing but defects. Those cloy you with sweets, and are “the very milk of human kindness,” flowing on in a stream of luscious panegyrics; these take delight in poisoning the sources of your satisfaction, and putting you out of conceit with nearly every author that comes in their way. The first are frequently actuated by personal friendship, the last by all the virulence of party spirit. Under the latter head would fall what may be termed “political criticism.”

===Chinese===

批评的行话却在问题的另一头；因为表现之力取决于艺术家力量的高下，对它的鉴别取决于你感受与辨析力的高下；但要立刻做起宏大风格的艺术家或鉴赏家，什么资历都无须分辨——前者只消选好题材，后者只消把信仰钉在那作品的崇高上，再双双俯视、以无以言表的轻蔑睥睨低微生活题材的画家与爱好者。记得有个苏格兰青年曾向我证明：迪肯斯夫人歌艺高于斯蒂芬斯小姐，因为前者擅圣乐而后者不擅。照这个路数，也就是说，倘若唱圣乐便占先，那么斯蒂芬斯小姐只消也唱圣乐，便可超越自己、同那位所谓的对手一较短长；因为这套理论意味着：一切圣乐都同样好，因而好过任何别的音乐。我承认，卡塔拉尼夫人唱圣乐胜过斯蒂芬斯小姐的谣曲，那是因为她的歌唱整体就更好，是一片声的海洋，比一泓甜美的和声之溪更奇。不久前唱《天佑吾王》末节时，她的声音凌驾于乐队整片嘈杂之上，如雄鹰穿云，向耳中倾泻“如此甜美的雷鸣”，令人惊异与狂喜交并！
有些批评过于乏味，正如另一些过于自作聪明。锋芒与扎实、气性与节制坦诚，不易兼得。许多人在作品里只看见美，另一些人只看见缺陷。前者拿甜腻腻的颂词的溪流把你齁住，是“人性之乳”本身；后者则以毒化你满足的源头为乐，叫你对他们遇到几乎每一位作者都倒了胃口。前者多出于私谊，后者则出于党派之毒的全部狠劲。归在后一类下的，可以称作“政治批评”。

The basis of this style of writing is a *caput mortuum* of impotent spite and dullness, till it is varnished over with the slime of servility, and thrown into a state of unnatural activity by the venom of the most rancorous bigotry. The eminent professors in this grovelling department are at first merely out of sorts with themselves, and vent their spleen in little interjections and contortions of phrase﻿—cry *Pish* at a lucky hit, and *Hem* at a fault, are smart on personal defects, and sneer at “Beauty out of favour and on crutches”﻿—are thrown into an ague-fit by hearing the name of a rival, start back with horror at any approach to their morbid pretensions, like Justice Woodcock with his gouty limbs﻿—rifle the flowers of the Della Cruscan school, and give you in their stead, as models of a pleasing pastoral style, “Verses Upon Anna”﻿—which you may see in the notes to the *Baviad* and *Maeviad*. All this is like the fable of “The Kitten and the Leaves.” But when they get their brass collar on and shake their bells of office, they set up their backs like the Great Cat Rodilardus, and pounce upon men and things. Woe to any little heedess reptile of an author that ventures across their path without a safe-conduct from the Board of Control. They snap him up at a mouthful, and sit licking their lips, stroking their whiskers, and rattling their bells over the imaginary fragments of their devoted prey, to the alarm and astonishment of the whole breed of literary, philosophical, and revolutionary vermin that were naturalised in this country by a Prince of Orange and an Elector of Hanover a hundred years ago.69 When one of these pampered, sleek, “demure-looking, spring-nailed, velvet-pawed, green-eyed” critics makes his King and Country parties to this sort of sport literary, you have not much chance of escaping out of his clutches in a whole skin. Treachery becomes a principle with them, and mischief a conscience, that is, a livelihood. They not only *damn* the work in the lump, but vilify and traduce the author, and substitute lying abuse and sheer malignity for sense and satire. To have written a popular work is as much as a man’s character is worth, and sometimes his life, if he does not happen to be on the right side of the question.

===Chinese===

这一路文字的底子，是无能的怨毒与迟钝的一具*残渣*（*caput mortuum*），直到涂上奴性的黏液，再被最刻毒的偏执的蛇毒激入一种反常的活跃。这一卑贱行当的知名教授们，起初只是自己同自己过不去，拿小小的感叹词与扭曲的措辞出气——碰上一记妙语便啐一声*呸*，遇上一处毛病便咳一声*哼*，专挖个人的缺陷，讪笑“失宠拄拐的美人”——听见对手的名字便打摆子，一有人逼近他们病态的自命便惊退，像那位害痛风的伍德科克治安官拖着两条病腿——他们劫掠德拉·克鲁斯卡派的花朵，回赠你《咏安娜》作可爱田园风格的典范——这些你可以在《巴维亚德》与《梅维亚德》（*Baviad* and *Maeviad*）的注里看到。这一切像那则“小猫与落叶”的寓言。可一旦套上黄铜项圈、摇起官铃，他们便像大猫罗迪拉都斯那样弓起背，向人与物猛扑。哪个不小心的爬虫般的作者，若无管制委员会颁发的通行证便敢横穿他们的路径，那就遭殃了。他们一口把他吞下，坐着舔嘴、捋须，在那祭品想象的残骸上摇铃，惊得百年前由一位奥兰治亲王与一位汉诺威选帝侯在这个国家入了籍的文学、哲学与革命的虫豸全族惶骇不已。69当这一类娇养、油光、“面目端凝、利爪弹簧、天鹅绒掌、绿眼睛”的批评家，把这种游戏办成他的国王与国家派的文学竞技，你想从他的爪下全身而退，机会不多。背信成了他们的原则，害人成了他们的良心——也就是生计。他们不但把作品一总*毙*掉，还诋毁诽谤作者本人，拿撒谎的谩骂与纯粹的恶意顶替见识与讽刺。写出一部风行的作品，若作者碰巧没站在问题“正确”的一边，便要押上他的名誉，有时还要押上性命。
