The way in which they set about *stultifying* an adversary is not to accuse you of faults, or to exaggerate those which you may really have, but they deny that you have any merits at all, least of all those that the world have given you credit for; bless themselves from understanding a single sentence in a whole volume; and unless you are ready to subscribe to all their articles of peace, will not allow you to be qualified to write your own name. It is not a question of literary discussion, but of political proscription. It is a mark of loyalty and patriotism to extend no quarter to those of the opposite party. Instead of replying to your arguments, they call you names, put words and opinions into your mouth which you have never uttered, and consider it a species of misprision of treason to admit that a Whig author knows anything of common sense or English. The only chance of putting a stop to this unfair mode of dealing would perhaps be to make a few reprisals by way of example. The Court party boast some writers who have a reputation to lose, and who would not like to have their names dragged through the kennel of dirty abuse and vulgar obloquy. What silenced the masked battery of *Blackwood’s Magazine* was the implication of the name of Sir Walter Scott in some remarks upon it﻿—(an honour of which it seems that extraordinary person was not ambitious)﻿—to be “pilloried on infamy’s high stage” was a distinction and an amusement to the other gentlemen concerned in that praiseworthy publication. I was complaining not long ago of this prostitution of literary criticism as peculiar to our own times, when I was told that it was just as bad in the time of Pope and Dryden, and indeed worse, inasmuch as we have no Popes or Drydens now on the obnoxious side to be nicknamed, metamorphosed into scarecrows, and impaled alive by bigots and dunces. I shall not pretend to say how far this remark may be true. The English (it must be owned) are rather a foul-mouthed nation.
Besides temporary or accidental biases of this kind, there seem to be sects and parties in taste and criticism (with a set of appropriate watchwords) coeval with the arts of composition, and that will last as long as the difference with which men’s minds are originally constituted. There are some who are all for the elegance of an author’s style, and some who are equally delighted with simplicity.

===Chinese===

他们*使人出丑*的办法，不是指摘你的过错，或夸大你也许真有的毛病，而是否认你有任何长处——尤其否认世人已经归到你名下的那些；他们庆幸自己读不通整卷书里的任何一句；除非你肯在他们的全部和约条款上签字，否则他们不承认你有资格签自己的名字。这不是文学讨论的问题，而是政治清洗的问题。对敌党一律不留活口，正是忠君与爱国的标志。他们不答复你的论证，只给你起诨名，把从未出口的话与见解塞进你嘴里，并认为承认一位辉格党作家懂点常识或英文，本身就是一种隐匿叛国罪。要煞住这种不公的行径，唯一的指望，或许是以牙还牙，杀一儆百。宫廷党也有几位惜名的作家，他们不会乐意自己的名字被拖过污言与俗诟的阴沟。使《布莱克伍德杂志》（*Blackwood's Magazine*）那门掩体炮台哑掉的，正是把沃尔特·司各特爵士的名字牵连进对它的几句评论——（这份殊荣，那位非凡人物似乎并不企慕）——至于“被枷在恶名的高台上示众”，对参与那份可嘉刊物的其余诸位先生，倒是一种勋衔与消遣。不久前我还在抱怨这种批评的卖淫乃我朝特产，就有人告诉我：蒲柏与德莱顿的时代同样糟糕，甚至更糟——因为如今遭忌的一方再没有蒲柏与德莱顿那样的人物，可供起诨名、扎成稻草人、被偏执鬼与蠢材们活活钉穿。这话有几分真，我不敢妄言。英格兰人（必须承认）是个嘴相当不干净的民族。
除了这类一时一事的偏向，趣味与批评之中似乎还有教派与党派（各有一套相应的口令），同写作技艺一样古老，也将同人心的天赋差异一样长久。有人一味推尊作者文笔的典雅，有人则同样醉心于质朴。

===Original===

The last refer you to Swift as a model of English prose, thinking all other writers sophisticated and naught; the former prefer the more ornamented and sparkling periods of Junius or Gibbon. It is to no purpose to think of bringing about an understanding between these opposite factions. It is a natural difference of temperament and constitution of mind. The one will never relish the antithetical point and perpetual glitter of the artificial prose style; as the plain, unperverted English idiom will always appear trite and insipid to the others. A toleration, not an uniformity of opinion, is as much as can be expected in this case; and both sides may acknowledge, without imputation on their taste or consistency, that these different writers excelled each in their way. I might remark here that the epithet “elegant” is very sparingly used in modern criticism. It has probably gone out of fashion with the appearance of the “Lake School,” who, I apprehend, have no such phrase in their vocabulary. Mr. Rogers was, I think, almost the last poet to whom it was applied as a characteristic compliment. At present it would be considered as a sort of diminutive of the title of poet, like the terms “pretty” or “fanciful,” and is banished from the *haut ton* of letters. It may perhaps come into request at some future period. Again, the dispute between the admirers of Homer and Virgil has never been settled and never will, for there will always be minds to whom the excellences of Virgil will be more congenial, and therefore more objects of admiration and delight than those of Homer, and vice versa. Both are right in preferring what suits them best, the delicacy and selectness of the one, or the fullness and majestic flow of the other. There is the same difference in their tastes that there was in the genius of their two favourites. Neither can the disagreement between the French and English school of tragedy ever be reconciled till the French become English or the English French.70 Both are right in what they admire, both are wrong in condemning the others for what they admire. We see the defects of Racine, they see the faults of Shakespeare probably in an exaggerated point of view.

===Chinese===

后者请你以斯威夫特为英语散文的典范，认为其余作家皆矫饰而不堪；前者则偏爱尤尼乌斯或吉本那更藻饰、更闪耀的句子。想叫这两大敌对宗派达成谅解，是徒劳的。那是气质与心性的天然差异。这一方永远不会欣赏人工散文那种对仗的锋芒与无休止的闪光；正如素朴未凿的英语习语在那一方眼里，永远显得陈腐乏味。在这种事情上，所能指望的是相容，不是舆论一律；双方都可以承认——不致连累自己的趣味或操守——这些不同的作家各擅胜场。
这里不妨提一句：“优雅”这个考语，现代批评已很少使用。它多半是随“湖畔派”的出现而过时的；据我揣想，那一派的词汇表里就没有这个词。罗杰斯先生，我想，几乎是最后一位被以它为特色赞语的诗人。如今它会被当作“诗人”头衔的爱称，同“俊俏”或“空灵”之类字眼一样，已被逐出文坛的*上流*。也许将来某个时期，它还会重新走俏。
再者，荷马与维吉尔的崇拜者之间的争论从未了结，也永不会了结；因为总会有那样的心灵，维吉尔的卓越于他们更相契，因而更是叹赏与喜悦的对象，胜过荷马的卓越；反之亦然。双方各有其是：各选其最相宜者——一位的精致与精纯，或另一位의饱满与庄严的流势。他们趣味之别，正如他们两位偶像的天才之别。法兰西与英格兰悲剧学派之间的龃龉，也永无调和之日，除非法国人变成英国人、英国人变成法国人。70双方之所赞各是其是；双方之斥对方之所赞，则各非其是。我们看到拉辛的缺陷，他们看莎士比亚的毛病，恐怕也是戴了放大镜。

===Original===

But we may be sure of this, that when we see nothing but grossness and barbarism, or insipidity and verbiage, in a writer that is the god of a nation’s idolatry, it is we and not they who want true taste and feeling. The controversy about Pope and the opposite school in our own poetry comes to much the same thing. Pope’s correctness, smoothness, etc., are very good things and much to be commended in him. But it is not to be expected or even desired that others should have these qualities in the same paramount degree, to the exclusion of everything else. If you like correctness and smoothness of all things in the world, there they are for you in Pope. If you like other things better, such as strength and sublimity, you know where to go for them. Why trouble Pope or any other author for what they have not, and do not profess to give? Those who seem to imply that Pope possessed, besides his own peculiar, exquisite merits, all that is to be found in Shakespeare or Milton, are, I should hardly think, in good earnest. But I do not therefore see that, because this was not the case, Pope was no poet. We cannot by a little verbal sophistry confound the qualities of different minds, nor force opposite excellences into a union by all the intolerance in the world. We may pull Pope in pieces as long as we please for not being Shakespeare or Milton, as we may carp at them for not being Pope, but this will not make a poet equal to all three. If we have a taste for someone precise style or manner, we may keep it to ourselves and let others have theirs. If we are more catholic in our notions, and want variety of excellence and beauty, it is spread abroad for us to profusion in the variety of books and in the several growth of men’s minds, fettered by no capricious or arbitrary rules. Those who would proscribe whatever falls short of a given standard of imaginary perfection do so, not from a higher capacity of taste or range of intellect than others, but to destroy, to “crib and cabin in” all enjoyments and opinions but their own.
We find people of a decided and original, and others of a more general and versatile taste. I have sometimes thought that the most acute and original-minded men made bad critics. They see everything too much through a particular medium. What does not fall in with their own bias and mode of composition strikes them as commonplace and factitious.

===Chinese===

但有一点我们可以确信：当我们在一个被举国奉若神明的作家身上只看见粗鄙与野蛮、或乏味与芜累时，缺了真正的趣味与感受的，是我们，不是他们。
我们自己诗坛上关于蒲柏与其对垒学派的争论，也大体如此。蒲柏的精确、圆熟等等，都是好东西，在他身上也颇值得称道。但既不能指望、也不必期望别人也在同等的压倒程度上具备这些品质，以致排除其余一切。倘若普天之下你最爱的就是精确与圆熟，蒲柏那里尽有你受用。倘若你更爱别的，比如力量与崇高，你也知道该往哪里去寻。何必拿他们本没有、也从未自称能给的，去为难蒲柏或任何别的作者？至于那些似乎在暗示蒲柏除了自己独特而精致的优点之外，还兼有莎士比亚或弥尔顿的一切的人——我想，多半不是认真的。但我并不因此就认为，既然事实并非如此，蒲柏便不是诗人。凭一点言语上的诡辩，我们混淆不了不同心灵的品质；使出天底下全部的不宽容，也逼不合相反的卓越。我们可以随意把蒲柏拆解，怪他不是莎士比亚或弥尔顿；也可以挑剔那两位，怪他们不是蒲柏；但这样拆来拆去，也拼不出一位等于三人合璧的诗人。我们若偏爱某一特定的风格或路数，尽可自守己好，也让人家各得其好。我们若胸怀更广，想要多样卓越与多样之美，那就在书籍的多样与人心各自的生长间为我们铺张到泛滥，不受任何任性专断的规则拘束。至于那些要把一切够不上某个想象的完善标准的东西都禁绝的人，他们这样做，并非趣味更高、智识更广，而是要摧毁、要“捆死框牢”一切他人的乐趣与见解，只留他们自己的。
有的人趣味决绝而独到，有的人则更宽泛而多能。我有时想，最敏锐、最有创见的人反而做不好批评家。他们看一切都太隔着一片特定的介质。凡不合他们自己的偏向与写作方式的，在他们眼里便平庸而做作。

===Original===

What does not come into the direct line of their vision, they regard idly, with vacant, “lacklustre eye.” The extreme force of their original impressions, compared with the feebleness of those they receive at secondhand from others, oversets the balance and just proportion of their minds. Men who have fewer native resources, and are obliged to apply oftener to the general stock, acquire by habit a greater aptitude in appreciating what they owe to others. Their taste is not made a sacrifice to their egotism and vanity, and they enrich the soil of their minds with continual accessions of borrowed strength and beauty. I might take this opportunity of observing, that the person of the most refined and least contracted taste I ever knew was the late Joseph Fawcett, the friend of my youth. He was almost the first literary acquaintance I ever made, and I think the most candid and unsophisticated. He had a masterly perception of all styles and of every kind and degree of excellence, sublime or beautiful, from Milton’s *Paradise Lost* to Shenstone’s *Pastoral Ballad*, from Butler’s *Analogy* down to *Humphrey Clinker*. If you had a favourite author, he had read him too, and knew all the best morsels, the subtle traits, the capital touches. “Do you like Sterne?” “Yes, to be sure,” he would say; “I should deserve to be hanged if I didn’t!” His repeating some parts of *Comus* with his fine, deep, mellow-toned voice, particularly the lines, “I have heard my mother Circe with the Sirens three,” etc., and the enthusiastic comments he made afterwards, were a feast to the ear and to the soul. He read the poetry of Milton with the same fervour and spirit of devotion that I have since heard others read their own. “That is the most delicious feeling of all,” I have heard him explain, “to like what is excellent, no matter whose it is.” In this respect he practised what he preached. He was incapable of harbouring a sinister motive, and judged only from what he felt. There was no flaw or mist in the clear mirror of his mind. He was as open to impressions as he was strenuous in maintaining them. He did not care a rush whether a writer was old or new, in prose or in verse﻿—“What he wanted,” he said, “was something to make him think.” Most men’s minds are to me like musical instruments out of tune. Touch a particular key, and it jars and makes harsh discord with your own.

===Chinese===

凡不落入他们视线正方向的，他们便漠然视之，带着空洞的“无光之眼”。他们原创印象的极端强力，同从他人那里二手得来的印象的孱弱相比，颠覆了他们心灵的平衡与合度。天赋资源较少、不得不更常求助于公共库存的人，反而由习惯养成了更敏于赏识外借之物的能力。他们的趣味不曾做了自我主义与虚荣的祭品；他们以源源不断借来的力与美，肥沃着自己心田的土壤。
借此机会我可以说一句：我所识得趣味最精微、最少偏狭的人，是已故的约瑟夫·福西特，我青年时代的朋友。他差不多是我结识的第一位文学之交，我想也是最坦白、最不染尘习的一位。对一切风格、一切品类与等级的卓越——无论崇高还是优美——从弥尔顿的《失乐园》到申斯通的《牧歌谣》，从巴特勒的《类比》到《汉弗莱·克林克》，他都有大师级的鉴识。你若有偏爱的作家，他也读过，且熟知其中全部最佳的片段、细微的笔致、点睛的落笔。“你可喜欢斯特恩？”“喜欢，当然，”他会说；“不喜欢就该绞死我！”他用他那美妙、深沉、圆润的嗓音诵起《科玛斯》的若干段落——特别是“我听我母亲喀耳同三位塞壬”数行——随后再加的热烈评点，是耳朵与灵魂的一场盛宴。他读弥尔顿的诗，那份虔诚与热忱，与我后来听旁人读自己的诗时一般无二。“那才是最甘美的感觉，”我听他解释过，“爱那卓越之物，无论它属于谁。”在这方面，他言出而行随。他心里容不下一个邪念，只凭自己所感下判断。他心头的明镜，没有一丝瑕疵与雾翳。他领受印象何其敞开，持守印象也何其坚定。作家是古是今、是散文是韵文，他一概不问——“他要的，”他说，“是能让他想的东西。”大多数人的头脑，在我听来像走了调的乐器。碰某一个键，它便刺耳，同你自己的琴音格格不入。

===Original===

They like *Gil Blas*, but can see nothing to laugh at in *Don Quixote*: they adore Richardson, but are disgusted with Fielding. Fawcett had a taste accommodated to all these. He was not exceptious. He gave a cordial welcome to all sort, provided they were the best in their kind. He was not fond of counterfeits or duplicates. His own style was laboured and artificial to a fault, while his character was frank and ingenuous in the extreme. He was not the only individual whom I have known to counteract their natural disposition in coming before the public, and by avoiding what they perhaps thought an inherent infirmity, debar themselves of their real strength and advantages. A heartier friend or honester critic I never coped withal. He has made me feel (by contrast) the want of genuine sincerity and generous sentiment in some that I have listened to since, and convinced me (if practical proof were wanting) of the truth of that text of Scripture﻿—“That had I all knowledge and could speak with the tongues of angels, yet without charity I were nothing!” I would rather be a man of disinterested taste and liberal feeling, to see and acknowledge truth and beauty wherever I found it, than a man of greater and more original genius, to hate, envy, and deny all excellence but my own﻿—but that poor scanty pittance of it (compared with the whole) which I had myself produced!
There is another race of critics who might be designated as the “Occult School”﻿—*vere adepti*. They discern no beauties but what are concealed from superficial eyes, and overlook all that are obvious to the vulgar part of mankind. Their art is the transmutation of styles. By happy alchemy of mind they convert dross into gold﻿—and gold into tinsel. They see farther into a millstone than most others. If an author is utterly unreadable, they can read him forever: his intricacies are their delight, his mysteries are their study. They prefer Sir Thomas Browne to the *Rambler* by Dr. Johnson, and Burton’s *Anatomy of Melancholy* to all the writers of the Georgian Age. They judge of works of genius as misers do of hid treasure﻿—it is of no value unless they have it all to themselves. They will no more share a book than a mistress with a friend. If they suspected their favourite volumes of delighting any eyes but their own, they would immediately discard them from the list.

===Chinese===

他们喜欢《吉尔·布拉斯》（*Gil Blas*），却看不出《堂吉诃德》（*Don Quixote*）有什么可笑；他们崇拜理查逊，却嫌菲尔丁讨厌。福西特的趣味兼收这一切。他不挑眼。只要是同类之冠，他都诚心接纳。他不喜赝品与复本。他自己的文风刻意而人工到了过头的地步，为人却坦率真挚到了极点。因当众发表而逆着自己的天性行事的人，我所识不止他一位：为回避某种自认的痼疾，反倒把自己真正的力量与长处拒之门外。更热肠的朋友、更诚实的批评家，我从未遇过。正是靠了对照，他让我在此后听过的某些人身上，觉出了真纯与慷慨之情的匮乏；也让我（倘若还需要实证的话）确信了《圣经》那句经文——“我若有万般知识、能说天使的言语，却没有爱，我就算不得什么！”我宁做一个趣味无私、胸怀宽廓的人，无论在哪里遇见真与美，都能看见、都能承认；也不做才具更高、创见更多的人——恨、妒、否认一切非我所有的卓越，只剩我自己产出的那可怜的一小份（同全体相比）！
还有一族批评家，或可名之曰“秘传学派”——*确然入门者*（*vere adepti*）。他们只辨认那些藏起来、浅眼看不见的美，而越过一切对凡俗众生昭然可见的美。他们的艺术是风格的炼金术。凭着心智的快乐炼金，他们把渣滓炼成金子——也把金子炼成锡箔。他们看磨盘也比别人看得深。一位作者倘若全然读不下去，他们倒能读他一辈子：他的晦涩是他们的欢愉，他的玄秘是他们的功课。他们宁取托马斯·布朗爵士，不取约翰逊博士的《漫步者》（*Rambler*）；宁取伯顿的《忧郁的解剖》（*Anatomy of Melancholy*），不取乔治王朝时代的全部作家。他们品评天才之作，如守财奴品评窖藏——不归他们独有，便一文不值。一本书，同一位情妇一样，他们绝不肯与朋友共享。倘若疑心他们心爱的书卷竟也悦了别人的眼，他们会立刻把它从名单上勾掉。

===Original===

Theirs are superannuated beauties that everyone else has left off intriguing with, bedridden hags, a “stud of nightmares.” This is not envy or affectation, but a natural proneness to singularity, a love of what is odd and out of the way. They must come at their pleasures with difficulty, and support admiration by an uneasy sense of ridicule and opposition. They despise those qualities in a work which are cheap and obvious. They like a monopoly of taste and are shocked at the prostitution of intellect implied in popular productions. In like manner, they would choose a friend or recommend a mistress for gross defects; and tolerate the sweetness of an actress’s voice only for the ugliness of her face. Pure pleasures are in their judgment cloying and insipid﻿—

> “An ounce of sour is worth a pound of sweet!”

Nothing goes down with them but what is caviar to the multitude. They are eaters of olives and readers of black-letter. Yet they smack of genius, and would be worth any money, were it only for the rarity of the thing!
The last sort I shall mention are “verbal critics”﻿—mere word-catchers, fellows that pick out a word in a sentence and a sentence in a volume, and tell you it is wrong.71 These erudite persons constantly find out by anticipation that you are deficient in the smallest things﻿—that you cannot spell certain words or join the nominative case and the verb together, because to do this is the height of their own ambition, and of course they must set you down lower than their opinion of themselves. They degrade by reducing you to their own standard of merit; for the qualifications they deny you, or the faults they object, are so very insignificant, that to prove yourself possessed of the one or free from the other is to make yourself doubly ridiculous. Littleness is their element, and they give a character of meanness to whatever they touch. They creep, buzz, and fly-blow. It is much easier to crush than to catch these troublesome insects; and when they are in your power your self-respect spares them. The race is almost extinct:﻿—one or two of them are sometimes seen crawling over the pages of the *Quarterly Review*!

===Chinese===

他们的是些过了气的美人，旁人早不再与之勾搭；是卧床不起的丑妪，“一厩的梦魇”。这不是嫉妒，也不是做作，而是一种天然的孤僻倾向，一种对奇僻冷僻之物的爱。他们的快乐必须来得艰难，他们的倾慕也须靠一种对讥嘲与反对的不安感来支撑。他们鄙视作品中廉价而显豁的品质。他们喜欢趣味的垄断，风行之作里心智的“卖淫”令他们震骇。同样，他们择友或荐情人，专挑重大的短处；容忍一位女演员嗓音的甜美，只因她脸面的丑陋。在他们看来，纯粹的快乐腻人而寡淡——

> “一盎司酸，抵得一磅甜！”

合他们口味的，唯有大众敬而远之的鱼子酱。他们是吃橄榄的人，读黑体古本的人。然而他们身上自有天才的气味；单凭这物以稀为贵，也值大价钱！
我要提的最后一种，是“字句批评家”——纯粹的捉字虱者：从句子里捉出一个词、从书卷里捉出一个句子，告诉你它错了71的家伙。这些博学之士总能预先发现你在最小的事上有欠缺——某些词你不会拼、主语和动词你连不到一起——因为做到这些已是他们野心的绝顶，自然要把你放到低于他们自我评价的位置上。他们把你拉到他们自己的功过标准上来贬损你；因为他们否认你具备的资格、指摘你的过失，都微末到极点——你若去证明自己有此一长、无此一短，反倒是双倍的可笑。渺小是他们的元素；凡经他们一碰，无不带上卑琐的印记。他们爬行、嗡营、产蛆。这些恼人的虫豸，碾死容易，捉住难；而一旦落入你手中，你的自尊又不屑弄死它们。这一族已近绝灭：——偶尔还能看见一两只，在《每季评论》（*Quarterly Review*）的书页上爬！

### On Effeminacy of Character / 论性格之柔靡
===Original===

Effeminacy of character arises from a prevalence of the sensibility over the will; or it consists in a want of fortitude to bear pain or to undergo fatigue, however urgent the occasion. We meet with instances of people who cannot lift up a little finger to save themselves from ruin, nor give up the smallest indulgence for the sake of any other person. They cannot put themselves out of their way on any account. No one makes a greater outcry when the day of reckoning comes, or affects greater compassion for the mischiefs they have occasioned; but till the time comes, they feel nothing, they care for nothing. They live in the present moment, are the creatures of the present impulse (whatever it may be)﻿—and beyond that, the universe is nothing to them. The slightest toy countervails the empire of the world; they will not forego the smallest inclination they feel, for any object that can be proposed to them, or any reasons that can be urged for it. You might as well ask of the gossamer not to wanton in the idle summer air, or of the moth not to play with the flame that scorches it, as ask of these persons to put off any enjoyment for a single instant, or to gird themselves up to any enterprise of pith or moment. They have been so used to a studied succession of agreeable sensations that the shortest pause is a privation which they can by no means endure﻿—it is like tearing them from their very existence﻿—they have been so inured to ease and indolence, that the most trifling effort is like one of the tasks of Hercules, a thing of impossibility, at which they shudder. They lie on beds of roses, and spread their gauze wings to the sun and summer gale, and cannot bear to put their tender feet to the ground, much less to encounter the thorns and briars of the world. Life for them

> “Rolls o’er Elysian flowers its amber stream,”

and they have no fancy for fishing in troubled waters. The ordinary state of existence they regard as something importunate and vain, and out of nature. What must they think of its trials and sharp vicissitudes? Instead of voluntarily embracing pain, or labour, or danger, or death, every sensation must be wound up to the highest pitch of voluptuous refinement, every motion must be grace and elegance; they live in a luxurious, endless dream, or

> “Die of a rose in aromatic pain!”

===Chinese===

性格的柔靡，源于感受力凌驾于意志之上；或者说，它在于无论情势多么急迫，都缺乏承受痛苦、经受劳顿的坚忍。我们见过这样的人：哪怕为免于毁灭，也不肯抬一抬小指；为了任何人，也不肯放弃最小的一点纵容。无论为了什么，他们都不能委屈自己一下。清算的日子一到，谁也不及他们叫得响，也不及他们对自己惹下的祸害装得更悲痛；可在那日子到来之前，他们无所感，也无所惜。他们活在此刻，是此刻冲动（不管什么冲动）的造物——超出此刻，宇宙于他们便什么都不是。一件最轻微的小玩物，也抵得过整个世界的帝国；他们绝不肯为他们感受到的最小的意愿让步——无论你向他们提出什么目标、摆出什么理由。要这种人把任何享乐推迟哪怕一瞬，或振作起来干一件有分量的、要紧的事业，无异于要求游丝不在夏日闲风中嬉戏，要求飞蛾不扑那灼身的火焰。他们太惯于精心安排的一连串适意感觉，最短的间歇也成了断供，万万忍受不了——那像把他们从存在本身撕下来——他们太惯于安逸与疏懒，最轻微的费力也像赫拉克勒斯的劳役，是一桩不可能之事，想起来就发抖。他们卧在玫瑰花榻上，向太阳与夏风张开薄纱的翅膀，连把娇嫩的脚踏到地上都受不了，更别说去迎世界的荆棘与野蔷薇了。生命于他们

> “在极乐仙花之上淌过它琥珀色的溪流”，

他们毫无在浑水里摸鱼的兴致。寻常的生存状态，他们视为纠缠而虚妄的东西，有悖自然。那么他们又该如何看待人世的磨难与陡然的荣枯？他们非但不主动拥抱痛苦、劳作、危险或死亡，反而要把每一种感觉上到奢靡精致的最高音；每一个动作都须优雅典雅；他们活在一场奢华而无尽的梦里，或者——

> “在一朵玫瑰的芬芳疼痛中死去！”

===Original===

Siren sounds must float around them; smiling forms must everywhere meet their sight; they must tread a soft measure on painted carpets or smooth-shaven lawns; books, arts, jests, laughter occupy every thought and hour﻿—what have they to do with the drudgery, the struggles, the poverty, the disease or anguish which are the common lot of humanity? These things are intolerable to them, even in imagination. They disturb the enchantment in which they are lapt. They cause a wrinkle in the clear and polished surface of their existence. They exclaim with impatience and in agony, “Oh, leave me to my repose!” How “they shall discourse the freezing hours away, when wind and rain beat dark December down,” or “bide the pelting of the pitiless storm,” gives them no concern, it never once enters their heads. They close the shutters, draw the curtains, and enjoy or shut out the whistling of the approaching tempest “They take no thought for the morrow,” not they. They do not anticipate evils. Let them come when they will come, they will not run to meet them. Nay more, they will not move one step to prevent them, nor let anyone else. The mention of such things is shocking; the very supposition is a nuisance that must not be tolerated. The idea of the obviate disagreeable consequences oppresses them to death, is an exertion too great for their enervated imaginations. They are not like Master Barnardine in *Measure for Measure*, who would not “get up to be hanged”﻿—they would not get up to avoid being hanged. They are completely wrapped up in themselves; but then all their self-love is concentrated in the present minute. They have worked up their effeminate and fastidious appetite of enjoyment to such a pitch that the whole of their existence, every moment of it, must be made up of these exquisite indulgences; or they will fling it all away, with indifference and scorn. They stake their entire welfare on the gratification of the passing instant. Their senses, their vanity, their thoughtless gaiety have been pampered till they ache at the smallest suspension of their perpetual dose of excitement, and they will purchase the hollow happiness of the next five minutes by a mortgage on the independence and comfort of years. They must have their will in everything, or they grow sullen and peevish like spoiled children.

===Chinese===

塞壬的歌声须在他们四周飘荡；含笑的身影须处处入眼；他们必须在彩绘的地毯上、在修剪平整的草坪上踩着轻柔的步子；书籍、艺术、谐谑、欢笑占尽每一缕思绪、每一个钟头——人类的共同命运，苦役、挣扎、贫乏、疾病与创痛，与他们何干？这些东西，他们连想想都受不了。它们搅扰了裹着他们的魔法。它们在他们生存那澄澈光洁的表面激起一道皱纹。他们焦躁而痛苦地喊：“哦，让我安息吧！”至于“当风和雨把晦暗的十二月打下来时，他们该如何清谈消磨冻人的时辰”，或如何“忍受无情风暴的捶打”，他们毫不上心，头脑里从不曾有一次想到。他们关上百叶窗，拉上帘幕，把逼近的风暴的呼啸或享用、或隔绝在外。“不为明天忧虑”——说的正是他们。他们不预想灾祸。要来就让它来，他们绝不去迎接。非但如此，他们也绝不挪一步去预防，也不许别人去。提起这些就令人震骇；光是这样假设，就是不容姑息的冒犯。光是去想避开不快的后果，这念头本身就把他们压得要死——对他们委顿的想象力，这是一场太过费力的举动。他们不像《一报还一报》（*Measure for Measure*）里的巴纳丁，是“不肯起来受绞刑”——他们是起来躲避绞刑都不肯。他们整个儿裹在自己里；但他们全部的自爱，又都凝在此刻这一分钟。他们把那柔靡而挑剔的享乐胃口养到了这样的高度：他们的全部存在、存在的每一刻，都必须由这些精致的纵情组成；否则，他们便漠然、轻蔑地把它整个抛开。他们把全部福祉押在转瞬即逝的满足上。他们的感官、虚荣与无思虑的欢快被养得娇惯已极，那永不间断的兴奋剂哪怕停供最小的一剂，他们便浑身作痛；他们肯拿多年自立与安逸的抵押，去买下一个五分钟空洞的幸福。事事都得如他们的意，否则就像惯坏的孩子一样变得阴沉、易怒。

===Original===

Whatever they set their eyes on, or make up their minds to, they must have that instant. They may pay for it hereafter. But that is no matter. They snatch a joy beyond the reach of fate, and consider the present time sacred, inviolable, unaccountable to that hard, churlish, niggard, inexorable taskmaster, the future. *Now or never* is their motto. They are madly devoted to the plaything, the ruling passion of the moment. What is to happen to them a week hence is as if it were to happen to them a thousand years hence. They put off the consideration for another day, and their heedless unconcern laughs at it as a fable. Their life is “a cell of ignorance, travelling abed”; their existence is ephemeral; their thoughts are insect-winged; their identity expires with the whim, the folly, the passion of the hour.
Nothing but a miracle can rouse such people from their lethargy. It is not to be expected, nor is it even possible in the natural course of things. Pope’s striking exclamation,

> “Oh! blindness to the future kindly given,

That each may fill the circuit mark’d by Heaven!”

===Chinese===

凡是他们看上眼的、拿定主意的，必须立刻到手。日后付出代价？那不要紧。他们抢夺命运够不着的欢乐，视现在为神圣、不可侵犯，无须向那个严苛、乖吝、小气、铁面无情的监工——未来——交代。*此时不干，更待何时*是他们的座右铭。他们疯狂地拜倒在此刻的玩物、此刻的主宰激情之下。一周后将要落到他们头上的事，与千年后的事没有两样。他们把掂量推给明天，而那浑不在意的漠然把它当笑谈。他们的生命是“一间隔着无知的牢房，躺在床上旅行”；他们的存在朝生暮死；他们的思想生着虫豸的翅膀；他们的自我，随一时的兴致、愚行与激情一同到期。
唯有奇迹能唤醒这类人的沉睡。那不能指望，在事物的自然进程里甚至不可能。蒲柏那动人的咏叹——

> “哦！上天仁慈地赐予我们对未来的盲昧，

好教人人填满天定的范围！”

===Original===

hardly applies here; namely, to evils that stare us in the face, and that might be averted with the least prudence or resolution. But nothing can be done. How should it? A slight evil, a distant danger, will not move them; and a more imminent one only makes them turn away from it in greater precipitation and alarm. The more desperate their affairs grow, the more averse they are to look into them; and the greater the effort required to retrieve them, the more incapable they are of it. At first, they will not do anything; and afterwards, it is too late. The very motives that imperiously urge them to self-reflection and amendment, combine with their natural disposition to prevent it. This amounts pretty nearly to a mathematical demonstration. Ease, vanity, pleasure are the ruling passions in such cases. How will you conquer these, or wean their infatuated votaries from them? By the dread of hardship, disgrace, pain? They turn from them, and you who point them out as the alternative, with sickly disgust; and instead of a stronger effort of courage or self-denial to avert the crisis, hasten it by a wilful determination to pamper the disease in every way, and arm themselves, not with fortitude to bear or to repel the consequences, but with judicial blindness to their approach. Will you rouse the indolent procrastinator to an irksome but necessary effort, by showing him how much he has to do? He will only draw back the more for all your entreaties and representations. If of a sanguine turn, he will make a slight attempt at a new plan of life, be satisfied with the first appearance of reform, and relapse into indolence again. If timid and undecided, the hopelessness of the undertaking will put him out of heart with it, and he will stand still in despair. Will you save a vain man from ruin, by pointing out the obloquy and ridicule that await him in his present career? He smiles at your forebodings as fantastical; or the more they are realised around him, the more he is impelled to keep out the galling conviction, and the more fondly he clings to flattery and death.

===Chinese===

——在此几乎用不上；这里说的是那些瞪眼望着我们的、只消最少的审慎或决断便可避开的祸事。可什么也做不成。又怎么能做成？小小的祸患、遥远的危险，撼不动他们；更迫近的，也只会叫他们更仓皇、更惊惶地掉头回避。事情越绝望，他们越不愿正视；挽回所需的努力越大，他们越无力做到。起初，他们什么也不肯做；到后来，已经太迟。恰恰是那些严令他们自省与悔改的动机，同他们的天然习性联手，阻止了自省与悔改。这几乎就是一条数学式的证明。安逸、虚荣、享乐，是这类情形里的主宰激情。你怎么征服它们，或把执迷的信徒从中劝出来？靠对困苦、耻辱、痛苦的畏惧吗？他们带着病态的厌恶掉头避开这些，也避开你这个把它们当作另一条路指给他们的人；非但不鼓起更大的勇气或自我克制去化解危局，反而存心把病往各处娇养，反而加速危局；他们武装自己的，不是承受或击退后果的坚忍，而是对后果之来临的官方式的视而不见。你想让那位懒散的拖延者看清他有多少事要做，以此催他做那桩烦人却必需的努力吗？任你怎样恳求与陈说，他只会愈发退缩。他若性子乐观，便对新的生活计划稍作尝试，见了点改良的影子便心满意足，重新瘫回懒散里去。他若胆怯而无决断，事情的无望又叫他心灰，他便绝望地立在原地。你想指明眼前这条路尽头等着他的谤毁与讥嘲，救一个虚荣的人免于毁灭吗？他把你的预卜当作奇谈一笑置之；或者，预兆在他四周应验得越多，他越是被逼着拒斥那难堪的确信，越是痴恋地抱紧谄媚与死亡。

===Original===

He will not make a bold and resolute attempt to recover his reputation, because that would imply that it was capable of being soiled or injured; or he no sooner meditates some desultory project, than he takes credit to himself for the execution, and is delighted to wear his unearned laurels while the thing is barely talked of. The chance of success relieves the uneasiness of his apprehensions; so that he makes use of the interval only to flatter his favourite infirmity again. Would you wean a man from sensual excesses by the inevitable consequences to which they lead?﻿—What holds more antipathy to pleasure than pain? The mind given up to self-indulgence revolts at suffering, and throws it from it as an unaccountable anomaly, as a piece of injustice when it comes. Much less will it acknowledge any affinity with or subjection to it as a mere threat. If the prediction does not immediately come true, we laugh at the prophet of ill: if it is verified, we hate our adviser proportionably, hug our vices the closer, and hold them dearer and more precious the more they cost us. We resent wholesome counsel as an impertinence, and consider those who warn us of impending mischief as if they had brought it on our heads. We cry out with the poetical enthusiast﻿—

> “And let us nurse the fond deceit;

And what if we must die in sorrow?

Who would not cherish dreams so sweet,

Though grief and pain should come tomorrow?”

===Chinese===

他不会奋起一击以挽回名誉，因为那便等于承认名誉是可玷污、可损伤的；又或者，他刚冒出一个散漫的计划，便已把执行之功记在自己账上，事情才刚有人议论，他就乐得戴上那顶未挣来的桂冠。成功的一线可能，纾解了他担忧的不安；于是他把这段间隙只用来再度娇纵他心爱的痼疾。你想用纵欲不可避免的后果，劝一个人戒除恶习吗？——还有什么比痛苦更与快乐相仇？委身于自我放纵的心灵，一遇苦难便起而反叛，把它当作无由解释的变例抛在一边；它真来临时，又把它当作一桩不义。至于仅仅作为威胁的它，心灵更不肯承认与它有任何亲缘、任何臣属。预言若不立刻应验，我们笑那凶言的先知；若应验了，我们便相应地恨那进言的人，把恶习搂得更紧——它们让我们付出的越多，我们越觉得它们可贵、越珍重。我们把有益的忠告当无礼来怨，把警告大祸将临的人，看作仿佛是那祸事由他亲手加到我们头上。我们同那位诗意的狂热者一起喊——

> “且让我们把这痴心的骗局看护；

纵然明天要在悲伤中死去又如何？

谁不肯珍藏这般甜美的梦，

哪怕忧愁与痛苦明天就会到来？”

===Original===

But oh thou! who didst lend me speech when I was dumb, to whom I owe it that I have not crept on my belly all the days of my life like the serpent, but sometimes lift my forked crest or tread the empyrean, wake thou out of thy midday slumbers! Shake off the heavy honeydew of thy soul, no longer lulled with that Circean cup, drinking thy own thoughts with thy own ears, but start up in thy promised likeness, and shake the pillared rottenness of the world! Leave not thy sounding words in air, write them in marble, and teach the coming age heroic truths! Up, and wake the echoes of Time! Rich in deepest lore, die not the bed-rid churl of knowledge, leaving the survivors unblest! Set, set as thou didst rise in pomp and gladness! Dart like the sunflower one broad, golden flash of light; and ere thou ascendest thy native sky, show us the steps by which thou didst scale the Heaven of philosophy, with Truth and Fancy for thy equal guides, that we may catch thy mantle, rainbow-dipped, and still read thy words dear to Memory, dearer to Fame!
There is another branch of this character, which is the trifling or dilatory character. Such persons are always creating difficulties, and unable or unwilling to remove them. They cannot brush aside a cobweb, and are stopped by an insect’s wing. Their character is imbecility, rather than effeminacy. The want of energy and resolution in the persons last described arises from the habitual and inveterate predominance of other feelings and motives; in these it is a mere want of energy and resolution, that is, an inherent natural defect of vigour of nerve and voluntary power. There is a specific levity about such persons, so that you cannot propel them to any object, or give them a decided momentum in any direction or pursuit. They turn back, as it were, on the occasion that should project them forward with manly force and vehemence. They shrink from intrepidity of purpose, and are alarmed at the idea of attaining their end too soon. They will not act with steadiness or spirit, either for themselves or you. If you chalk out a line of conduct for them, or commission them to execute a certain task, they are sure to conjure up some insignificant objection or fanciful impediment in the way, and are withheld from striking an effectual blow by mere feebleness of character.

===Chinese===

但是你啊！当我还喑哑时赐我以言语的你——我之所以不曾像蛇一样终生以腹爬行，而能时而昂起我分叉的头冠、踏足九天，全赖有你——从你正午的酣睡中醒来吧！抖落你灵魂上沉重的甘露，别再被那喀耳刻的杯盏催眠、拿自己的耳朵啜饮自己的思想；起来，显出你应许的模样，摇撼这世界柱石般的朽坏！别让你铿锵的言语散在空中，把它们刻上大理石，教给来代以英雄的真理！起来，唤醒时间的回声！你怀最深奥的学问之富，切莫做知识的卧床老吝啬鬼死去，不遗后人以福！落下去吧，像你升起时那样堂皇而欢欣地落下去！像向日葵般投出一大片金色的光闪；在你升返本乡的天空之前，把你攀上哲学之天的阶蹬指给我们——真理与幻想是你同等的向导——好让我们接住你那蘸过虹彩的衣钵，仍旧诵读你的话语：它们亲于记忆，更亲于声名！
这一性格还有另一个分支，即琐屑或拖沓的性格。这样的人总是制造困难，又无力或不愿排除它们。他们掸不开一张蛛网，一片昆虫的翅膀就能拦住他们。他们的性格是孱弱，而非柔靡。前一类人的精力与决断之匮乏，源于别种情感与动机的习惯而根深蒂固的宰制；在这些人身上，则纯然是精力与决断的匮乏，即神经活力与意志力天生固有的欠缺。这类人身上有一种特有的轻浮，你无法把他们推向任何目标，无法在任何方向或追求上给他们一个确定的冲量。本该以丈夫的气力与猛势把他们抛向前去的时机，反倒叫他们朝后折返。他们畏避果敢的目的，一想到太早达到目的反会惊慌。无论为他们自己还是为你，他们都不肯沉稳地、振作地行事。你若替他们规划一条行动路线，或委托他们办一件事，他们准会变出一条无足轻重的异议或一个想入非非的障碍横在路上，单凭性格的孱弱，就打不出一记有效的出手。

===Original===

They may be officious, good-natured, friendly, generous in disposition, but they are of no use to anyone. They will put themselves to twice the trouble you desire, not to carry your point, but to defeat it; and in obviating needless objections, neglect the main business. If they do what you want, it is neither at the time nor in the manner that you wish. This timidity amounts to treachery; for by always anticipating some misfortune or disgrace, they realise their unmeaning apprehensions. The little bears sway in their minds over the great: a small inconvenience outweighs a solid and indispensable advantage; and their strongest bias is uniformly derived from the weakest motive. They hesitate about the best way of beginning a thing till the opportunity for action is lost, and are less anxious about its being done than the precise manner of doing it. They will destroy a passage sooner than let an objectionable word pass; and are much less concerned about the truth or the beauty of an image than about the reception it will meet with from the critics. They alter what they write, not because it is, but because it may possibly be wrong; and in their tremulous solicitude to avoid imaginary blunders, run into real ones. What is curious enough is, that with all this caution and delicacy, they are continually liable to extraordinary oversights. They are, in fact, so full of all sorts of idle apprehensions, that they do not know how to distinguish real from imaginary grounds of apprehension; and they often give some unaccountable offence, either from assuming a sudden boldness half in sport, or while they are secretly pluming themselves on their dexterity in avoiding everything exceptionable; and the same distraction of motive and shortsightedness which gets them into scrapes hinders them from seeing their way out of them. Such persons (often of ingenious and susceptible minds) are constantly at cross-purposes with themselves and others; will neither do things nor let others do them; and whether they succeed or fail, never feel confident or at their case. They spoil the freshness and originality of their own thoughts by asking contradictory advice; and in befriending others, while they are *about it and about it*, you might have done the thing yourself a dozen times over.
There is nothing more to be esteemed than a manly firmness and decision of character.

===Chinese===

他们或许多事、好心、友善、天性慷慨，但对谁都无用。他们肯花双倍于你所愿的麻烦，不为办成你的事，而为办砸它；在排除不必要的异议时，把正事撂在一边。即便做了你要的事，也不在你盼的时候、不合你愿的方式。这种怯懦近乎背叛；因为他们总在预想某种灾祸或羞辱，结果把自己无谓的忧惧一一兑现。在他们心里，小的压倒大的：一点小小的不便，胜过一个坚实而不可或缺的好处；而他们最强的偏向，一概出自最弱的动机。一件事怎样开头最好，他们踌躇再三，直到行动的时机失掉；对事情办成与否，他们倒不及对办事的确切方式那样挂心。他们宁可毁掉一段文字，也不肯放一个可议的词过关；对一个意象的真与美，他们的关切远不及对批评家对它将作何反应。他们改动所写的东西，不因为它错了，而因为它可能错；在战战兢兢避免想象中的失误时，栽进真正的失误。够奇怪的是，有这万般的小心与精细，他们却不断犯下非同小可的疏失。事实上，他们满心是各式各样无谓的忧惧，以致分不清忧虑的根据是真是幻；他们又常莫名地开罪于人——或是半开玩笑地摆出一阵突然的胆大，或是正暗自得意于自己躲开一切可议之物的机巧；而正是那使他们陷入窘境的动机涣散与目光短浅，也使他们看不见脱身之路。这样的人（常是心灵灵巧而敏感的）不断同自己、也同旁人拧着劲；事情既不肯自己做，也不让别人做；无论成败，从无自信，也从不安泰。他们四处征询互相矛盾的意见，把自己思想的新鲜与独创败坏净尽；受人之托帮人做事时，他们*绕啊绕啊*兜圈子——你自己的话，那件事早办完一打了。
没有什么比丈夫气的坚定与果决的性格更值得敬重。

===Original===

I like a person who knows his own mind and sticks to it; who sees at once what is to be done in given circumstances and does it. He does not beat about the bush for difficulties or excuses, but goes the shortest and most effectual way to work to attain his own ends or to accomplish a useful object. If he can serve you, he will do so; if he cannot, he will say so without keeping you in needless suspense, or laying you under pretended obligations. The applying to him in any laudable undertaking is not like stirring “a dish of skimmed milk.” There is stuff in him, and it is of the right practicable sort. He is not all his life at hawk-and-buzzard whether he shall be a Whig or a Tory, a friend or a foe, a knave or a fool; but thinks that life is short, and that there is no time to play fantastic tricks in it, to tamper with principles, or trifle with individual feelings. If he gives you a character, he does not add a damning clause to it: he does not pick holes in you lest others should, or anticipate objections lest he should be thought to be blinded by a childish partiality. His object is to serve you; and not to play the game into your enemies’ hands.

> “A generous friendship no cold medium knows,

Burns with one love, with one resentment glows.”

===Chinese===

我喜欢那种心里有数而守定不动的人：他一眼看清在既定情势下该做什么，便去做。他不绕着弯子找困难或借口，而是走最短、最有效的路去达到自己的目的、办成有益的事。若能帮你，他便帮；若不能，他便明说，不叫你无谓地悬着心，也不叫你欠下一份虚情的人情。任何正当的事去找他，绝不像“搅一盘脱脂奶”。他身上有料，而且是那种恰恰使得上劲的料。他不会一辈子首鼠两党，一会儿辉格一会儿托利、亦友亦敌、非奸即愚地摇摆；他知道人生苦短，没有工夫在里面变戏法、拿原则做交易、拿他人的感情当儿戏。他若为你写品行鉴定，不会附加一条把你毁掉的但书：他不会先自挑你的毛病、以防旁人来挑，也不会抢先历数反对之辞、生怕被人说成幼稚的偏爱迷了眼。他的目的是帮你，而不是把球送进你仇家的门里。

> “慷慨的友谊不识冷淡的中间地带，

一种爱在燃烧，一种恨在发光。”

===Original===

I should be sorry for anyone to say what he did not think of me; but I should not be pleased to see him slink out of his acknowledged opinion, lest it should not be confirmed by malice or stupidity. He who is well acquainted and well inclined to you ought to give the tone, not to receive it from others, and may set it to what key he pleases in certain cases.
There are those of whom it has been said, that to them an obligation is a reason for not doing anything, and there are others who are invariably led to do the reverse of what they should. The last are perverse, the first impracticable people. Opposed to the effeminate in disposition and manners are the coarse and brutal. As those were all softness and smoothness, these affect or are naturally attracted to whatever is vulgar and violent, harsh and repulsive in tone, in modes of speech, in forms of address, in gesture and behaviour. Thus there are some who ape the lisping of the fine lady, the drawling of the fine gentleman, and others who all their life delight in and catch the uncouth dialect, the manners and expressions of clowns and hoydens. The last are governed by an instinct of the disagreeable, by an appetite and headlong rage for violating decorum and hurting other people’s feelings, their own being excited and enlivened by the shock. They deal in home truths, unpleasant reflections, and unwelcome matters of fact; as the others are all compliment and complaisance, insincerity and insipidity.
We may observe an effeminacy of style, in some degree corresponding to effeminacy of character. Writers of this stamp are great interliners of what they indite, alterers of indifferent phrases, and the plague of printers’ devils. By an effeminate style I would be understood to mean one that is all florid, all fine; that cloys by its sweetness, and tires by its sameness. Such are what Dryden calls “calm, peaceable writers.” They only aim to please, and never offend by truth or disturb by singularity. Every thought must be beautiful per se, every expression equally fine. They do not delight in vulgarisms, but in commonplaces, and dress out unmeaning forms in all the colours of the rainbow. They do not go out of their way to think﻿—that would startle the indolence of the reader: they cannot express a trite thought in common words﻿—that would be a sacrifice of their own vanity.

谁若对我说言不由衷的话，我自然遗憾；但看到他从自己已然承认的见解里溜走、唯恐那见解得不到恶意或愚蠢的认可，我同样不快。深知你而心怀好意的人，应当定调子，而不是从旁人那里接调子；在某些情形下，他尽可以把调门定在他喜欢的任何一键上。
有人说过这样一类人：受人之托，反成了他们什么都不做的理由；还有一类人，永远做出与本应做的相反的事。后者是乖张，前者是不堪任事。与性情举止上的柔靡相对的，是粗粝与横暴。前者一味软与滑，后者则癖好——或天然被吸引于——一切粗俗而狂暴、生硬而拒人的东西：腔调里、谈吐里、称呼里、手势与做派里。于是，有人学时髦太太的嗲声、时髦绅士的拖腔，也有人一辈子偏爱并仿效村夫乡姑的土话、举止与腔口。后者受一种“惹人嫌”的本能支配，怀着一种冒犯体统、刺伤他人感情的胃口与横冲直撞的狂热——他人的震动反而使他们自己兴奋活跃。他们专营逆耳的实话、不快的议论、不受欢迎的事实；正如前者专营恭维与殷勤、虚情与乏味。
我们还可在文风上观察到一种柔靡，与性格的柔靡不无对应。这一路的作家，写起来尽在字里行间加行插字，对无关痛痒的措辞改了又改，是排字学徒的灾星。我所谓的柔靡文风，指的是那种通篇绚烂、通篇精致的风格；甜得发腻，千篇一律得使人疲倦。他们便是德莱顿所谓的“平静、温和的作家”。他们只求取悦，从不用真话冒犯人，也不用独特搅扰人。每一个念头都必须自身即美，每一个措辞都必须同样漂亮。他们不喜俗语，而喜套语，给无意义的空壳披上彩虹的全部颜色。他们不特意去想——那会惊扰读者的怠惰；他们又不能用平常的话说出平常的意思——那有损他们的虚荣。

===Original===

They are not sparing of tinsel, for it costs nothing. Their works should be printed, as they generally are, on hot-pressed paper, with vignette margins. The Della Cruscan school comes under this description, which is now nearly exploded. Lord Byron is a pampered and aristocratic writer, but he is not effeminate, or we should not have his works with only the printer’s name to them! I cannot help thinking that the fault of Mr. Keats’s poems was a deficiency in masculine energy of style. He had beauty, tenderness, delicacy, in an uncommon degree, but there was a want of strength and substance. His “Endymion” is a very delightful description of the illusions of a youthful imagination given up to airy dreams﻿—we have flowers, clouds, rainbows, moonlight, all sweet sounds and smells, and Oreads and Dryads flitting by﻿—but there is nothing tangible in it, nothing marked or palpable﻿—we have none of the hardy spirit or rigid forms of antiquity. He painted his own thoughts and character, and did not transport himself into the fabulous and heroic ages. There is a want of action, of character, and so far of imagination, but there is exquisite fancy. All is soft and fleshy, without bone or muscle. We see in him the youth without the manhood of poetry. His genius breathed “vernal delight and joy.” “Like Maia’s son he stood and shook his plumes,” with fragrance filled. His mind was redolent of spring. He had not the fierceness of summer, nor the richness of autumn, and winter he seemed not to have known till he felt the icy hand of death!

===Chinese===

他们锡箔用得不吝惜——反正不值钱。他们的作品照例要印在砑光纸上，页边饰一圈小花图。德拉·克鲁斯卡派正属此类，如今差不多已销声匿迹。拜伦勋爵是位娇纵而贵族气的作家，但他并不柔靡——否则，他的作品就不会只署印刷商的名字了！
我不免认为，济慈先生的诗的毛病，正在文风上丈夫气能量的欠缺。他有不寻常程度的美、温婉、细腻，却缺少力量与实体。他的《恩底弥翁》是一卷极可喜的写照，写沉溺于缥缈之梦的青春想象的幻境——花、云、虹、月色，一切甜美的声响与芬芳，山宁芙与树宁芙翩然掠过——但其中没有一点可触的东西，没有一点醒豁或切实的东西——全无古人那种坚劲的精神、刚硬的形式。他画的是自己的心思与性格，并不把自己搬进传说与英雄的时代。其中缺动作、缺性格，也就缺了想象力（就此而论），却有无上的幻想。一切皆软而多肉，无骨无肌。我们在他身上看到的是诗的青春，而无诗的壮年。他的天才吐纳着“春日的欢愉与欣悦”。“他如迈亚之子昂立，抖动羽翎”，满载芬芳。他的心灵馥郁如春。他没有夏的炽烈，没有秋的丰饶；至于冬，他仿佛直到触到死亡冰冷的手，才认识了它！

### On Familiar Style / 论平易的文体
===Original===

It is not easy to write a familiar style. Many people mistake a familiar for a vulgar style, and suppose that to write without affectation is to write at random. On the contrary, there is nothing that requires more precision, and, if I may so say, purity of expression, than the style I am speaking of. It utterly rejects not only all unmeaning pomp, but all low, cant phrases, and loose, unconnected, *slipshod* allusions. It is not to take the first word that offers, but the best word in common use; it is not to throw words together in any combinations we please, but to follow and avail ourselves of the true idiom of the language. To write a genuine familiar or truly English style is to write as anyone would speak in common conversation who had a thorough command and choice of words, or who could discourse with ease, force, and perspicuity, setting aside all pedantic and oratorical flourishes. Or, to give another illustration, to write naturally is the same thing in regard to common conversation as to read naturally is in regard to common speech. It does not follow that it is an easy thing to give the true accent and inflection to the words you utter, because you do not attempt to rise above the level of ordinary life and colloquial speaking. You do not assume, indeed, the solemnity of the pulpit, or the tone of stage-declamation; neither are you at liberty to gabble on at a venture, without emphasis or discretion, or to resort to vulgar dialect or clownish pronunciation. You must steer a middle course. You are tied down to a given and appropriate articulation, which is determined by the habitual associations between sense and sound, and which you can only hit by entering into the author’s meaning, as you must find the proper words and style to express yourself by fixing your thoughts on the subject you have to write about. Anyone may mouth out a passage with a theatrical cadence, or get upon stilts to tell his thoughts; but to write or speak with propriety and simplicity is a more difficult task. Thus it is easy to affect a pompous style, to use a word twice as big as the thing you want to express: it is not so easy to pitch upon the very word that exactly fits it.

===Chinese===

平易的文体并不好写。许多人把平易误当粗俗，以为不带做作地写，就是信笔乱写。恰恰相反，再没有比我说的这种文体更需要精确、更需要（容我这样说）表达之纯正的了。它断然拒斥的不仅是无谓的铺张，还有一切低级的行话切口，以及散漫、无着落的*拖沓*的引喻。它不是抓起头一个送上门的词，而是取通行用语中最好的那个词；不是把词随我们的意胡乱拼凑，而是遵循并善用这门语言真正的习语。写出地道的平易文体、真正的英国文体，就是像一位彻底掌握并善于选择词语的人在日常谈话中说话那样去写——抛开一切掉书袋与演说腔的花饰，谈得从容、有力而明白。或者换个比方：写作之求自然，对于日常交谈，正如朗读之求自然对于日常言语。不能因为你并不想超出日常生活与口语的水平，就以为给你吐出的字眼配上真正恰当的重音与语调是件容易事。诚然，你不必摆出讲坛的庄严、舞台朗诵腔的调门；但你也无权信口唠叨，不讲重音、不知取舍，更无权去用俚俗的方言或村夫的发音。你必须执中而行。你被限定在一种确当而合宜的发音方式上，它由意义与声音之间习惯性的联结所决定；要命中它，唯有深入作者的意思——正如要找到表达自己的恰当词语与文体，唯有把心思钉在你要写的题目上。谁都会拿戏腔的抑扬把一段文字念得铿锵作响，或踩着高跷发表感想；但要写得或说得得体而简洁，却是更难的功课。所以，装出一副浮夸的文体容易——用一个大上一倍的词去说你想说的事；难的是拣中那个恰恰合身的词。

===Original===

Out of eight or ten words equally common, equally intelligible, with nearly equal pretensions, it is a matter of some nicety and discrimination to pick out the very one the preferableness of which is scarcely perceptible, but decisive. The reason why I object to Dr. Johnson’s style is that there is no discrimination, no selection, no variety in it. He uses none but “tall, opaque words,” taken from the “first row of the rubric”﻿—words with the greatest number of syllables, or Latin phrases with merely English terminations. If a fine style depended on this sort of arbitrary pretension, it would be fair to judge of an author’s elegance by the measurement of his words and the substitution of foreign circumlocutions (with no precise associations) for the mother-tongue.77 How simple is it to be dignified without case, to be pompous without meaning! Surely it is but a mechanical rule for avoiding what is low, to be always pedantic and affected. It is clear you cannot use a vulgar English word if you never use a common English word at all. A fine tact is shown in adhering to those which are perfectly common, and yet never falling into any expressions which are debased by disgusting circumstances, or which owe their signification and point to technical or professional allusions. A truly natural or familiar style can never be quaint or vulgar, for this reason, that it is of universal force and applicability, and that quaintness and vulgarity arise out of the immediate connection of certain words with coarse and disagreeable or with confined ideas. The last form what we understand by “cant” or “slang” phrases.﻿—To give an example of what is not very clear in the general statement, I should say that the phrase “To cut with a knife,” or “To cut a piece of wood,” is perfectly free from vulgarity, because it is perfectly common; but “to cut an acquaintance” is not quite unexceptionable, because it is not perfectly common or intelligible, and has hardly yet escaped out of the limits of slang phraseology. I should hardly, therefore, use the word in this sense without putting it in italics as a license of expression, to be received *cum grano salis*. All provincial or bye-phrases come under the same mark of reprobation﻿—all such as the writer transfers to the page from his fireside or a particular coterie, or that he invents for his own sole use and convenience.

===Chinese===

八个十个同样常见、同样易懂、资历几乎相当的词里，挑出那一个——它的优越几乎察觉不出、却一锤定音——是一件颇需精细与辨别力的事。
我之所以不喜约翰逊博士的文体，是因为其中没有辨别、没有拣选、没有变化。他用的无一不是“高个的、不透明的词”，取自“红字栏的头一排”——音节最多的词，或只是缀上英文词尾的拉丁短语。倘若漂亮的文体系于这一类任意的做派，那么以量词的长短、以外国语的迂说法（并无精确联想的）替换母语来评判一位作者的雅致，便也算公道了。77不费力气就得庄严，没有意思也能铺张，何其省事！永远掉书袋、永远做作， surely 只是回避俚俗的一条机械规则。显然，你若压根不用常见的英文词，也就用不上俚俗的英文词了。恪守那些十足常见的词，却又绝不落入那些被可厌的语境玷辱过的、或其意义与锋芒全系于行话或专门引喻的表达——这里正见出精微的分寸。真正自然或平易的文体绝不会古怪或俚俗，理由是：它具有普遍的力量与适用性；而古怪与俚俗，则生于某些词同粗鄙可厌的观念、或偏狭的观念的直接勾连。后者便构成了我们所谓的“行话”或“黑话”。——为把一般说法里不甚明了处说清，试举一例：“用刀切”或“切一块木头”，全然不涉俚俗，因为它十足常见；但“切掉一个熟人”（to cut an acquaintance，绝交之意）便不无可议，因为它并不十足常见或易懂，还没完全脱出黑话的范围。因此，我几乎不会在这个意义上使用这个词——除非以斜体标出，视为一处破格，请读者*加盐领受*（*cum grano salis*）。一切外省话、旁门语，都同样该打——凡作者从自家炉边或某个小圈子搬上纸面的，或为自家一己之便生造的，皆是。

===Original===

I conceive that words are like money, not the worse for being common, but that it is the stamp of custom alone that gives them circulation or value. I am fastidious in this respect, and would almost as soon coin the currency of the realm as counterfeit the King’s English. I never invented or gave a new and unauthorised meaning to any word but one single one (the term “impersonal” applied to feelings), and that was in an abstruse metaphysical discussion to express a very difficult distinction. I have been (I know) loudly accused of revelling in vulgarisms and broken English. I cannot speak to that point; but so far I plead guilty to the determined use of acknowledged idioms and common elliptical expressions. I am not sure that the critics in question know the one from the other, that is, can distinguish any medium between formal pedantry and the most barbarous solecism. As an author I endeavour to employ plain words and popular modes of construction, as, were I a chapman and dealer, I should common weights and measures.
The proper force of words lies not in the words themselves, but in their application. A word may be a fine-sounding word, of an unusual length, and very imposing from its learning and novelty, and yet in the connection in which it is introduced may be quite pointless and irrelevant. It is not pomp or pretension, but the adaptation of the expression to the idea, that clenches a writer’s meaning:﻿—as it is not the size or glossiness of the materials, but their being fitted each to its place, that gives strength to the arch; or as the pegs and nails are as necessary to the support of the building as the larger timbers, and more so than the mere showy, unsubstantial ornaments. I hate anything that occupies more space than it is worth. I hate to see a load of bandboxes go along the street, and I hate to see a parcel of big words without anything in them. A person who does not deliberately dispose of all his thoughts alike in cumbrous draperies and flimsy disguises may strike out twenty varieties of familiar everyday language, each coming somewhat nearer to the feeling he wants to convey, and at last not hit upon that particular and only one which may be said to be identical with the exact impression in his mind. This would seem to show that Mr. Cobbett is hardly right in saying that the first word that occurs is always the best.

===Chinese===

我以为，词就像钱，并不因常见而贬值；赋予它们流通与价值的，唯独习俗的钤印。在这上头我十分挑剔：私铸王国货币的事，我几乎也肯干；伪造国王的英语，我可不肯。我从不曾发明、也从不曾给任何词一个新的、无据的新义——只有一处例外（把“非人称”一词用于情感）；那是在一次艰深的形而上学讨论里，为表达一个非常困难的区分。我知道，我曾被人高声指控沉溺于俚语与破体英语。这一点我不辩白；但就我认罪的部分而言，我认的是坚决使用公认习语与寻常省略式表达这一条。我不敢肯定那几位批评家分得清这两者——也就是说，分得清正式的掉书袋与最野蛮的文法误用之间还有任何中间地带。作为作者，我力求用平易的词、通行的句式，正如我若是个小贩商贾，便用官定的度量衡。
词的真正力量不在词本身，而在它的运用。一个词可以音调铿锵、长得罕见，凭其学问与新奇颇为唬人，然而放进具体的上下文里，却可能全然无的、文不对题。坐实作者意思的，不是铺张或自命，而是表达与意念的相称：——正如拱的力道不在于石料之巨与光泽，而在于每一块都各得其所；正如木钉铁钉之于房屋的支撑，与大木料同等必要，更胜过那些徒有其表的虚饰。我恨一切占的地方比它的价值还多的东西。我恨看见一车纸帽盒招摇过市，也恨看见一堆大词，里面空空如也。一个人若不故意给所有想法一律裹上累赘的帔帛、罩上轻薄的伪装，他可以一连打出二十种家常日用的说法，每一种都比前一种更贴近他想传达的情感，而到头来仍未必命中那独一无二的一个——同他心中确切的印痕可说是同一个东西的那一个。这似乎表明，科贝特先生说头一个冒出来的词永远是最好的，未必妥当。

===Original===

It may be a very good one; and yet a better may present itself on reflection or from time to time. It should be suggested naturally, however, and spontaneously, from a fresh and lively conception of the subject. We seldom succeed by trying at improvement, or by merely substituting one word for another that we are not satisfied with, as we cannot recollect the name of a place or person by merely plaguing ourselves about it. We wander farther from the point by persisting in a wrong scent; but it starts up accidentally in the memory when we least expected it, by touching some link in the chain of previous association.
There are those who hoard up and make a cautious display of nothing but rich and rare phraseology﻿—ancient medals, obscure coins, and Spanish pieces of eight. They are very curious to inspect, but I myself would neither offer nor take them in the course of exchange. A sprinkling of archaisms is not amiss, but a tissue of obsolete expressions is more fit *for keep than wear*. I do not say I would not use any phrase that had been brought into fashion before the middle or the end of the last century, but I should be shy of using any that had not been employed by any approved author during the whole of that time. Words, like clothes, get old-fashioned, or mean and ridiculous, when they have been for some time laid aside. Mr. Lamb is the only imitator of old English style I can read with pleasure; and he is so thoroughly imbued with the spirit of his authors that the idea of imitation is almost done away. There is an inward unction, a marrowy vein, both in the thought and feeling, an intuition, deep and lively, of his subject, that carries off any quaintness or awkwardness arising from an antiquated style and dress. The matter is completely his own, though the manner is assumed. Perhaps his ideas are altogether so marked and individual as to require their point and pungency to be neutralised by the affectation of a singular but traditional form of conveyance. Tricked out in the prevailing costume, they would probably seem more startling and out of the way. The old English authors, Burton, Fuller, Coryate, Sir Thomas Browne, are a kind of mediators between us and the more eccentric and whimsical modern, reconciling us to his peculiarities. I do not, however, know how far this is the case or not, till he condescends to write like one of us.

===Chinese===

它也许很好；然而更好的，也许会在斟酌之后、或过些时候自行出现。不过，它应当自然地、自发地从对题目清新而活泼的构想里冒出来。硬求改进、或仅仅拿一个词换掉我们不满意的另一个，很少能成——正如一个地名或人名想不起来，光是苦苦折磨自己也无济于事。循着错误的气味穷追，只会离目标更远；可等到无意间碰到先前联想之链上的某一环，它又会在最不指望的时候，冷不丁从记忆里跳出来。
也有人专事囤积、又小心翼翼炫示的，唯有富丽而珍罕的词藻——古钱章、冷门钱币、西班牙八里亚尔银元。拿来把玩固然新奇，只是我自己在流通中既不付这种钱、也不收这种钱。古语点缀一二无妨；可满纸废弃的表达，便*只宜收藏、不宜穿戴*了。我不是说，凡在上世纪中叶或末叶以前流行过的短语我便一概不用；但若有哪个短语在整个这段时期里不曾被任何可许的作者用过，我便要存几分戒心。词同衣裳一样，搁置日久，便过时了，或变得寒碜可笑。
兰姆先生是唯一一位让我读来愉悦的旧英文风格的摹仿者；他把那些作者的精魂浸润得如此透彻，“摹仿”这个念头几乎消融殆尽。他的思想与情感里都有一层内在的膏泽、一条多髓的矿脉，对题材有一种深而活泼的直觉——这就把旧式文体与装束可能带来的任何古怪与笨拙全数带走了。方式虽是借的，血肉却全然是他自己的。也许他的见解本就太鲜明、太个人，倒需要借一种奇特而承自旧统的传达形式的做作，来中和它们的锋芒与辛辣。若给它们穿上时下的衣装，恐怕反而更显突兀、更不入流。那些旧英文作者——伯顿、富勒、科里亚特、托马斯·布朗爵士——是我们同这位更古怪、更任性的现代作家之间的调解人，使我们同他的癖性和解。不过，这个判断究竟成不成立，我还说不好——除非他肯屈尊，像我们中的一个那样写点什么。

I must confess that what I like best of his papers under the signature of Elia (still I do not presume, amidst such excellence, to decide what is most excellent) is the account of “Mrs. Battle’s Opinions on Whist,” which is also the most free from obsolete allusions and turns of expression﻿—

> “A well of native English undefiled.”

===Chinese===

我必须承认，在他署名伊利亚的那些文字里，我最喜欢的是《巴特尔太太论惠斯特牌》一篇（在如此多的佳构之间，我当然不敢妄断哪一篇最佳）——而这一篇，恰恰也最没有废旧的引喻与旧式的措辞——

> “一口未经玷污的本土英语之井。”

===Original===

To those acquainted with his admired prototypes, these *Essays* of the ingenious and highly gifted author have the same sort of charm and relish that Erasmus’s *Colloquies* or a fine piece of modern Latin have to the classical scholar. Certainly, I do not know any borrowed pencil that has more power or felicity of execution than the one of which I have here been speaking.
It is as easy to write a gaudy style without ideas as it is to spread a pallet of showy colours or to smear in a flaunting transparency. “What do you read?” “Words, words, words.”﻿—“What is the matter?” “*Nothing*,” it might be answered. The florid style is the reverse of the familiar. The last is employed as an unvarnished medium to convey ideas; the first is resorted to as a spangled veil to conceal the want of them. When there is nothing to be set down but words, it costs little to have them fine. Look through the dictionary, and cull out a *florilegium*, rival the *tulippomania*. *Rouge* high enough, and never mind the natural complexion. The vulgar, who are not in the secret, will admire the look of preternatural health and vigour; and the fashionable, who regard only appearances, will be delighted with the imposition. Keep to your sounding generalities, your tinkling phrases, and all will be well. Swell out an unmeaning truism to a perfect tympany of style. A thought, a distinction is the rock on which all this brittle cargo of verbiage splits at once. Such writers have merely *verbal* imaginations, that retain nothing but words. Or their puny thoughts have dragon-wings, all green and gold. They soar far above the vulgar failing of the *Sermo humi obrepens*﻿—their most ordinary speech is never short of an hyperbole, splendid, imposing, vague, incomprehensible, magniloquent, a cento of sounding commonplaces. If some of us, whose “ambition is more lowly,” pry a little too narrowly into nooks and corners to pick up a number of “unconsidered trifles,” they never once direct their eyes or lift their hands to seize on any but the most gorgeous, tarnished, threadbare, patchwork set of phrases, the left-off finery of poetic extravagance, transmitted down through successive generations of barren pretenders.

===Chinese===

对熟知他所宗法的那些范本的人而言，这位才思横溢、天纵之才的作者的这些《随笔》（*Essays*），其魅力与滋味，正如伊拉斯谟的《对话录》（*Colloquies*）或一篇漂亮的近代拉丁文之于古典学者。当然，就我所知，再没有一支借来的笔，比我方才谈到的这一支更具力量或更得心应手。
写一种没有思想的浮艳文体，同在调色板上摊开一片俗丽的颜色、往一幅招摇的灯彩上涂抹一样容易。“您在读什么？”“词，词，词。”——“写的是什么？”“*什么也没有*。”不妨这样回答。藻丽文体正与平易文体相反。后者用作传递思想的素朴媒介；前者则当作一件缀满亮片的纱幕，好遮掩思想的阙如。既然要落笔的除了词什么都没有，把词弄得漂亮些，自然花不了几个钱。把词典翻个遍，精选出一部*群芳谱*，去同那场*郁金香狂热*争个高下。*胭脂*尽管搽厚，天生什么面色，不必理会。不明就里的俗众，会赞叹那超乎自然的健康与红润；只看表象的时髦人，也会为这场骗局心花怒放。只管抱着你铿锵的泛论、叮当作响的短语，一切便都平安。把一句无谓的老生常谈，吹胀成文体上一场十足的鼓胀病。一个思想、一层区分，便是这块怕碰的废话货载触之即碎的礁石。
这类作家只有*文字上*的想象力，留得住的只有词。或者说，他们孱弱的思想生着龙的翅膀，通体青金。它们翱翔在高天，远隔*贴地爬行的言语*这种俗人的毛病——他们最寻常的言谈也从不缺一份夸张：辉煌、唬人、空洞、费解、张大其词，一篇铿锵套话的集锦。我们有些人“志向较为卑微”，专爱往旮旯缝隙里细瞧，去拾取一些“未经虑及的琐屑”；他们却从不曾把目光或手指对准别的，只认那最华丽、最晦暗、最磨旧、补丁摞补丁的一套短语——诗界奢靡留下的旧衣裳，在一辈又一辈贫瘠的冒牌家手里世代相传。

===Original===

If they criticise actors and actresses, a huddled phantasmagoria of feathers, spangles, floods of light, and oceans of sound float before their morbid sense, which they paint in the style of Ancient Pistol. Not a glimpse can you get of the merits or defects of the performers: they are hidden in a profusion of barbarous epithets and wilful rhodomontade. Our hypercritics are not thinking of these little fantoccini beings﻿—

> “That strut and fret their hour upon the stage﻿—”

but of tall phantoms of words, abstractions, genera and species, sweeping clauses, periods that unite the Poles, forced alliterations, astounding antitheses﻿—

> “And on their pens *Fustian* sits plumed.”

===Chinese===

他们批评男女演员时，一团纷乱的幻灯景象——羽毛、亮片、光的洪流、声的海洋——浮在他们病态的感官前，再用毕斯托大尉的腔调描绘一番。演员的优劣，你连一瞥也得不到：全埋在大批野蛮的形容词与一意孤行的浮夸大话里。我们的超级批评家心里想的根本不是这些小小的傀儡——

> “在台上神气活现、焦躁不安地过完他们的一刻钟——”

而是词的高大幽灵、抽象物、属与种、横扫的从句、连通两极的长句、生硬的头韵、惊世的对偶——

> “而在他们的笔上，*浮夸*昂着羽冠端坐。”

===Original===

If they describe kings and queens, it is an Eastern pageant. The Coronation at either House is nothing to it. We get at four repeated images﻿—a curtain, a throne, a sceptre, and a footstool. These are with them the wardrobe of a lofty imagination; and they turn their servile strains to servile uses. Do we read a description of pictures? It is not a reflection of tones and hues which “nature’s own sweet and cunning hand laid on,” but piles of precious stones, rubies, pearls, emeralds, Golconda’s mines, and all the blazonry of art. Such persons are in fact besotted with words, and their brains are turned with the glittering but empty and sterile phantoms of things. Personifications, capital letters, seas of sunbeams, visions of glory, shining inscriptions, the figures of a transparency, Britannia with her shield, or Hope leaning on an anchor, make up their stock-in-trade. They may be considered as *hieroglyphical* writers. Images stand out in their minds isolated and important merely in themselves, without any groundwork of feeling﻿—there is no context in their imaginations. Words affect them in the same way, by the mere sound, that is, by their possible, not by their actual application to the subject in hand. They are fascinated by first appearances, and have no sense of consequences. Nothing more is meant by them than meets the ear: they understand or feel nothing more than meets their eye. The web and texture of the universe, and of the heart of man, is a mystery to them: they have no faculty that strikes a chord in unison with it. They cannot get beyond the daubings of fancy, the varnish of sentiment. Objects are not linked to feelings, words to things, but images revolve in splendid mockery, words represent themselves in their strange rhapsodies. The categories of such a mind are pride and ignorance﻿—pride in outside show, to which they sacrifice everything, and ignorance of the true worth and hidden structure both of words and things. With a sovereign contempt for what is familiar and natural, they are the slaves of vulgar affectation﻿—of a routine of high-flown phrases. Scorning to imitate realities, they are unable to invent anything, to strike out one original idea. They are not copyists of nature, it is true; but they are the poorest of all plagiarists, the plagiarists of words.

===Chinese===

他们描写国王王后，便是一场东方的盛典。两院各自的加冕礼也比不上它。我们得到的是四个翻来覆去的意象——帏幔、宝座、权杖、脚凳。这些便是他们崇高想象力的全部行头；他们把奴态的诗章派上奴态的用场。他们描述绘画又如何？那不是对“自然自己的巧手甜心”敷上的色调与光影的映照，而是一堆堆宝石——红宝石、珍珠、祖母绿、戈尔康达的矿藏，外加艺术纹章学的全套排场。
这类人其实是被词灌醉了，被事物那些闪光而空洞、贫瘠的幻影搅昏了头。拟人、大写字母、阳光之海、荣耀的幻象、闪亮的题铭、灯彩上的人形、持盾的不列颠尼亚、倚锚的希望——这些便是他们的全部存货。他们可以被看作*象形*作家。意象在他们心中凸现，孤立而自以为重，底下没有情感的根基——他们的想象里没有上下文。词也以同样的方式作用于他们：凭声音本身，也就是说，凭它们可能的、而非实际对眼下题目的运用。他们为第一眼的表象所惑，毫无后果之感。他们的话，耳朵听到多少，意思便只有多少；他们理解或感受的，眼睛看到多少，便只有多少。宇宙的经纬、人心的经纬，于他们是一团谜：他们没有一根弦能与之共振。他们越不出幻想的涂抹、情感的清漆。对象不与情感相连，词不与事物相连；意象只在做着辉煌的嘲弄里打转，词在他们怪诞的狂诗中只代表它们自己。
这种心灵的范畴，是骄傲与无知——为外表的排场而牺牲一切的骄傲，以及对词与事物的真正价值与隐秘构造的无知。他们怀着对平易自然之物的高傲的轻蔑，自己却做着俗气做作的奴隶——做着一套高调短语之成规的奴隶。耻于摹仿实在，他们又发明不出任何东西，打不出一个原创的念头。诚然，他们不是自然的抄手；但他们是天下最贫瘠的剽窃者——词的剽窃者。

===Original===

All is far-fetched, dear bought, artificial, oriental in subject and allusion; all is mechanical, conventional, vapid, formal, pedantic in style and execution. They startle and confound the understanding of the reader by the remoteness and obscurity of their illustrations; they soothe the ear by the monotony of the same everlasting round of circuitous metaphors. They are the mock-school in poetry and prose. They flounder about between fustian in expression and bathos in sentiment. They tantalise the fancy, but never reach the head nor touch the heart. Their Temple of Fame is like a shadowy structure raised by Dullness to Vanity, or like Cowper’s description of the Empress of Russia’s palace of ice, “as worthless as in show ’twas glittering”﻿—

> “It smiled, and it was cold!”

===Chinese===

题材与引喻，无不牵强、昂价、人工、东方；文体与手法，无不着实机械、因袭、乏味、呆板、掉书袋。他们用例证之辽远与晦暗惊扰、搅乱读者的理智；又用同样那套永远绕圈子的比喻的单调，抚慰读者的耳朵。他们是诗歌与散文中的仿英雄派。他们在表达的浮夸与情感的突降之间扑腾。他们撩拨幻想，却永远够不着头脑、碰不到心。他们的声名之殿，像“愚钝”为“虚荣”造起的一座幽影建筑，或像柯珀笔下俄国女皇的冰宫——“表观何等晶耀，内里便何等无价值”——

> “它笑着，而它是冷的！”

### On Genius and Common Sense / 论天才与常识
===Original===

We hear it maintained by people of more gravity than understanding, that genius and taste are strictly reducible to rules, and that there is a rule for everything. So far is it from being true that the finest breath of fancy is a definable thing, that the plainest common sense is only what Mr. Locke would have called a “mixed mode,” subject to a particular sort of acquired and undefinable tact. It is asked, “If you do not know the rule by which a thing is done, how can you be sure of doing it a second time?” And the answer is, “If you do not know the muscles by the help of which you walk, how is it you do not fall down at every step you take?” In art, in taste, in life, in speech, you decide from feeling, and not from reason; that is, from the impression of a number of things on the mind, from which impression is true and well founded, though you may not be able to analyse or account for it in the several particulars. In a gesture you use, in a look you see, in a tone you hear, you judge of the expression, propriety, and meaning from habit, not from reason or rules; that is to say, from innumerable instances of like gestures, looks, and tones, in innumerable other circumstances, variously modified, which are too many and too refined to be all distinctly recollected, but which do not therefore operate the less powerfully upon the mind and eye of taste. Shall we say that these impressions (the immediate stamp of nature) do not operate in a given manner till they are classified and reduced to rules, or is not the rule itself grounded, upon the truth and certainty of that natural operation?
How then can the distinction of the understanding as to the manner in which they operate be necessary to their producing their due and uniform effect upon the mind? If certain effects did not regularly arise out of certain causes in mind as well as matter, there could be no rule given for them: nature does not follow the rule, but suggests it. Reason is the interpreter and critic of nature and genius, not their lawgiver and judge. He must be a poor creature indeed whose practical convictions do not in almost all cases outrun his deliberate understanding, or who does not feel and know much more than he can give a reason for. Hence the distinction between eloquence and wisdom, between ingenuity and common sense.

===Chinese===

我们听人说——这些人庄重有余、明白不足——天才与趣味皆可严格还原为规则，凡事皆有一条规则。说幻想最精微的一息是个可界定的东西，固然不真；其实，最寻常的常识，也不过像洛克先生（Mr. Locke）会说的那种“混合样式”，系于一种后天的、无法界定的机敏。有人问：“你若不知道一件事据以做成的规则，怎能保证第二次还能做成？”回答是：“你若不知道走路时借助的是哪些肌肉，怎么没有每走一步摔一跤？”在艺术里、在趣味里、在生活里、在言谈里，你凭感觉、而非凭理性作判断；也就是说，凭众多事物打在心上的印痕——那印痕真实而有根据，尽管你未必能逐项分析或说明它。你做一个手势、看一个眼神、听一个声调，对其表情、得体与否与含意，你是凭习惯判断，不是凭理性或规则；也就是说，凭无数别的情境中、经过种种变化的无数类似的手势、眼神与声调——它们太多、太精微，无法一一清晰忆起，但并不因此而在趣味的头脑与眼光里少一分效力。难道我们该说，这些印象（自然的直接钤印）在被分类、被归纳为规则之前，就不按确定的方式起作用吗？规则本身，难道不正是植根于那自然运作的真实与确定吗？
那么，理解力对它们运作方式的分析，又怎会是它们在心上产生应有效果的必要条件？倘若在心灵同在物质中一样，某些效果并不规律地生于某些原因，那么根本无从为它们立规则：自然不遵循规则，而是暗示规则。理性是自然与天才的诠释者与批评者，不是它们的立法者与裁判官。倘若一个人的实际确信在几乎所有事情上不超出他深思后的理解，倘若他不觉得、不知道远多于他所能说明理由的东西，那他必定是个可怜的家伙。由此而有雄辩与智慧之分、机巧与常识之别。

===Original===

A man may be dexterous and able in explaining the grounds of his opinions, and yet may be a mere sophist, because he only sees one-half of a subject. Another may feel the whole weight of a question, nothing relating to it may be lost upon him, and yet he may be able to give no account of the manner in which it affects him, or to drag his reasons from their silent lurking-places. This last will be a wise man, though neither a logician nor rhetorician. Goldsmith was a fool to Dr. Johnson in argument; that is, in assigning the specific grounds of his opinions: Dr. Johnson was a fool to Goldsmith in the fine tact, the airy, intuitive faculty with which he skimmed the surfaces of things, and unconsciously formed his opinions. Common sense is the just result of the sum total of such unconscious impressions in the ordinary occurrences of life, as they are treasured up in the memory, and called out by the occasion. Genius and taste depend much upon the same principle exercised on loftier ground and in more unusual combinations.
I am glad to shelter myself from the charge of affectation or singularity in this view of an often debated but ill-understood point, by quoting a passage from Sir Joshua Reynolds’s *Discourses*, which is full, and, I think, conclusive to the purpose. He says:﻿—
“I observe, as a fundamental ground common to all the Arts with which we have any concern in this Discourse, that they address themselves only to two faculties of the mind, its imagination and its sensibility.
“All theories which attempt to direct or to control the Art, upon any principles falsely called rational, which we form to ourselves upon a supposition of what ought in reason to be the end or means of Art, independent of the known first effect produced by objects on the imagination, must be false and delusive. For though it may appear bold to say it, the imagination is here the residence of truth. If the imagination be affected, the conclusion is fairly drawn; if it be not affected, the reasoning is erroneous, because the end is not obtained; the effect itself being the test, and the only test, of the truth and efficacy of the means.

一个人陈述起自己见解的根据来可以又敏捷又能干，却依然不过是个诡辩家，因为他只看见题目的一半。另一个人或能感到一个问题的全部分量，与之相关的一切都不曾漏过他，却说不清它如何打动了他，也无力把他的理由从沉默的潜伏处拖出来。后者才是智者，尽管既非逻辑家，也非雄辩家。论争辩，哥尔德斯密斯在约翰逊博士面前是个傻瓜——也就是在指明见解的具体根据上；论那种精细的分寸、那种轻灵而直觉的能力——凭它掠过事物的表面、不自觉地产出见解——约翰逊博士在哥尔德斯密斯面前才是傻瓜。常识，是生活寻常境遇中这类不自觉印象的总和所结出的正当结果——它们珍存在记忆里，因时而起。天才与趣味，大抵依凭同一条原理，只是行在更高处、见于更不寻常的组合。
在这个常被争论却少被理解的题目上，我很乐意引一段雷诺兹爵士《讲演录》（*Discourses*）里的话，来庇护自己免遭矫饰或立异的指责——这段话说得充分，我想，也足以结论。他说：——
“我注意到一条根本的共同基础，适用于本讲所论的一切艺术：它们只诉诸心灵的两种官能——想象力与感受力。
“一切试图指导或控制艺术的理论，凡建立在我们凭空设想、被妄称为理性的原则之上的——设想艺术按理应当以什么为目的、以什么为手段，而不管对象作用于想象力的已知的第一效果——必定虚假而惑人。这话虽或显得大胆：想象力正是真理的住处。想象力若被触动了，结论便是公允地得出的；若不曾被触动，那推理便错了，因为目的没有达到；效果本身，乃是手段之真实与效力的试金石，而且是唯一的试金石。”

===Original===

“There is in the commerce of life, as in Art, a sagacity which is far from being contradictory to right reason, and is superior to any occasional exercise of that faculty which supersedes it and does not wait for the slow progress of deduction, but goes at once, by what appears a kind of intuition, to the conclusion. A man endowed with this faculty feels and acknowledges the truth, though it is not always in his power, perhaps, to give a reason for it; because he cannot recollect and bring before him all the materials that gave birth to his opinion; for very many and very intricate considerations may unite to form the principle, even of small and minute parts, involved in, or dependent on, a great many things:﻿—though these in process of time are forgotten, the right impression still remains fixed in his mind.
“This impression is the result of the accumulated experience of our whole life, and has been collected, we do not always know how or when. But this mass of collective observation, however acquired, ought to prevail over that reason, which, however powerfully exerted on any particular occasion, will probably comprehend but a partial view of the subject; and our conduct in life, as well as in the arts, is or ought to be generally governed by this habitual reason: it is our happiness that we are enabled to draw on such funds. If we were obliged to enter into a theoretical deliberation on every occasion before we act, life would be at a stand, and Art would be impracticable.
“It appears to me therefore” (continues Sir Joshua) “that our first thoughts, that is, the effect which anything produces on our minds on its first appearance, is never to be forgotten; and it demands for that reason, because it is the first, to be laid up with care. If this be not done, the artist may happen to impose on himself by partial reasoning; by a cold consideration of those animated thoughts which proceed, not perhaps from caprice or rashness (as he may afterwards conceit), but from the fullness of his mind, enriched with the copious stores of all the various inventions which he had ever seen, or had ever passed in his mind. These ideas are infused into his design, without any conscious effort; but if he be not on his guard, he may reconsider and correct them, till the whole matter is reduced to a commonplace invention.

“在人生的交道中，同在艺术中一样，存在一种明察；它绝不与正当的理性相悖，却胜过理性一时的运用——它取代理性，不等演绎的缓慢进程，而是仿佛凭着一种直觉，径直走向结论。禀有这种能力的人感到并承认真理，尽管他未必总能为之说明理由；因为他无法回忆并摆出曾催生其见解的全部材料；须知，即便涉及或依赖于许多事物的小而又小的部分，其原理也可能由许许多多、盘根错节的考量汇合而成——这些考量的痕迹随岁月淡忘了，正确的印象却依然固守在他心里。
“这印象是我们一生积累的经验的结果，如何积来、何时积来，我们并不尽知。但这一大团集合的观察，无论怎样得来，都应当压倒那理性——理性无论在某一场合发挥得多么有力，对题目多半只见到片面；我们一生的行止，同艺术中的作为一样，通常受、也应受这习惯的理性支配：我们能支取这样一笔基金，是我们的幸福。倘若每次行动之前都必须先来一番理论的斟酌，人生将陷于停顿，艺术也将无从施行。
“因此在我看来”（雷诺兹爵士继续说），“我们的第一念，即任何事物初现时在我们心上产生的效果，是永远不该忘记的；正因为它居先，就更要求被郑重收藏。不这样做，艺术家便可能以片面的推理自欺；以冷冰冰的掂量，对待那些活跃的念头——它们未必出自任性或轻率（如他日后自忖的那样），而是出自他心灵的充盈：那心灵因他见过、想过的一切形形色色构象的丰饶蕴藏而富足。这些意念不假有意的努力，便注入他的设计；但他若不加提防，又可能三思而改之，直到整件事缩成一件平庸的造物。”

===Original===

“This is sometimes the effect of what I mean to caution you against; that is to say, an unfounded distrust of the imagination and feeling, in favour of narrow, partial, confined, argumentative theories, and of principles that seem to apply to the design in hand, without considering those general impressions on the fancy in which real principles of *sound reason*, and of much more weight and importance, are involved, and, as it were, lie hid under the appearance of a sort of vulgar sentiment. Reason, without doubt, must ultimately determine everything; at this minute it is required to inform us when that very reason is to give way to feeling.”16
Mr. Burke, by whom the foregoing train of thinking was probably suggested, has insisted on the same thing, and made rather a perverse use of it in several parts of his *Reflections on the French Revolution*; and Windham in one of his *Speeches* has clenched it into an aphorism﻿—“There is nothing so true as habit.” Once more I would say, common sense is tacit reason. Conscience is the same tacit sense of right and wrong, or the impression of our moral experience and moral apprehensions on the mind, which, because it works unseen, yet certainly, we suppose to be an instinct, implanted in the mind; as we sometimes attribute the violent operations of our passions, of which we can neither trace the source nor assign the reason, to the instigation of the Devil!
I shall here try to go more at large into this subject, and to give such instances and illustrations of it as occur to me.
One of the persons who had rendered themselves obnoxious to Government and been included in a charge for high treason in the year 1794, had retired soon after into Wales to write an epic poem and enjoy the luxuries of a rural life. In his peregrinations through that beautiful scenery, he had arrived one fine morning at the inn at Llangollen, in the romantic valley of that name. He had ordered his breakfast, and was sitting at the window in all the dalliance of expectation when a face passed, of which he took no notice at the instant﻿—but when his breakfast was brought in presently after, he found his appetite for it gone﻿—the day had lost its freshness in his eye﻿—he was uneasy and spiritless; and without any cause that he could discover, a total change had taken place in his feelings.

===Chinese===

“这有时正是我要你们提防的东西造成的结果：也就是说，对想象力与情感的一种无根据的不信任，偏袒那些狭隘、片面、局促、好辩的理论，偏袒那些看似适用于手头设计的原理，却不顾想象之上那些总体的印象——*健全理性*的真正原理、远更重要而沉重的原理，正包孕其间，仿佛藏在一层庸俗情调的外观之下。理性无疑终须裁定一切；而此刻，它正须告知我们：理性本身何时该给情感让路。”16
雷诺兹那套想法多半出自伯克先生的启发；伯克本人坚持过同样的意思，并在《法国革命感想录》（*Reflections on the French Revolution*）的好几处对它作了颇为乖谬的运用；温德姆则在一次《演说》里把它锤成一句格言——“没有比习惯更真的东西。”我要再说一遍：常识就是缄默的理性。良心则是同一种缄默的善恶之感，是我们的道德经验与道德识见打在心上的印痕；正因为它在看不见处却确凿地运作，我们便以为它是植入心中的一种本能；正如我们有时把自己激情的暴烈发作——既寻不着源头、也说不出理由——归之于魔鬼的煽动！
这里我想把这个问题展开一些，举出我想到的例证与说明。
1794 年，有一位因开罪政府而被列入叛逆罪指控的人，不久便退隐威尔士，去写一部史诗、享受田园生活的奢华。在那片秀色中漫游时，一个晴朗的早晨，他来到了兰戈伦谷——那名字浪漫的山谷——里的客栈。他点了早饭，正坐在窗前满怀期待地消磨时光，一张面孔从窗外经过，他当时并未在意——可待早饭端上来，他发觉胃口没了——眼中的天色也失了清朗——他烦躁而无精打采；找不出任何缘故，他的感受却整个变了。

===Original===

While he was trying to account for this odd circumstance, the same face passed again﻿—it was the face of Taylor the spy; and he was longer at a loss to explain the difficulty. He had before caught only a transient glimpse, a passing side-view of the face; but though this was not sufficient to awaken a distinct idea in his memory, his feelings, quicker and surer, had taken the alarm; a string had been touched that gave a jar to his whole frame, and would not let him rest, though he could not at all tell what was the matter with him. To the flitting, shadowy, half-distinguished profile that had glided by his window was linked unconsciously and mysteriously, but inseparably, the impression of the trains that had been laid for him by this person;﻿—in this brief moment, in this dim, illegible shorthand of the mind he had just escaped the speeches of the Attorney and Solicitor-General over again; the gaunt figure of Mr. Pitt glared by him; the walls of a prison enclosed him; and he felt the hands of the executioner near him, without knowing it till the tremor and disorder of his nerves gave information to his reasoning faculties that all was not well within. That is, the same state of mind was recalled by one circumstance in the series of association that had been produced by the whole set of circumstances at the time, though the manner in which this was done was not immediately perceptible. In other words, the feeling of pleasure or pain, of good or evil, is revived, and acts instantaneously upon the mind, before we have time to recollect the precise objects which have originally given birth to it.17 The incident here mentioned was merely, then, one case of what the learned understand by the *association of ideas*: but all that is meant by feeling or common sense is nothing but the different cases of the association of ideas, more or less true to the impression of the original circumstances, as reason begins with the more formal development of those circumstances, or pretends to account for the different cases of the association of ideas. But it does not follow that the dumb and silent pleading of the former (though sometimes, nay often, mistaken) is less true than that of its babbling interpreter, or that we are never to trust its dictates without consulting the express authority of reason.

他正琢磨这桩怪事，那张脸又经过了一次——那是密探泰勒的脸；他越发不解了。先前他只匆匆瞥见那张脸的侧影一晃而过；这虽不足以在记忆里唤起一个清晰的观念，他的感觉却更快、更准，已然拉响了警报；有一根弦被拨动，震得他周身发颤，叫他不得安宁，尽管他全然说不出自己是怎么了。
同那掠过窗前、影影绰绰、依稀难辨的侧影，不自觉而神秘地、却不可分解地系在一起的，是此人为他布下圈套的印象——在这短短一瞬，在这心灵的昏昧难辨的速记里，他刚刚再度逃过检察长与副检察长的控词；皮特先生瘦削的身影瞪视而过；监狱的四壁围拢过来；他感到刽子手的手近在身旁——他自己并不知道，直到神经的震颤与紊乱向他的理性官能报信：内里出了岔子。
这就是说，当初整套情势在心中造成的联想系列里的一个环节，又唤回了同一种心境——只是唤回的方式并不即刻可见。换言之，苦乐之感、善恶之感复活了，即刻作用于心灵，快得叫我们来不及追忆起最初孕育它的那些确切对象。17那么，上面这件事不过是学者们所谓*观念联想*的一例：而所谓情感或常识，无非是观念联想的种种情形——对原初情势的印象或真或假；至于理性，则从那些情势更正式的展开起步，或妄图为观念联想的种种情形给出说明。但并不能因此说，前者（虽有时、不，常常出错）那喑哑无声的申辩，就比它那饶舌的译述人更不真实；也不能说，我们非得请教理性的明示权威，才可听从它的指令。
