他不是对自己怀着一份不成比例的观念，就是对身处的世界一无所知。生来便以为宇宙是为他们而造的那一等人大有其人，有一等就已经够受了！——再者，一个人若总把自己的真实长处拖到前台来，仿佛俗话在这里也应验——“眼不见，心不念”——这也未免显出缺乏安宁、自信，与对自身实在价值的坚定信念。譬如说，他是否以为，若非他亲自反复吟诵、强加于人，就再没有人会想起他的诗？他是否相信，一切竞争、一切对他人长处的承认，于他都是致命的？他是否必须像《乡下姑娘》里的穆迪那样，把他崇拜者们的官能统统锁起来，不叫他们知道绘画、音乐、古物这一切别的美好事物，唯恐他们逃学离他而去？我想，这样的行径，于他自己的天才、于他们的趣味，都不是什么好的评价：它有失庄严，也有失体统。诚然，一个人若确信自己真有所得，便受得住不必每分钟听人提起。他若知道自己在某方面确有无可置疑的优势，便不会因为遇见的人个个不识内情而不安，也不会因为传闻有敌手之才而动摇。当代第一流的数学家兼古典学者之一，曾把一件事当作对他的恭维讲给人听：他的一个表妹，一个刚出学堂的姑娘，对他说：“您知道，（曼宁）是个挺平常、挺好的年轻人，可一点儿也没有什么过人之处。”利·亨特（Leigh Hunt）有一回对我说：“真奇怪，从前竟从没听你谈过这个题目，你好像对它下过不少功夫。”我答道：“唉，据我所知，我们还不至于落到那个地步！”——
还有一种人，虽算不上犯这里所说的毛病，却也要“为同样大的罪孽记账”；他们谈吐并不乏味单调，而是活泼的做派家、过分的自我主义者。他们虽出于一时高兴能把一千个题目跑个遍，乐趣却仍旧出自同一个观念，那就是他们自己。随便翻开哪一页，总有一幅他们自己的卷首插画正对着你的脸。他们有点像“绿衣杰克”一流的角色：插一枝月桂，缀一点锡箔，抹一点黑灰，一面翻着跟头、一刻不停地蹦跳，好引人注目，逼你赏出你那一星半点的赞许。

===Original===

Whether they talk of the town or the country, poetry or politics, it comes to much the same thing. If they talk to you of the town, its diversions, “its palaces, its ladies, and its streets,” they are the delight, the grace, and ornament of it. If they are describing the charms of the country, they give no account of any individual spot or object or source of pleasure but the circumstance of their being there. “With them conversing, we forget all place, all seasons, and their change.” They perhaps pluck a leaf or a flower, patronise it, and hand it you to admire, but select no one feature of beauty or grandeur to dispute the palm of perfection with their own persons. Their rural descriptions are mere landscape backgrounds with their own portraits in an engaging attitude in front. They are not observing or enjoying the scene, but doing the honours as masters of the ceremonies to nature, and arbiters of elegance to all humanity. If they tell a love-tale of enamoured princesses, it is plain they fancy themselves the hero of the piece. If they discuss poetry, their encomiums still turn on something genial and unsophisticated, meaning their own style. If they enter into politics, it is understood that a hint from them to the potentates of Europe is sufficient. In short, as a lover (talk of what you will) brings in his mistress at every turn, so these persons contrive to divert your attention to the same darling object﻿—they are, in fact, in love with themselves, and, like lovers, should be left to keep their own company.

===Chinese===

无论他们谈的是城市还是乡野，是诗还是政治，落到头来都是一回事。倘若他们同你谈城市，谈它的行乐，“它的宫殿、它的淑女和它的街衢”，那么城市的欢愉、风致与点缀便是他们本人。倘若他们描摹乡野的胜景，那么任何一处具体的所在、一件具体的景物、一样具体的赏心乐事，他们都交代不出，除了“他们本人在那里”这一情节。“与他们交谈，我们忘了一切处所，一切季节，和季节的更迭。”他们或许摘一片叶、一朵花，垂青一番，递到你手上让你赏鉴，却决不挑出任何一样美的或壮丽的景致，来同他们本人的仪表争夺完美的桂冠。他们的乡野描写不过是风景衬底，前面是姿态动人的他们自己的肖像。他们不是在观赏、享受眼前的景致，而是在替自然尽地主之谊，充当全体人类的礼仪官与风雅的总裁判。倘若他们讲一个热恋中的公主们的爱情故事，那分明是他们把自己当成了戏里的主角。倘若他们议论诗，他们的颂词仍然落在某种亲切而不做作的东西上——意思是他们自己的风格。倘若他们谈政治，那意思是明白的：由他们向欧洲的列强们递一句话就够了。总之，正如情人（随你谈什么）动不动就把他的情人牵进来，这些人也有本事把你的注意引到同一个心爱的对象上——他们其实是爱上了他们自己；而既然是情人，就该让他们自己去陪伴自己吧。

### On the Aristocracy of Letters / 论文坛贵族
===Original===

> “Ha! here’s three of us are sophisticated:﻿—off, you lendings.”

There is such a thing as an aristocracy or privileged order in letters which has sometimes excited my wonder, and sometimes my spleen. We meet with authors who have never done anything, but who have a vast reputation for what they could have done. Their names stand high, and are in everybody’s mouth, but their works are never heard of, or had better remain undiscovered for the sake of their admirers.﻿—*Stat nominis umbra*﻿—their pretensions are lofty and unlimited, as they have nothing to rest upon, or because it is impossible to confront them with the proofs of their deficiency. If you inquire farther, and insist upon some act of authorship to establish the claims of these Epicurean votaries of the Muses, you find that they had a great reputation at Cambridge, that they were senior wranglers or successful prize-essayists, that they visit at Holland House, and, to support that honour, must be supposed, of course, to occupy the first rank in the world of letters.65 It is possible, however, that they have some manuscript work in hand, which is of too much importance (and the writer has too much at stake in publishing it) hastily to see the light: or perhaps they once had an article in the *Edinburgh Review*, which was much admired at the time, and is kept by them ever since as a kind of diploma and unquestionable testimonial of merit. They are not like Grub Street authors, who write for bread, and are paid by the sheet. Like misers who hoard their wealth, they are supposed to be masters of all the wit and sense they do not impart to the public. “Continents have most of what they contain,” says a considerable philosopher; and these persons, it must be confessed, have a prodigious command over themselves in the expenditure of light and learning. The Oriental curse, “O that mine enemy had written a book!” hangs suspended over them. By never committing themselves, they neither give a handle to the malice of the world, nor excite the jealousy of friends; and keep all the reputation they have got, not by discreetly blotting, but by never writing a line. Someone told Sheridan, who was always busy about some new work and never advancing any farther in it, that he would not write because he was afraid of the author of the *School for Scandal*.

===Chinese===

> “哈！这儿就有咱们三个是装点过的：——脱掉吧，你们这些借来的行头。”

文坛上也确有一种贵族、一种特权阶层，它有时激起我的惊异，有时激起我的怒气。我们常遇到一些从没写过什么东西的作者，却凭着他们本可以写出来的东西享有莫大的名声。他们的大名高高在上，人人挂在嘴边，他们的著作却无人听见，或者为了他们崇拜者的利益，最好永远别被发现。——*声名不过是一道影子*（Stat nominis umbra）——他们的声索高迈而无边，正因为它们无所依凭，或者说，正因为你无法拿他们欠缺的凭据来同他们对质。倘若你进一步追问，坚持要这些缪斯的伊壁鸠鲁式信徒拿出一点著述的实绩来确立他们的权利，你会发现：他们当年在剑桥大名鼎鼎，是数学甲等的头名、或是征文得奖的高手，他们出入霍兰德府（Holland House），而为了撑起这份体面，当然就得假定他们位居文坛的第一等了。65 不过，他们也未必没有一部什么手稿在进行之中，只是分量太重（而出版它，作者押上的赌注也太大），不便贸然问世；或者，他们当年在《爱丁堡评论》（Edinburgh Review）上发表过一篇文章，当时颇受赞赏，从此便被他们当作一纸文凭、一份不容置疑的才具证明保存至今。他们不似格拉布街的作者们，为面包而写，按印张领钱。他们像囤积财富的守财奴，被认作掌管着一切他们不肯给予公众的机智与见识。“蓄得最满的，装得最多”，一位颇可观的哲学家如是说；而必须承认，这些人在消耗光与学问方面，对自己有着惊人的克制力。那句东方的咒语——“噢，但愿我的仇人写过一本书！”——悬在他们头顶。他们从不把自己交出去，既不给世人的恶意留把柄，也不惹朋友的嫉妒；他们保住已经到手的名声，靠的不是审慎地涂改，而是一行也不写。有人对谢里丹（Sheridan）说——此人总在忙一部什么新著、却从没推进一步——他之所以不写，是因为他怕《造谣学校》的作者。

===Original===

So these idle pretenders are afraid of undergoing a comparison with themselves in something they have never done, but have had credit for doing. They do not acquire celebrity, they assume it; and escape detection by never venturing out of their imposing and mysterious incognito. They do not let themselves down by everyday work: for them to appear in print is a work of supererogation as much as in lords and kings; and like gentlemen with a large landed estate, they live on their established character, and do nothing (or as little as possible) to increase or lose it. There is not a more deliberate piece of grave imposture going. I know a person of this description who has been employed many years (by implication) in a translation of Thucydides, of which no one ever saw a word, but it does not answer the purpose of bolstering up a factitious reputation the less on that account. The longer it is delayed and kept sacred from the vulgar gaze, the more it swells into imaginary consequence; the labour and care required for a work of this kind being immense;﻿—and then there are no faults in an unexecuted translation. The only impeccable writers are those that never wrote. Another is an oracle on subjects of taste and classical erudition, because (he says at least) he reads Cicero once a year to keep up the purity of his Latinity. A third makes the indecency pass for the depth of his researches and for a high gusto in *virtu*, till, from his seeing nothing in the finest remains of ancient art, the world by the merest accident find out that there is nothing in him. There is scarcely anything that a grave face with an impenetrable manner will not accomplish, and whoever is weak enough to impose upon himself will have wit enough to impose upon the public﻿—particularly if he can make it their interest to be deceived by shallow boasting, and contrives not to hurt their self-love by sterling acquirements. Do you suppose that the understood translation of Thucydides costs its supposed author nothing? A select party of friends and admirers dine with him once a week at a magnificent town mansion, or a more elegant and picturesque retreat in the country. They broach their Horace and their old hock, and sometimes allude with a considerable degree of candour to the defects of works which are brought out by contemporary writers﻿—the ephemeral offspring of haste and necessity!

===Chinese===

于是，这班游手好闲的冒牌人物，害怕的是同自己从未做过、却享着做过之名的事情来一番比较。他们的名声不是挣来的，是摆出来的；他们从不走出那副威严而神秘的隐姓埋名，所以永远不会露馅。他们决不拿日常的活计贬低自己：对他们来说，付梓印行是分外之事，一如对公卿帝王；他们像坐拥大片地产的绅士，靠既立的名分过活，对这名分，则尽可能地无所增减。世上再没有比这更处心积虑的、板着脸的招摇撞骗了。我认得一位这一流的人物，多年来（就默认而言）一直在从事一部修昔底德（Thucydides）的译本，谁也没见过其中一个字，但这份差事照样替他撑起一份人为的名声。事情拖得越久、越是藏得远远的不许俗眼窥看，它在想象中便膨胀得越有分量；这样一部著作，所需的辛劳与用心自然是巨大的；——况且，一部没有动工的译本里，是找不出毛病来的。唯一全无瑕疵的作家，是从没写过的那些。另一位是鉴赏与古典学问方面的神谕，因为他（至少他自己说）每年通读一遍西塞罗（Cicero），以保持他拉丁文的纯正。第三位拿他的不成体统冒充他研究的深度、冒充他对古物（virtu）的高级趣味，直到——由于他在古代艺术最精美的遗迹里看不出任何东西——世人碰巧之至地发现：他肚子里本来就没有任何东西。一张板起的脸、一副莫测高深的做派，几乎没有办不成的事；凡是糊涂到能骗过自己的人，也就聪明到足以骗过公众——尤其倘若他能叫公众觉得受浅薄大话的欺骗于己有利，又能小心不叫真才实学伤了他们的自尊。你以为那部传说中的修昔底德译本，不曾教它传说中的作者破费分文么？一伙精选的朋友与崇拜者，每周一次在他城里的华宅、或乡下更雅致如画的别业里同他共餐。他们开他的贺拉斯（Horace）和陈年莱茵酒，有时还带着相当可观的坦率，议论当代作家们抛出的著作的种种缺陷——那些仓促与穷迫生出的朝生暮死的产品！

===Original===

Among other things, the learned languages are a ready passport to this sort of unmeaning, unanalysed reputation. They presently lift a man up among the celestial constellations, the signs of the zodiac (as it were) and third heaven of inspiration, from whence he looks down on those who are toiling on in this lower sphere, and earning their bread by the sweat of their brain, at leisure and in scorn. If the graduates in this way condescend to express their thoughts in English, it is understood to be *infra dignitatem*﻿—such light and unaccustomed essays do not fit the ponderous gravity of their pen﻿—they only draw to advantage and with full justice to themselves in the bow of the ancients. Their native tongue is to them strange, inelegant, unapt, and crude. They “cannot command it to any utterance of harmony. They have not the skill.” This is true enough; but you must not say so, under a heavy penalty﻿—the displeasure of pedants and blockheads. It would be sacrilege against the privileged classes, the Aristocracy of Letters. What! will you affirm that a profound Latin scholar, a perfect Grecian, cannot write a page of common sense or grammar? Is it not to be presumed, by all the charters of the Universities and the foundations of grammar-schools, that he who can speak a dead language must be *a fortiori* conversant with his own? Surely the greater implies the less. He who knows every science and every art cannot be ignorant of the most familiar forms of speech. Or if this plea is found not to hold water, then our scholastic bungler is said to be above this vulgar trial of skill, “something must be excused to want of practice﻿—but did you not observe the elegance of the Latinity, how well that period would become a classical and studied dress?” Thus defects are “monster’d” into excellences, and they screen their idol, and require you, at your peril, to pay prescriptive homage to false concords and inconsequential criticisms, because the writer of them has the character of the first or second Greek or Latin scholar in the kingdom. If you do not swear to the truth of these spurious credentials, you are ignorant and malicious, a quack and a scribbler﻿—*flagranti delicto*!

===Chinese===

在诸多事物之中，古典语言正是通往这种不知所云、无人细究的名声的一纸现成护照。它们立刻把一个人举上天界的星座、黄道的宫宿（不妨这样说）和灵感的第三重天，他从此居高临下，带着闲暇与轻蔑，俯视那些在下界辛苦跋涉、凭脑门的汗水挣面包的人。这一路的学位得主倘若肯屈尊用英语表达思想，那便被看作*有失身份*（infra dignitatem）——这样轻巧而生疏的试笔，配不上他们笔端的凝重庄严——他们唯有借古人的弓，才能画出自身，画得公道。母语在他们手里生疏、粗野、钝拙、生硬。他们“无法命令它说出任何和谐之音。他们没有那份技艺。”这话倒也不假；只是你万万说不得，说了便要重罚——触怒迂夫子与蠢材。那是对特权阶级、对文坛贵族的亵渎。什么！你竟敢断言，一位精深的拉丁学者、一位十全的希腊学家，写不出一页通顺的常识、合式的文法？凭大学的一切特许状、文法学校的一切基业，难道不该推定：会说死语言的人必定*更遑论*熟谙自己的语言？大者当然包含小者。通晓每一门科学、每一门艺术的人，总不至于连最寻常的说话方式也不会罢。倘若这层辩护理由站不住，人们便又替我们这位学界的笨伯说，他是不屑于这种通俗的技艺比试——“总要体谅他缺乏练习——可你难道没注意到那段拉丁文多么典雅，那个句子若换上古典而讲究的衣装该多么相称？”于是缺陷被“吹”成了长处；他们护住自己的偶像，要你冒着自己的危险，向假的一致关系、向文不对题的批评照例致敬，因为写出它们的人，有着干国第一或第二的希腊、拉丁学者的名头。你若不肯对这纸伪证起誓，你便是无知而恶毒，是江湖郎中、是无聊写手——*当场拿获*！

===Original===

Thus the man who can merely read and construe some old author is of a class superior to any living one, and, by parity of reasoning, to those old authors themselves: the poet or prose-writer of true and original genius, by the courtesy of custom, “ducks to the learned fool”; or, as the author of *Hudibras* has so well stated the same thing﻿—

> “He that is but able to express

No sense at all in several languages,

Will pass for learneder than he that’s known

To speak the strongest reason in his own.”

These preposterous and unfounded claims of mere scholars to precedence in the commonwealth of letters which they set up so formally themselves and which others so readily bow to, are partly owing to traditional prejudice: there was a time when learning was the only distinction from ignorance, and when there was no such thing as popular English literature. Again, there is something more palpable and positive in this kind of acquired knowledge, like acquired wealth, which the vulgar easily recognise. That others know the meaning of signs which they are confessedly and altogether ignorant of is to them both a matter of fact and a subject of endless wonder. The languages are worn like a dress by a man, and distinguish him sooner than his natural figure; and we are, from motives of self-love, inclined to give others credit for the ideas they have borrowed or have come into indirect possession of, rather than for those that originally belong to them and are exclusively their own. The merit in them and the implied inferiority in ourselves is less. Learning is a kind of external appendage or transferable property﻿—

> “ ’Twas mine, ’tis his, and may be any man’s.”

===Chinese===

于是，一个仅仅能读能解某位古人的人，便属于一个高于一切今人的阶级，而且照此推理，也高于那些古人自己：真正而有独创性的天才（Genius）诗人或散文家，承习俗之雅意，要向有学问的傻子“打躬”；或者，如《休迪布拉斯》的作者把同一件事说得那样好——

> “谁若能用好几种语言，

> 表达的全是不知所云，

> 便被当作比那人更有学问：

> 那人素来只用母语，

> 说出的道理最有力不过。”

单凭学问的人在文学共和国里要求的优先权——他们自己立得那样郑重，旁人又俯首得那样爽快——这些荒谬而毫无根据的声索，一部分要归因于传统的成见：曾有一个时代，学问是与愚昧相区别的唯一标识，那时还不存在通俗的英国文学这回事。再者，这一类后得的知识，如同后得的财富，有某种更着实、更具体的东西，庸众一望便知。旁人懂得那些符号的意义，而他们自己则自认全然不懂——这在他们既是事实，又是无穷惊叹的题目。语言像一件衣裳穿在人身上，比他本来的身段更早地把他标别出来；而出于自爱的动机，我们总乐于把旁人借来的、或辗转得来的观念记在旁人功劳簿上，却不肯承认那原本属于他们、独独属于他们的东西。那样，他们的功德与我们自认的低一等，都来得少些。学问是一种身外的附加物，一份可转让的财产——

> “从前是我的，如今是他的，也可能归任何人。”

===Original===

Genius and understanding are a man’s self, an integrant part of his personal identity; and the title to these last, as it is the most difficult to be ascertained, is also the most grudgingly acknowledged. Few persons would pretend to deny that Porson had more Greek than they; it was a question of fact which might be put to the immediate proof, and could not be gainsaid; but the meanest frequenter of the Cider Cellar or the Hole in the Wall would be inclined, in his own conceit, to dispute the palm of wit or sense with him, and indemnify his self-complacency for the admiration paid to living learning by significant hints to friends and casual droppers-in, that the greatest men, when you came to know them, were not without their weak sides as well as others. Pedants, I will add here, talk to the vulgar as pedagogues talk to schoolboys, on an understood principle of condescension and superiority, and therefore make little progress in the knowledge of men or things. While they fancy they are accommodating themselves to, or else assuming airs of importance over, inferior capacities, these inferior capacities are really laughing at them. There can be no true superiority but what arises out of the presupposed ground of equality: there can be no improvement but from the free communication and comparing of ideas. Kings and nobles, for this reason, receive little benefit from society﻿—where all is submission on one side, and condescension on the other. The mind strikes out truth by collision, as steel strikes fire from the flint!
There are whole families who are born classical, and are entered in the heralds’ college of reputation by the right of consanguinity. Literature, like nobility, runs in the blood. There is the Burney family. There is no end of it or its pretensions. It produces wits, scholars, novelists, musicians, artists in “numbers numberless.” The name is alone a passport to the Temple of Fame. Those who bear it are free of Parnassus by birthright. The founder of it was himself an historian and a musician, but more of a courtier and man of the world than either. The secret of his success may perhaps be discovered in the following passage, where, in alluding to three eminent performers on different instruments, he says: “These three illustrious personages were introduced at the Emperor’s court,” etc.

He towers above his fellows by all the height of the peerage. If the poet lends a grace to the nobleman, the nobleman pays it back to the poet with interest. What a fine addition is ten thousand a year and a title to the flaunting pretensions of a modern rhapsodist! His name so accompanied becomes the mouth well: it is repeated thousands of times, instead of hundreds, because the reader in being familiar with the Poet’s works seems to claim acquaintance with the Lord.

He smiles at the high-flown praise or petty cavils of little men. Does he make a slip in decorum, which Milton declares to be the principal thing? His proud crest and armorial bearings support him: no bend-sinister slurs his poetical escutcheon! Is he dull, or does he put of some trashy production on the public? It is not charged to his account, as a deficiency which he must make good at the peril of his admirers. His Lordship is not answerable for the negligence or extravagances of his Muse. He “bears a charmed reputation, which must not yield” like one of vulgar birth. The Noble Bard is for this reason scarcely vulnerable to the critics. The double barrier of his pretensions baffles their puny, timid efforts. Strip off some of his tarnished laurels, and the coronet appears glittering beneath: restore them, and it still shines through with keener lustre. In fact, his Lordship’s blaze of reputation culminates from his rank and place in society. He sustains two lofty and imposing characters; and in order to simplify the process of our admiration, and “leave no rubs or botches in the way,” we equalise his pretensions, and take it for granted that he must be as superior to other men in genius as he is in birth. Or, to give a more familiar solution of the enigma, the Poet and the Peer agree to honour each other’s acceptances on the bank of Fame, and sometimes cozen the town to some tune between them. Really, however, and with all his privileges, Lord Byron might as well not have written that strange letter about Pope. I could not afford it, poor as I am. Why does he pronounce, *ex cathedra* and robed, that Cowper is no poet? Cowper was a gentleman and of noble family like his critic. He was a teacher of morality as well as a describer of nature, which is more than his Lordship is. His *John Gilpin* will last as long as “Beppo,” and his verses to Mary are not less touching than the “Farewell.” If I had ventured upon such an assertion as this, it would have been worse for me than finding out a borrowed line in the “Pleasures of Hope.”
There is not a more helpless or more despised animal than a mere author, without any extrinsic advantages of birth, breeding, or fortune to set him off. The real ore of talents or learning must be stamped before it will pass current.

To be at all looked upon as an author, a man must be something more or less than an author﻿—a rich merchant, a banker, a lord, or a ploughman. He is admired for something foreign to himself, that acts as a bribe to the servility or a set-off to the envy of the community. “What should such fellows as we do, crawling betwixt heaven and earth”;﻿—“coining our hearts for drachmas”; now scorched in the sun, now shivering in the breeze, now coming out in our newest gloss and best attire, like swallows in the spring, now “sent back like hollowmas or shortest day”? Instead of this set of Grub Street authors, the mere *canaille* of letters, this corporation of Mendicity, this ragged regiment of genius suing at the corners of streets in *forma pauperis*, give me the gentleman and scholar, with a good house over his head and a handsome table “with wine of Attic taste” to ask his friends to, and where want and sorrow never come. Fill up the sparkling bowl; heap high the dessert with roses crowned; bring out the hot-pressed poem, the vellum manuscripts, the medals, the portfolios, the intaglios﻿—this is the true model of the life of a man of taste and *virtu*﻿—the possessors, not the inventors of these things, are the true benefactors of mankind and ornaments of letters. Look in, and there, amidst silver services and shining chandeliers, you will see the man of genius at his proper post, picking his teeth and mincing an opinion, sheltered by rank, bowing to wealth﻿—a poet framed, glazed, and hung in a striking light; not a straggling weed, torn and trampled on; not a poor *Kit-run-the-street*, but a powdered beau, a sycophant plant, an exotic reared in a glass case, hermetically sealed,

Unless an author has all establishment of his own, or is entered on that of some other person, he will hardly be allowed to write English or to spell his own name. To be well spoken of, he must enlist under some standard; he must belong to some coterie. He must get the *esprit de corps* on his side: he must have literary bail in readiness. Thus they prop up one another’s rickety heads at Murray’s shop, and a spurious reputation, like false argument, runs in a circle. Croker affirms that Gifford is sprightly, and Gifford that Croker is genteel; Disraeli that Jacob is wise, and Jacob that Disraeli is good-natured. A Member of Parliament must be answerable that you are not dangerous or dull before you can be of the entrée. You must commence toad-eater to have your observations attended to; if you are independent, unconnected, you will be regarded as a poor creature. Your opinion is honest, you will say; then ten to one it is not profitable. It is at any rate your own. So much the worse; for then it is not the world’s. Tom Hill is a very tolerable barometer in this respect. He knows nothing, hears everything, and repeats just what he hears; so that you may guess pretty well from this round-faced echo what is said by others! Almost everything goes by presumption and appearances. “Did you not think Mr. B﻿—﻿—’s language very elegant?”﻿—I thought he bowed very low. “Did you not think him remarkably well-behaved?”﻿—He was unexceptionably dressed. “But were not Mr. C﻿—﻿—’s manners quite insinuating?”﻿—He said nothing. “You will at least allow his friend to be a well-informed man.”﻿—talked upon all subjects alike. Such would be a pretty faithful interpretation of the tone of what is called “good society.” The surface is everything; we do not pierce to the core. The setting is more valuable than the jewel. Is it not so in other things as well as letters? Is not an R.A. by the supposition a greater man in his profession than anyone who is not so blazoned? Compared with that unrivalled list, Raphael had been illegitimate, Claude not classical, and Michelangelo admitted by special favour. What is a physician without a diploma? An alderman without being knighted? An actor whose name does not appear in great letters? All others are counterfeits﻿—men “of no mark or likelihood.”

We find a class of persons who labour under an obvious natural inaptitude for whatever they aspire to. Their manner of setting about it is a virtual disqualification. The simple affirmation, “What this man has said, I will do,” is not always considered as the proper test of capacity. On the contrary, there are people whose bare pretensions are as good or better than the actual performance of others. What I myself have done, for instance, I never find admitted as proof of what I shall be able to do: whereas I observe others who bring as proof of their competence to any task (and are taken at their word) what they have never done, and who gravely assure those who are inclined to trust them that their talents are exactly fitted for some post because they are just the reverse of what they have ever shown them to be. One man has the air of an editor as much as another has that of a butler or porter in a gentleman’s family. —﻿—﻿— is the model of this character, with a prodigious look of business, an air of suspicion which passes for sagacity, and an air of deliberation which passes for judgment. If his own talents are no ways prominent, it is inferred he will be more impartial and in earnest in making use of those of others. There is Britton, the responsible conductor of several works of taste and erudition, yet (God knows) without an idea in his head relating to any one of them. He is learned by proxy, and successful from sheer imbecility. If he were to get the smallest smattering of the departments which are under his control, he would betray himself from his desire to shine; but as it is, he leaves others to do all the drudgery for him. He signs his name in the title-page or at the bottom of a vignette, and nobody suspects any mistake. This contractor for useful and ornamental literature once offered me two guineas for a *Life and Character of Shakespeare*, with an admission to his *converzationi*. I went once.

===Chinese===

正因为如此，“北方的豺狼们”才那样起劲地想证明我已被《爱丁堡评论》扫地出门。惹他们恼恨的，不是那些文章的长处，而是文章登在那里。文风，他们一无所知；思想，他们毫不在意：他们知道的只是我在那家有势力的刊物上写稿——所以他们便一口咬定我没有！
我们见到一类人，对凡是他们心存觊觎的事，都怀着一种显而易见的天生的不称职。他们着手的方式本身就是一纸不合格的证明。“人家做过的事，我也做得到”——这样简单的自陈，并不总被当作能力的正当考验。恰恰相反，有些人光凭一口空话，就顶得上、还胜过旁人实实做出的成绩。譬如我自己做过的事，从不被承认为我将来能做什么的凭据；而我看旁人拿他们从未做过的事来担保自己什么都能做（居然还被人当真），还一本正经地向那些打算信他们的人保证：他们的才具恰好胜任某个职位，因为它恰恰同他们历来显露的东西相反。一个人有主编的气派，正如另一个人有绅士家总管或门房的气派。———先生正是这种性格的典范：一副不得了的事务神气，一脸疑虑——那被当作精明，一脸从容——那被当作决断。倘若他本人的才具毫不出众，人们便推断他使用旁人才具时反而更公正、更认真。还有布里顿，好几部风雅与博学之作的名义主持者，然而（天知道）他脑袋里同其中任何一部有关的思想一个也没有。他的学问是代理的，他的成功全凭彻底的低能。他但凡对经管的门类沾上一星半点，就会因急于露脸而露馅；但如今这样，他便把苦活脏活一概留给旁人做。他在扉页上、或小花饰底下签上名字，谁也不疑心有什么差错。这位有用而体面文学的包工头，有一次出两几尼的稿酬，要我写一部《莎士比亚（Shakespeare）的生平与品格》，附带请我出席他的“文艺座谈”（converzationi）。我去过一回。

===Original===

There was a collection of learned lumber, of antiquaries, lexicographers, and other “illustrious obscure,” and I had given up the day for lost, when in dropped Jack Taylor of the *Sun*﻿—(who would dare to deny that he was “the Sun of our table”?)﻿—and I had nothing now to do but hear and laugh. Mr. Taylor knows most of the good things that have been said in the metropolis for the last thirty years, and is in particular an excellent retailer of the humours and extravagances of his old friend Peter Pindar. He had recounted a series of them, each rising above the other in a sort of magnificent burlesque and want of literal preciseness, to a medley of laughing and sour faces, when on his proceeding to state a joke of a practical nature by the said Peter, a Mr. —﻿—﻿— (I forget the name) objected to the moral of the story, and to the whole texture of Mr. Taylor’s facetiae﻿—upon which our host, who had till now supposed that all was going on swimmingly, thought it time to interfere and give a turn to the conversation by saying, “Why, yes, gentlemen, what we have hitherto heard fall from the lips of our friend has been no doubt entertaining and highly agreeable in its way; but perhaps we have had enough of what is altogether delightful and pleasant and light and laughable in conduct. Suppose, therefore, we were to shift the subject, and talk of what is serious and moral and industrious and laudable in character﻿—Let us talk of Mr. Tomkins the Penman!”﻿—This staggered the gravest of us, broke up our dinner-party, and we went upstairs to tea. So much for the didactic vein of one of our principal guides in the embellished walks of modern taste, and master manufacturers of letters. He had found that gravity had been a never-failing resource when taken at a pinch﻿—for once the joke miscarried﻿—and Mr. Tomkins the Penman figures to this day nowhere but in Sir Joshua’s picture of him!
To complete the natural Aristocracy of Letters, we only want a Royal Society of Authors!

===Chinese===

满座是一堆学问的杂木：古物家、词典家，还有别的“显赫的无名氏”；这一天使我认定是白费了，不想《太阳报》的杰克·泰勒飘然而至——（谁敢否认他是“我们餐桌上的太阳”呢？）——从此我便只消听着、笑着。泰勒先生记得京城三十年来流传的绝大多数妙语，尤其是他老友彼得·平达的谐趣与狂态的一位上好的转述人。他正讲着一连串，每一桩比前一桩更高妙，带着一种壮丽的滑稽与不拘字句的精确，讲给一片有笑有酸的脸听；当他要接着讲那位彼得的一桩实用性质的玩笑时，一位———先生（我忘了名字）对故事的寓意、对泰勒先生笑谈的整个格调提出了异议——于是我们的主人，他直到此刻还以为一切都进行得顺顺当当，觉得该出面把话头转一转了，便说：“呃，是啊，诸位，方才从我们朋友唇边听来的种种，无疑自成一路地有趣、极为可喜；不过，纯乎是快意的、好听的、轻松的、好笑的行事，我们或许听得够了。不如换个题目，谈谈品性中严肃的、道德的、勤勉的、可敬的一面吧——让我们来谈谈缮写员汤姆金斯先生！”——这话把我们在场最持重的人都惊得站立不稳，宴席就此散了，我们上楼喝茶去了。这位现代风雅幽径上的主要向导之一、文学制造业的大师傅，其教训的笔调，不过如此。他早发现，情急之时摆出一副道学面孔是万试万灵的灵药——只是这一回玩笑演砸了——缮写员汤姆金斯先生至今只在一个地方露面：乔舒亚爵士画的那张像里！
要凑齐这天然的文坛贵族，我们只差一所皇家作家协会了！

### On the Disadvantages of Intellectual Superiority / 论智力超群的弊害
===Original===

The chief disadvantage of knowing more and seeing farther than others, is not to be generally understood. A man is, in consequence of this, liable to start paradoxes, which immediately transport him beyond the reach of the commonplace reader. A person speaking once in a slighting manner of a very original-minded man, received for answer, “He strides on so far before you that he dwindles in the distance!”
Petrarch complains that “Nature had made him different from other people”﻿—*singular’ d’ altri genti.* The great happiness of life is, to be neither better nor worse than the general run of those you meet with. If you are beneath them, you are trampled upon; if you are above them, you soon find a mortifying level in their difference to what you particularly pique yourself upon. What is the use of being moral in a night-cellar, or wise in Bedlam? “To be honest, as this world goes, is to be one man picked out of ten thousand.” So says Shakespeare; and the commentators have not added that, under these circumstances, a man is more likely to become the butt of slander than the mark of admiration for being so. “How now, thou particular fellow?”83 is the common answer to all such out-of-the-way pretensions. By not doing as those at Rome do, we cut ourselves off from good-fellowship and society. We speak another language, have notions of our own, and are treated as of a different species. Nothing can be more awkward than to intrude with any such far-fetched ideas among the common herd, who will be sure to

> “Stand all astonished, like a sort of steers,

’Mongst whom some beast of strange and foreign race

Unwares is chanced, far straying from his peers:

So will their ghastly gaze betray their hidden fears.”

===Chinese===

比旁人知道得多、看得远的主要坏处，是不被一般人所理解。一个人因此动辄抛出些奇论，一下子便把自己送到了寻常读者够不着的地方。有人曾以轻蔑的口气议论一位极有创见的人，得到的回答是：“他在你们前头跨得太远，远得在天边缩成了一个小点！”
彼特拉克（Petrarch）抱怨说，“自然（Nature）造得他与旁人不同”——*异于众族的人*（singular' d' altri genti）。人生的大幸福，是同你遇到的那一船人比，既不好些、也不坏些。你若在他们之下，便遭践踏；你若在他们之上，那么在你独自矜夸的那些地方，他们与你的悬隔很快便成了一件教你难堪的事。在夜半的地窖酒馆里讲道德，在疯人院里讲智慧，有什么用处？“照这世道的情形，诚实，是万人中挑出来的人。”莎士比亚（Shakespeare）如是说；而评注家们没有补充：在这种情形之下，一个人为此更可能成为诽谤的靶子，而不是钦佩的对象。“喂，你这个各别的人怎么着？”83——对一切这类出格的才具，这是通常的回答。不入乡随俗，我们便把自己逐出了交谊与社会。我们说着另一种语言，怀着自家的一套念头，被当作另一个物种对待。再没有比带着这类迂远的见解闯进芸芸众堆里更尴尬的了，众人必定——

> “全都怔住，像一群牛，

> 当中误闯进了一头异邦的怪兽，

> 离群走失，混在它们中间：

> 于是它们惨白的目光，泄出心底的惊惶。”

===Original===

Ignorance of another’s meaning is a sufficient cause of fear, and fear produces hatred: hence the suspicion and rancour entertained against all those who set up for greater refinement and wisdom than their neighbours. It is in vain to think of softening down this spirit of hostility by simplicity of manners, or by condescending to persons of low estate. The more you condescend, the more they will presume upon it; they will fear you less, but hate you more; and will be the more determined to take their revenge on you for a superiority as to which they are entirely in the dark, and of which you yourself seem to entertain considerable doubt. All the humility in the world will only pass for weakness and folly. They have no notion of such a thing. They always put their best foot forward; and argue that you would do the same if you had any such wonderful talents as people say. You had better, therefore, play off the great man at once﻿—hector, swagger, talk big, and ride the high horse over them: you may by this means extort outward respect or common civility; but you will get nothing (with low people) by forbearance and good-nature but open insult or silent contempt. Coleridge always talks to people about what they don’t understand: I, for one, endeavour to talk to them about what they do understand, and find I only get the more ill-will by it. They conceive I do not think them capable of anything better; that I do not think it worth while, as the vulgar saying is, to “throw a word to a dog.” I once complained of this to Coleridge, thinking it hard I should be sent to Coventry for not making a prodigious display. He said: “As you assume a certain character, you ought to produce your credentials. It is a tax upon people’s good-nature to admit superiority of any kind, even where there is the most evident proof of it; but it is too hard a task for the imagination to admit it without any apparent ground at all.”
There is not a greater error than to suppose that you avoid the envy, malice, and uncharitableness, so common in the world, by going among people without pretensions. There are no people who have no pretensions; or the fewer their pretensions, the less they can afford to acknowledge yours without some sort of value received.

===Chinese===

不懂旁人的意思，便是恐惧的一个充分原因，而恐惧生出仇恨：于是，凡自命比邻居更高雅、更明智的人，一概遭到猜疑与怨毒。想靠举止的平易、靠屈尊俯就地对待下层人来化解这股敌意，是徒劳的。你越屈尊，他们越放肆；他们对你的惧怕少了，恨却多了；并且越发打定主意，要为一项他们全然不明就里、连你本人似乎也颇有疑虑的优越向你报复。世上一切谦卑，只会被当作软弱与愚蠢。他们没有这种东西的概念。他们向来只把最好的脚伸在前头；他们认定，你若真像人们说的那样怀有不世之才，你也一定会这样做。所以你索性立刻摆出大人物来——咆哮、吹嘘、说大话、跨在他们头上作威作福：这样你倒或许能榨出一点表面的尊敬或寻常的客气；但对待下等人，你的克制与好心换来的，除了公然的侮辱，便是无声的轻蔑。柯尔律治同人们谈的，尽是他们不懂的东西；我呢，努力同他们谈他们懂的东西，却发现只落得更多的怨恨。他们以为我看死了他们拿不出更好的东西；以为照俗话说的，我不屑“赏狗一句话”。有一次我为此向柯尔律治诉苦，说不曾大展身手就被打入冷宫，实在冤枉。他说：“你既然摆出了一定的身份，就该拿出你的证件来。承认任何一种优越，都是对人们好心的一重课税，哪怕有最显明的凭据也是如此；若要他们毫无凭据地凭空承认，那想象力实在担当不起。”
以为混在没有声索的人们中间，就能躲开世间习见的嫉妒、恶毒与刻薄，再没有比这更大的错误了。没有一个人是没有声索的；或者说，声索越少的人，越要得了点好处，才承认得起你的声索。

===Original===

The more information individuals possess, or the more they have refined upon any subject, the more readily can they conceive and admit the same kind of superiority to themselves that they feel over others. But from the low, dull, level sink of ignorance and vulgarity, no idea or love of excellence can arise. You think you are doing mighty well with them; that you are laying aside the buckram of pedantry and pretence, and getting the character of a plain, unassuming, good sort of fellow. It will not do. All the while that you are making these familiar advances, and wanting to be at your ease, they are trying to recover the wind of you. You may forget that you are an author, an artist, or whatnot﻿—they do not forget that they are nothing, nor bate one jot of their desire to prove you in the same predicament. They take hold of some circumstance in your dress; your manner of entering a room is different from that of other people; you do not eat vegetables﻿—that’s odd; you have a particular phrase, which they repeat, and this becomes a sort of standing joke; you look grave, or ill; you talk, or are more silent than usual; you are in or out of pocket: all these petty, inconsiderable circumstances, in which you resemble, or are unlike other people, form so many counts in the indictment which is going on in their imaginations against you, and are so many contradictions in your character. In anyone else they would pass unnoticed, but in a person of whom they had heard so much they cannot make them out at all. Meanwhile, those things in which you may really excel go for nothing, because they cannot judge of them. They speak highly of some book which you do not like, and therefore you make no answer. You recommend them to go and see some picture in which they do not find much to admire. How are you to convince them that you are right? Can you make them perceive that the fault is in them, and not in the picture, unless you could give them your knowledge? They hardly distinguish the difference between a Correggio and a common daub. Does this bring you any nearer to an understanding?

===Chinese===

一个人的见识越多，或对某一题目钻研得越精，便越容易设想并承认那种他们自己凌驾于旁人时感到的优越，也会落到自己头上。而从愚昧与粗俗那低洼沉闷的洼地里，生不出对卓越的任何概念或爱慕。你自以为同他们处得极好：脱下了迂腐与做作的硬衬，得了个直白、谦和、好好先生的名声。这是行不通的。你这边一路亲热凑近、想随意自在，他们那边却在设法抢你的上风头。你尽可以忘了自己是作家、是艺术家、是什么人物——他们可忘不了自己什么也不是，也一分不减地想证明你同他们一样。他们抓住你衣着的某个细节不放；你进屋的姿势与旁人不同；你不吃素——这就怪了；你有个口头禅，他们学着说，从此成了一桩保留节目；你脸色沉，或是气色不好；你话多了，或是比平常更沉默；你手头宽了，或是紧了：这一干琐屑的小事——你与旁人相像或不相像的地方——都在他们心里那篇控诉你的状子上记下一款，也都是你性格上的一重矛盾。这些事换在旁人身上，根本无人理会；可在这个他们久闻大名的人身上，他们就全然想不通了。与此同时，你真正出众的那些地方一钱不值，因为他们无从判断。他们盛赞某本书，你不喜欢，便不答话。你推荐他们去看一幅画，他们却看不出有什么可赞美之处。你怎么说服他们你是对的呢？你能叫他们觉出毛病在他们、不在画么——除非你能把你的学问整个儿给他们？他们连柯勒乔（Correggio）与一幅寻常涂鸦的区别都分辨不出。这可让你离互相了解更近了一步么？

===Original===

The more you know of the difference, the more deeply you feel it, or the more earnestly you wish to convey it, the farther do you find yourself removed to an immeasurable distance from the possibility of making them enter into views and feelings of which they have not even the first rudiments. You cannot make them see with your eyes, and they must judge for themselves.
Intellectual is not like bodily strength. You have no hold of the understanding of others but by their sympathy. Your knowing, in fact, so much more about a subject does not give you a superiority, that is, a power over them, but only renders it the more impossible for you to make the least impression on them. Is it, then, an advantage to you? It may be, as it relates to your own private satisfaction, but it places a greater gulf between you and society. It throws stumbling-blocks in your way at every turn. All that you take most pride and pleasure in is lost upon the vulgar eye. What they are pleased with is a matter of indifference or of distaste to you. In seeing a number of persons turn over a portfolio of prints from different masters, what a trial it is to the patience, how it jars the nerves to hear them fall into raptures at some commonplace flimsy thing, and pass over some divine expression of countenance without notice, or with a remark that it is very singular-looking? How useless it is in such cases to fret or argue, or remonstrate? Is it not quite as well to be without all this hypercritical, fastidious knowledge, and to be pleased or displeased as it happens, or struck with the first fault or beauty that is pointed out by others? I would be glad almost to change my acquaintance with pictures, with books, and, certainly, what I know of mankind, for anybody’s ignorance of them!
It is recorded in the life of some worthy (whose name I forget) that he was one of those “who loved hospitality and respect”: and I profess to belong to the same classification of mankind. Civility is with me a jewel. I like a little comfortable cheer, and careless, indolent chat, I hate to be always wise, or aiming at wisdom. I have enough to do with literary cabals, questions, critics, actors, essay-writing, without taking them out with me for recreation, and into all companies. I wish at these times to pass for a good-humoured fellow; and goodwill is all I ask in return to make good company.

===Chinese===

你对这种差别知道得越多、感受得越深、或越急于把它传达出去，你便发现自己离“使他们领会”的可能隔着无限远：那些见解与感受，他们连最初的入门也没有。你不能叫他们用你的眼睛看，而他们又必须自己判断。
智力不比膂力。你把握旁人的理解力，唯有靠他们的同情。事实上，你在某门学问上多懂的那些，并不给你优越——也就是支配他们的权力——只是叫你愈发连最浅的一点印象也打不到他们心上。那么，这于你还算一桩好处么？就你一己的满足而言或许是；但它在你与社会之间掘下了更深的鸿沟。它一路上处处给你放绊脚石。你最为之骄傲、最为之欢喜的一切，在俗眼看来尽付东流。他们中意的东西，在你不是无关痛痒，便是倒胃口的滋事。看一群人翻检一夹子各家大师的版画，听他们对着某件平庸轻飘的东西如醉如痴，对某副天神般的面容却视若无睹、或评一句“样子很怪”，这是对耐性怎样的煎熬，怎样地硌人的神经！在这种场合，烦躁、争论、劝导，何济于事？全没有这一身挑剔苛细的学问，随遇而喜、随遇而厌，人家指出第一处毛病或好处来便惊叹领受，岂不也一样好、或者更好？我几乎情愿拿我对绘画、对书籍的修养——当然，还有我对人性的那点了解——去换随便哪个人的对此一无所知！
某位贤者（名字我忘了）的生平里记载，他是“爱好款客与礼敬”的那类人：我自认也归属人类的同一门类。客气在我是一件珠宝。我爱一点舒舒服服的小酌，一点无心无肺的闲聊；我恨老是做智者、老瞄着智慧不放。文字界的党争、论题、批评家、演员、写随笔，已经够我应付的了，我不想再带它们出去消遣，带进每一处人群。这种时候我只愿被当作一个好脾气的人；作为回报，我也只求人家报我以善意，好成一场好聚。

===Original===

I do not desire to be always posing myself or others with the questions of fate, free-will, foreknowledge absolute, etc. I must unbend sometimes. I must occasionally lie fallow. The kind of conversation that I affect most is what sort of a day it is, and whether it is likely to rain or hold up fine for tomorrow. This I consider as enjoying the *otium cum dignitate*, as the end and privilege of a life of study. I would resign myself to this state of easy indifference, but I find I cannot. I must maintain a certain pretension, which is far enough from my wish. I must he put on my defence, I must take up the gauntlet continually, or I find I lose ground. “I am nothing, if not critical.” While I am thinking what o’clock it is, or how I came to blunder in quoting a well-known passage, as if I had done it on purpose, others are thinking whether I am not really as dull a fellow as I am sometimes said to be. If a drizzling shower patters against the windows, it puts me in mind of a mild spring rain, from which I retired twenty years ago, into a little public-house near Wem in Shropshire, and while I saw the plants and shrubs before the door imbibe the dewy moisture, quaffed a glass of sparkling ale, and walked home in the dusk of evening, brighter to me than noonday suns at present are! Would I indulge this feeling? In vain. They ask me what news there is, and stare if I say I don’t know. If a new actress has come out, why must I have seen her? If a new novel has appeared, why must I have read it? I, at one time, used to go and take a hand at cribbage with a friend, and afterwards discuss a cold sirloin of beef, and throw out a few lackadaisical remarks, in a way to please myself, but it would not do long. I set up little pretension, and therefore the little that I did set up was taken from me. As I said nothing on that subject myself, it was continually thrown in my teeth that I was an author. From having me at this disadvantage, my friend wanted to peg on a hole or two in the game, and was displeased if I would not let him. If I won off him, it was hard he should be beat by an author. If he won, it would be strange if he did not understand the game better than I did. If I mentioned my favourite game of rackets, there was a general silence, as if this was my weak point. If I complained of being ill, it was asked why I made myself so.

===Chinese===

我不想老拿命运、自由意志、绝对的先知先觉这些问题来考问自己或旁人。我有时总得松弛松弛。我偶尔总得让地荒一茬。我最爱的谈话，是今天天气如何、明天会下雨还是放晴。我把这个当作享受*有尊严的闲暇*（otium cum dignitate），当作治学生涯的归宿与特权。我愿意把自己交给这种闲适无争的状态，却发现做不到。我必须撑着一定的架子，这同我的心愿相去甚远。我必须时时摆出防御的姿态，必须不断接下人家掷来的手套，不然我发现自己便节节败退。“我这个人，不挑剔便一文不值。”我这边正想着现在几点钟，或者想着怎么会把一段名言引岔了——引得仿佛是故意的——那边旁人正想着：我恐怕真是人家有时说的那种无趣的家伙。倘若一阵细雨敲打窗棂，我便想起二十年前一场温和的春雨，那时我躲进什罗普郡韦姆镇附近一家小酒店，看门前的花草灌木吸饮润泽的雨露，自己灌下一杯起沫的淡啤酒，趁暮色走回家去——那暮色，在我眼里比如今的正午太阳还亮堂！我想纵情在这份情怀里么？枉然。他们问我有什么新闻，我说不知道，他们便瞪眼。新出了个女演员，为什么我就一定看过？新出了本小说，为什么我就一定读过？有一阵子，我常去一位朋友家打克里比奇纸牌，随后切一块冷牛腰肉，懒懒地发几条议论，自得其乐，可这长不了。我本没摆什么架子，于是连我摆的那一点点也被夺走了。我自己从不提那一行，人家却动不动拿“你是个作家”堵我的嘴。朋友见我落在下风，便想在牌上再赢一两个孔，我不肯让，他就不高兴。我若赢了他，一个作家居然赢了他，实在说不过去。他若赢了，那他牌艺比我高，更是天经地义。我一提我心爱的墙网球，满座便一片沉默，仿佛这是我的软肋。我抱怨身体不好，人家便问：谁叫你把自己弄成这样的？

===Original===

If I said such an actor had played a part well, the answer was, there was a different account in one of the newspapers. If any allusion was made to men of letters, there was a suppressed smile. If I told a humorous story, it was difficult to say whether the laugh was at me or at the narrative. The wife hated me for my ugly face; the servants, because I could not always get them tickets for the play, and because they could not tell exactly what an author meant. If a paragraph appeared against anything I had written, I found it was ready there before me, and I was to undergo a regular *roasting*. I submitted to all this till I was tired, and then I gave it up.
One of the miseries of intellectual pretensions is, that nine-tenths of those you come in contact with do not know whether you are an impostor or not. I dread that certain anonymous criticisms should get into the hands of servants where I go, or that my hatter or shoemaker should happen to read them, who cannot possibly tell whether they are well or ill founded. The ignorance of the world leaves one at the mercy of its malice. There are people whose good opinion or goodwill you want, setting aside all literary pretensions; and it is hard to lose by an ill report (which you have no means of rectifying) what you cannot gain by a good one. After a diatribe in the *Quarterly* (which is taken in by a gentleman who occupies my old apartments on the first floor), my landlord brings me up his bill (of some standing), and on my offering to give him so much in money and a note of hand for the rest, shakes his head, and says he is afraid he could make no use of it. Soon after, the daughter comes in, and, on my mentioning the circumstance carelessly to her, replies gravely, “that indeed her father has been almost ruined by bills.” *This is the unkindest cut of all.* It is in vain for me to endeavour to explain that the publication in which I am abused is a mere government engine﻿—an organ of a political faction. They know nothing about that. They only know such and such imputations are thrown out; and the more I try to remove them, the more they think there is some truth in them. Perhaps the people of the house are strong Tories﻿—government agents of some sort. Is it for me to enlighten their ignorance?

===Chinese===

我说某位演员某个角色演得好，回答是：报纸上的说法不一样。话头一带到文人，便有人抿嘴一笑。我讲一个滑稽的故事，难说笑声是冲着我还是冲着故事。主妇恨我，因为我的脸丑；仆人们恨我，因为我不能老给他们弄到戏票，也因为他们摸不清作家到底是什么意思。只要登出一段攻讦我文字的短评，我发现它早已等在那里，我便要照例受一番*炮烙*。这一切我都忍着，忍到腻了，便不再去了。
智力上负有声索的一大苦处是：你交往的人里，十个有九个不知道你是不是个骗子。我怕某些匿名的批评文章落到我去的那家人家仆人手里，或者怕我的帽商、鞋商碰巧读到——他们根本无从判断那些话有根没根。世人的无知，把人交给世人的恶意去摆布。撇开一切文字上的声索，总有一些人，你是想要他们的好感与善意的；靠好评挣不来的东西，却会因为一纸你无从辩白的恶评而失去，这实在难堪。《每季评论》上骂过我一篇雄文之后（那刊物由住我原先二楼房间的一位绅士订阅），我的房东便把账单（积欠有些日子了）拿上来，我提出付一部分现钱、其余立一张字据，他直摇头，说恐怕用不上它。过后不久，女儿进来，我随口向她提起这事，她一本正经地答道：“可不，我爹就是叫字据害得差点儿破了产。”*这是最狠心的一刀。*我竭力解释：骂我的那家刊物不过是政府的机器——一个政治派别的喉舌。全是白费。他们不懂这些。他们只知道人家抛出了这样那样的罪名；我越想洗刷，他们越觉得事出有因。说不定这一家人还是死硬的托利党徒——某种政府的眼线呢。难道要我去启蒙他们的无知么？

===Original===

If I say, I once wrote a thing called *Prince Maurice’s Parrot*, and an *Essay on the Regal Character*, in the former of which allusion is made to a noble marquis, and in the latter to a great personage (so at least, I am told, it has been construed), and that Mr. Croker has peremptory instructions to retaliate, they cannot conceive what connection there can be between me and such distinguished characters. I can get no farther. Such is the misery of pretensions beyond your situation, and which are not backed by any external symbols of wealth or rank, intelligible to all mankind!
The impertinence of admiration is scarcely more tolerable than the demonstrations of contempt. I have known a person whom I had never seen before besiege me all dinnertime with asking what articles I had written in the *Edinburgh Review*? I was at last ashamed to answer to my splendid sins in that way. Others will pick out something not yours, and say they are sure no one else could write it. By the first sentence they can always tell your style. Now I hate my style to be known, as I hate all *idiosyncrasy*. These obsequious flatterers could not pay me a worse compliment. Then there are those who make a point of reading everything you write (which is fulsome); while others, more provoking, regularly lend your works to a friend as soon as they receive them. They pretty well know your notions on the different subjects, from having heard you talk about them. Besides, they have a greater value for your personal character than they have for your writings. You explain things better in a common way, when you are not aiming at effect. Others tell you of the faults they have heard found with your last book, and that they defend your style in general from a charge of obscurity. A friend once told me of a quarrel he had had with a near relation, who denied that I knew how to spell the commonest words. These are comfortable confidential communications to which authors who have their friends and excusers are subject. A gentleman told me that a lady had objected to my use of the word *learneder* as bad grammar. He said he thought it a pity that I did not take more care, but that the lady was perhaps prejudiced, as her husband held a government office. I looked for the word, and found it in a motto from Butler.

===Chinese===

倘若我说，我曾经写过一篇叫《莫里斯亲王的鹦鹉》的东西，又写过一篇《论帝王的品格》，前一篇里影射到一位尊贵的侯爵，后一篇里影射到一位大人物（至少人家告诉我，它是这样被解读的），而克罗克先生奉有严令要报复——他们便想不通，我这样的人同那等显赫人物之间能有什么干系。我就到此为止，再进不得一步。这就是声索越出自己身份、又没有全人类都看得懂的财富或门第的外在标记来撑腰的悲哀！
钦慕的无礼，几乎不比轻蔑的表演更可忍受。我认得一个人，素昧平生，一顿饭的工夫缠住我不放，问我《爱丁堡评论》上哪些文章是我写的？我到末了都不好意思一一招认我那些风光的罪过。另一些人专挑不是你的东西，说除了你谁也写不出来。凭头一句他们总能认出你的笔调。而我恨我的笔调被人认出，一如我恨一切*个人癖性*（idiosyncrasy）。这班胁肩谄媚之徒，再想不出更糟的恭维了。还有一种人，定要把你写的东西读个遍（腻死人）；另有更气人的一种，一收到你的书就按例借给朋友。你的各路见解，他们听你谈过，早摸得烂熟。再说，他们看重你的为人，胜过看重你的文章。你不刻意求效果的时候，用平常话说理反倒更明白。还有人告诉你，你上一本书被人挑出了什么毛病，又说他们如何替你的文笔辩护，顶住了“晦涩”的指控。一位朋友有回告诉我，他同一位近亲吵了一架，因为那位断言我连最普通的字都不会拼。这便是身边有朋友、有辩护士的作家们享受的贴心话。有位绅士告诉我，一位女士指责我用*learneder*这个词是文法错误。他说他觉得我不多加小心实在可惜，不过那位女士或许存有偏见，因为她丈夫在政府里当差。我查了查那个词，发现它出自巴特勒（Butler）的题词。

===Original===

I was piqued, and desired him to tell the fair critic that the fault was not in me, but in one who had far more wit, more learning, and loyalty than I could pretend to. Then, again, some will pick out the flattest thing of yours they can find to load it with panegyrics; and others tell you (by way of letting you see how high they rank your capacity) that your best passages are failures. Lamb has a knack of tasting (or as he would say, *palating*) the insipid. Leigh Hunt has a trick of turning away from the relishing morsels you put on his plate. There is no getting the start of some people. Do what you will, they can do it better; meet with what success you may, their own good opinion stands them in better stead, and runs before the applause of the world. I once showed a person of this overweening turn (with no small triumph, I confess) a letter of a very flattering description I had received from the celebrated Count Stendhal, dated Rome. He returned it with a smile of indifference, and said, he had had a letter from Rome himself the day before, from his friend S﻿—﻿—! I did not think this “germane to the matter.” Godwin pretends I never wrote anything worth a farthing but my answers to Vetus, and that I fail altogether when I attempt to write an essay, or anything in a short compass.
What can one do in such cases? Shall I confess a weakness? The only set-off I know to these rebuffs and mortifications is sometimes in an accidental notice or involuntary mark of distinction from a stranger. I feel the force of Horace’s *digito monstrari*﻿—I like to be pointed out in the street, or to hear people ask in Mr. Powell’s court, “Which is Mr. Hazlitt?” This is to me a pleasing extension of one’s personal identity. Your name so repeated leaves an echo like music on the ear: it stirs the blood like the sound of a trumpet. It shows that other people are curious to see you; that they think of you, and feel an interest in you without your knowing it. This is a bolster to lean upon; a lining to your poor, shivering, threadbare opinion of yourself. You want some such cordial to exhausted spirits, and relief to the dreariness of abstract speculation. You are something; and, from occupying a place in the thoughts of others, think less contemptuously of yourself. You are the better able to run the gauntlet of prejudice and vulgar abuse.

===Chinese===

我气不过，请他转告那位漂亮的批评家：错不在我，而在一位才思、学问、忠贞都远非我敢企及的人。再者，有些人专从你的文字里拣出最淡而无味的一篇，加以盛赞；另一些人则告诉你（好让你看看他们把你的才具摆在多高），你最好的段落其实是失败。兰姆（Lamb）有一种本领，专会品味（或者照他自己的说法，*尝调*〔palating〕）那淡乎寡味的。利·亨特（Leigh Hunt）有个习惯，你搁在他盘子里最有滋味的一箸，他偏要掉头不顾。有些人你永远抢不到他们前头去。你做什么，他们做得更好；你怎样成功，他们自家的好评也比全世界的掌声跑得更快、更顶用。我曾给一位这路自负的人物看（我承认，不无得意）一封大加揄扬的信，是那位大名鼎鼎的司汤达伯爵（Count Stendhal）从罗马写给我的。他把信递还我，淡淡一笑，说：他前天自己也从罗马收到了一封信，是他的朋友S——写的！我不觉得这与本题“有何相干”。葛德文（Godwin）一口咬定，我写的东西里，除了答复维图斯（Vetus）的那几篇，一便士也不值；还说我一动笔写随笔、写任何短章，便一败涂地。
这种时候有什么办法？要不要我招认一个弱点？据我所知，抵消这些冷遇与羞辱的，有时是陌生人偶然的注目、不由自主的敬意的表示。我领教过贺拉斯（Horace）那句*被手指指点*（digito monstrari）的分量——我喜欢在街上被人指认，喜欢在鲍威尔先生（Mr. Powell）的场子里听人问：“哪一位是哈兹里特先生（Mr. Hazlitt）？”这于我是一种愉快的自我身分的延展。你的名字这样被念着，在耳畔留下一缕乐音般的回响：它像号角一样催动血脉。这说明旁人好奇想见你；他们想着你，不知不觉对你有一份关切。这是一条可以倚靠的垫枕；给你那身寒碜打颤、捉襟见肘的自我评价衬一层里子。心力交瘁之时，你需要这样一杯提神酒；玄思的荒凉里，你需要这样一点排遣。你是个人物；因为在旁人的思虑里占了一个位置，你对自己的轻蔑便少了几分。你也更能挺身闯过偏见与流俗辱骂的那道夹鞭刑。

===Original===

It is pleasant in this way to have your opinion quoted against yourself, and your own sayings repeated to you as good things. I was once talking to an intelligent man in the pit, and criticising Mr. Knight’s performance of Filch. “Ah!” he said, “little Simmons was the fellow to play that character.” He added, “There was a most excellent remark made upon his acting it in the *Examiner* (I think it was)﻿—*That he looked as if he had the gallows in one eye and a pretty girl in the other.*” I said nothing, but was in remarkably good humour the rest of the evening. I have seldom been in a company where Fives-playing has been talked of, but someone has asked, in the course of it, “Pray, did anyone ever see an account of one Cavanagh that appeared some time back in most of the papers? Is it known who wrote it?” These are trying moments. I had a triumph over a person, whose name I will not mention, on the following occasion. I happened to be saying something about Burke, and was expressing my opinion of his talents in no measured terms, when this gentleman interrupted me by saying he thought, for his part, that Burke had been greatly overrated, and then added, in a careless way, “Pray, did you read a character of him in the last number of the —﻿—﻿—?” “I wrote it!”﻿—I could not resist the antithesis, but was afterwards ashamed of my momentary petulance. Yet no one that I find ever spares me.
Some persons seek out and obtrude themselves on public characters in order, as it might seem, to pick out their failings, and afterwards betray them. Appearances are for it, but truth and a better knowledge of nature are against this interpretation of the matter. Sycophants and flatterers are undesignedly treacherous and fickle. They are prone to admire inordinately at first, and not finding a constant supply of food for this kind of sickly appetite, take a distaste to the object of their idolatry. To be even with themselves for their credulity, they sharpen their wits to spy out faults, and are delighted to find that this answers better than their first employment. It is a course of study, “lively, audible, and full of vent.” They have the organ of wonder and the organ of fear in a prominent degree.

===Chinese===

自己的高见被人引来反驳自己，自己的妙语被人当作好话讲给自己听，也是一件快事。有一回我在正厅后排同一位明白人聊天，批评奈特先生（Mr. Knight）演的菲尔奇。“啊！”他说，“演那个角色，还得数小个子的西蒙斯。”他又说：“有一句话评他这出戏，评得再好不过了，登在《考察家》（Examiner）上（我记得是）——*他那只模样，一只眼睛里像装着绞架，另一只里像装着一个俏姑娘。*”我一声没吭，那一晚余下的时间心情却好得出奇。凡有谈壁球戏的场合，我很少不听到有人插问一句：“请问，前一阵各家报纸都登过一篇写一个叫卡瓦纳的人的文章，有谁见过么？可知道是谁写的？”这些时刻可真难熬。还有一回，我胜过一个人一筹——姓名我不提了。我当时正说着柏克（Burke），正毫不节制地称道他的才具，这位先生打断我说，依他看，柏克的名气被抬得太高了；随后又漫不经心地添一句：“请问，最近一期《———》上有一篇写他的文字，您读过了么？”“正是我写的！”——这个对句我忍不住说了，过后又为那一刻的意气惭愧。然而，据我所见，可从没有谁饶过我。
有些人钻营着凑到名人跟前，看样子是为了挑出毛病、日后再出卖他们。表面如此，但事情的真相与对自然更深的了解却不肯这样解释。谄媚之徒的负心与善变，多半出于无心。他们起先容易钦慕得过分，待这种病胃口的粮草接济不上，便对偶像生厌。为了同自己的轻信算清账，他们磨尖了心智去窥探过失，又惊喜地发现这营生比原先那桩更有出息。这是一门功课，“活泼、响亮、一肚子的气要出”。他们身上的惊奇官能和恐惧官能都格外发达。

===Original===

The first requires new objects of admiration to satisfy its uneasy cravings: the second makes them crouch to power wherever its shifting standard appears, and willing to curry favour with all parties, and ready to betray any out of sheer weakness and servility. I do not think they mean any harm: at least, I can look at this obliquity with indifference in my own particular case. I have been more disposed to resent it as I have seen it practised upon others, where I have been better able to judge of the extent of the mischief, and the heartlessness and idiot folly it discovered.
I do not think great intellectual attainments are any recommendation to the women. They puzzle them, and are a diversion to the main question. If scholars talk to ladies of what they understand, their hearers are none the wiser: if they talk of other things, they prove themselves fools. The conversation between Angelica and Foresight in *Love for Love* is a receipt in full for all such overstrained nonsense: while he is wandering among the signs of the zodiac, she is standing a-tiptoe on the earth. It has been remarked that poets do not choose mistresses very wisely. I believe it is not choice, but necessity. If they could throw the handkerchief like the Grand Turk, I imagine we should see scarce mortals, but rather goddesses, surrounding their steps, and each exclaiming, with Lord Byron’s own Ionian maid﻿—

> “So shalt thou find me ever at thy side,

Here and hereafter, if the last may be!”

===Chinese===

前者需要不断更新的钦慕对象，来喂它无休无止的馋；后者使他们一见那面飘忽不定的权力大旗，便匍匐在地，愿意向各党各派讨好，又出于纯粹的软弱与奴性，随时可以出卖任何一方。我并不认为他们安着什么坏心：至少这种心术歪斜落到我自己头上时，我还能淡然处之。看到它施在旁人身上，我才更动气——那时我更能掂出祸害的大小，掂出它暴露出的凉薄与痴愚。
我不认为渊深的智力造诣于女人是什么推荐。她们被弄糊涂了，正题倒教它岔开了。学者同淑女们谈他们懂的东西，听的人一个字也没多明白；谈别的吧，又证明自己是傻瓜。《以爱还爱》里安杰莉卡与福赛特的对话，把这类牵强过头的胡话一总结清：他在黄道十二宫里漫游，她踮着脚尖站在地上。常有人说诗人挑情人不大高明。我看那不是挑选，是不得已。倘若他们能像土耳其大帝那样抛得出手帕，我想他们脚边围着的便几乎不是凡人，而是众位女神了，每一位都学着拜伦勋爵自家的爱奥尼亚少女嚷道——

> “你将发现我永远在你身旁，

> 今世与来世——若真有来世的话！”

===Original===

Ah! no, these are bespoke, carried of by men of mortal, not of ethereal mould, and thenceforth the poet from whose mind the ideas of love and beauty are inseparable as dreams from sleep, goes on the forlorn hope of the passion, and dresses up the first Dulcinea that will take compassion on him in all the colours of fancy. What boots it to complain if the delusion lasts for life, and the rainbow still paints its form in the cloud?
There is one mistake I would wish, if possible, to correct. Men of letters, artists, and others not succeeding with women in a certain rank of life, think the objection is to their want of fortune, and that they shall stand a better chance by descending lower, where only their good qualities or talents will be thought of. Oh! worse and worse. The objection is to themselves, not to their fortune﻿—to their abstraction, to their absence of mind, to their unintelligible and romantic notions. Women of education may have a glimpse of their meaning, may get a clue to their character, but to all others they are thick darkness. If the mistress smiles at their ideal advances, the maid will laugh outright; she will throw water over you, get her sister to listen, send her sweetheart to ask you what you mean, will set the village or the house upon your back; it will be a farce, a comedy, a standing jest for a year, and then the murder will out. Scholars should be sworn at Highgate. They are no match for chambermaids, or wenches at lodging-houses. They had better try their hands on heiresses or ladies of quality. These last have high notions of themselves that may fit some of your epithets! They are above mortality; so are your thoughts! But with low life, trick, ignorance, and cunning, you have nothing in common. Whoever you are, that think you can make a compromise or a conquest there by good nature or good sense, be warned by a friendly voice, and retreat in time from the unequal contest.
If, as I have said above, scholars are no match for chambermaids, on the other hand gentlemen are no match for blackguards. The former are on their honour, act on the square; the latter take all advantages, and have no idea of any other principle. It is astonishing how soon a fellow without education will learn to cheat. He is impervious to any ray of liberal knowledge; his understanding is

> “Not pierceable by power of any star﻿—”

===Chinese===

啊！不。这班女神早被人订下了，让凡胎、而非灵质的人抢了去；从此，那位心中爱与美的观念如梦之于睡眠、须臾不可分离的诗人，便踏上了这桩痴情的敢死队之旅，把头一个肯怜悯他的杜尔西内娅，用想象的一切色彩装扮起来。倘若这迷误能伴人终身，倘若长虹至今仍在云间画出它的形影，抱怨又有何益？
有一个误会，倘若可能，我愿纠正。文人、艺术家，还有那些在某一阶层的女子那里不得志的人，总以为人家嫌的是他们没钱，以为往低处走、走到只看人品才具的地方，机会便好些。啊！越弄越糟。人家嫌的是他们本人，不是他们的钱袋——嫌他们的心不在焉，嫌他们的神不守舍，嫌他们那些谁也听不懂的浪漫念头。受过教育的女子或许能对他们的意思窥见一斑，或许摸得到他们性格的一点头绪；对其余的女子，他们便是一团浓黑。女主人对你的理想式殷勤还肯微笑，女仆可要笑出声来；她会兜头泼你一盆水，拉她姐妹来听，派她的情郎来问你到底什么意思，会挑动全村或全家与你作对；这将是一出闹剧、一场喜剧、一年的保留笑柄，然后真相大白、东窗事发。学者们真该在海格特宣个誓。他们斗不过女仆，斗不过寄宿人家的丫头。他们不如到女继承人或贵妇人身上去碰碰运气。后者的自我期许才当得起你们的某些形容词！她们超乎凡俗之上；你们的思想也是！可是同下等生活、同狡计、愚昧与刁滑，你们毫无共通之处。无论你是谁，只要你以为凭好脾气或好见识，便能在那边来一场调和或一场征服，就听友好的一声忠告，趁早从这场力量悬殊的较量里退出来。
倘若如我上文所说，学者斗不过女仆，那么反过来说，绅士也斗不过流氓。前者顾惜名誉，行事光明正大；后者占尽便宜，此外不知还有什么原则。一个没有受过教育的小子学会坑蒙拐骗，其快令人吃惊。他刀枪不入于一切开明学问的光线；他的理解力——

> “任什么星宿的法力也穿不透——”

===Original===

but it is porous to all sorts of tricks, chicanery, stratagems, and knavery, by which anything is to be got. Mrs. Peachum, indeed, says, that to succeed at the gaming-table, the candidate should have the education of a nobleman. I do not know how far this example contradicts my theory. I think it is a rule that men in business should not be taught other things. Anyone will be almost sure to make money who has no other idea in his head. A college education, or intense study of abstract truth, will not enable a man to drive a bargain, to overreach another, or even to guard himself from being overreached. As Shakespeare says, that “to have a good face is the effect of study, but reading and writing come by nature”; so it might be argued, that to be a knave is the gift of fortune, but to play the fool to advantage it is necessary to be a learned man. The best politicians are not those who are deeply grounded in mathematical or in ethical science. Rules stand in the way of expediency. Many a man has been hindered from pushing his fortune in the world by an early cultivation of his moral sense, and has repented of it at leisure during the rest of his life. A shrewd man said of my father, that he would not send a son of his to school to him on any account, for that by teaching him to speak the truth he would disqualify him from getting his living in the world!
It is hardly necessary to add any illustration to prove that the most original and profound thinkers are not always the most successful or popular writers. This is not merely a temporary disadvantage; but many great philosophers have not only been scouted while they were living, but forgotten as soon as they were dead. The name of Hobbes is perhaps sufficient to explain this assertion. But I do not wish to go farther into this part of the subject, which is obvious in itself. I have said, I believe, enough to take off the air of paradox which hangs over the title of this essay.

===Chinese===

可是对一切能捞到东西的圈套、诡辩、计谋与欺诈，它却处处透风。皮丘姆太太（Mrs. Peachum）固然说过，要在赌桌上发迹，进身者须受贵族的教育。这个例子在多大程度上反驳了我的理论，我不得而知。我以为有一条定则：生意人不应再教他别的东西。一个人只要脑子里再没有别的念头，几乎稳赚钱钱。大学教育，或对抽象真理的深钻，不能使人做成一桩好买卖、算计倒旁人，甚至不能叫他防住旁人的算计。莎士比亚说过：“有一张好看的脸是修来的，读书写字才是天生的”；照此也可以说：做无赖是天赋的运气，而要把傻瓜当得漂亮，非做学问人不可。最好的政客，并不是深通数学或伦理科学的人。规矩挡着权变的道。多少人因为早年修养了道德感，一生在世界里进取无路，只好在余生里从容悔恨。一位精明人说起我父亲：他说无论如何不肯把儿子送到他的学校去，因为他教孩子讲真话，等于断绝了孩子日后在世界上的生计！
最独创、最深刻的思想家未必是最成功、最走红的作家——这一点几乎不必再举例了。这不只是一时的吃亏：许多大哲学家不但生前备受摈斥，死后也随即被人忘却。霍布斯（Hobbes）这个名字，或许足以为这一断语作注了。但这个题目本身的显豁，使我不愿再多说。我相信，已经说得够多了——足够抹去悬在这篇随笔题目上的那层故作奇论之气了。

### On the Fear of Death / 论怕死
===Original===

> “And our little life is rounded with a sleep.”

===Chinese===

> “我们这短短的一生，前后都环绕在酣睡之中。”

===Original===

Perhaps the best cure for the fear of death is to reflect that life has a beginning as well as an end. There was a time when we were not: this gives us no concern﻿—why, then, should it trouble us that a time will come when we shall cease to be? I have no wish to have been alive a hundred years ago, or in the reign of Queen Anne: why should I regret and lay it so much to heart that I shall not be alive a hundred years hence, in the reign of I cannot tell whom?
When Bickerstaff wrote his *Essays* I knew nothing of the subjects of them; nay, much later, and but the other day, as it were, in the beginning of the reign of George III, when Goldsmith, Johnson, Burke, used to meet at the Globe, when Garrick was in his glory, and Reynolds was over head and ears with his portraits, and Sterne brought out the volumes of *Tristram Shandy* year by year, it was without consulting me: I had not the slightest intimation of what was going on: the debates in the House of Commons on the American War, or the firing at Bunker’s Hill, disturbed not me: yet I thought this no evil﻿—I neither ate, drank, nor was merry, yet I did not complain: I had not then looked out into this breathing world, yet I was well; and the world did quite as well without me as I did without it! Why, then, should I make all this outcry about parting with it, and being no worse off than I was before? There is nothing in the recollection that at a certain time we were not come into the world that “the gorge rises at”﻿—why should we revolt at the idea that we must one day go out of it? To die is only to be as we were before we were born; yet no one feels any remorse, or regret, or repugnance, in contemplating this last idea. It is rather a relief and disburdening of the mind: it seems to have been holiday-time with us then: we were not called to appear upon the stage of life, to wear robes or tatters, to laugh or cry, be hooted or applauded; we had lain *perdus* all this while, snug, out of harm’s way; and had slept out our thousands of centuries without wanting to be waked up; at peace and free from care, in a long nonage, in a sleep deeper and calmer than that of infancy, wrapped in the softest and finest dust. And the worst that we dread is, after a short, fretful, feverish being, after vain hopes and idle fears, to sink to final repose again, and forget the troubled dream of life!﻿ ﻿…

===Chinese===

医治怕死，最好的药方或许是想一想：生命有始，亦有终。曾有一个时候，我们还不存在：这并不使我们挂心——那么，将来有一个时候我们将不复存在，又何必为此烦恼呢？我并不希望在一百年前、在安妮女王当政的时候活过；那么，我将不能在一百年后、在我说不准哪位当政的时候活着，又何必这样懊丧、这样痛心呢？
比克斯塔夫（Bickerstaff）写他的《随笔》时，那些题目我一无所知；不但如此，晚得多的时候——简直就像前几天，乔治三世登基之初——哥尔德斯密斯、约翰逊、柏克常在地球酒馆聚首，加里克正当盛名，雷诺兹埋首于他的肖像画，斯特恩一年一卷地推出《项狄传》，这一切都没有请教过我：事情进行到哪一步，我一点风声也没有；下院关于美洲战争的辩论，邦克山的炮声，都不曾惊动我：可我并不以此为苦——我不吃、不喝、也不行乐，却也不抱怨；那时我还没有望进这个呼吸的世界，我却安然无恙；世界没有我过得照样好，我没有世界也过得照样好！那么，如今要与它分手、回到先前那种不好不坏的状态，我又何必这样大喊大叫呢？回想自己在某一时刻尚未降生人世，这里头没有一点叫人“反胃”的东西——那么想到有一天必须离开人世，我们又何必反感呢？死，不过是回到我们出生之前的那个样子；然而在凝思后面这个念头时，谁也不觉得有一点悔恨、惋惜或厌恶。它毋宁是心灵的一种解脱与卸除：那时候，我们过的仿佛是假期：没有人唤我们上台，去穿锦袍或挂破布，去笑去哭，去挨嘘或受捧；我们一直潜伏着，安安稳稳，祸害沾不了身；我们睡足了千万个世纪，也不想有人来叫醒；太平安然，无忧无虑，处在一个漫长的未成年期，一场比婴儿的睡眠更深更稳的睡眠里，裹在最细软的尘土中。而我们最怕的，不过是经过短促、焦躁、发热的一生，经过虚妄的希望与无谓的恐惧之后，重新沉入最后的安息，忘掉人生这场烦扰的梦！……

===Original===

Ye armed men, knights templars, that sleep in the stone aisles of that old Temple church, where all is silent above, and where a deeper silence reigns below (not broken by the pealing organ), are ye not contented where ye lie? Or would you come out of your long homes to go to the Holy War? Or do ye complain that pain no longer visits you, that sickness has done its worst, that you have paid the last debt to nature, that you hear no more of the thickening phalanx of the foe, or your lady’s waning love; and that while this ball of earth rolls its eternal round, no sound shall ever pierce through to disturb your lasting repose, fixed as the marble over your tombs, breathless as the grave that holds you! And thou, oh! thou, to whom my heart turns, and will turn while it has feeling left, who didst love in vain, and whose first was thy last sigh, wilt not thou too rest in peace (or wilt thou cry to me complaining from thy clay-cold bed) when that sad heart is no longer sad, and that sorrow is dead which thou wert only called into the world to feel!
It is certain that there is nothing in the idea of a preexistent state that excites our longing like the prospect of a posthumous existence. We are satisfied to have begun life when we did; we have no ambition to have set out on our journey sooner; and feel that we have had quite enough to do to battle our way through since. We cannot say,

> “The wars we well remember of King Nine,

Of old Assaracus and Inachus divine.”

===Chinese===

你们这些披甲的人、圣殿骑士们，长眠在圣殿老教堂的石砌侧廊里——上面万籁俱寂，下面更是深不可测的寂静（风琴的轰鸣也惊不破它）——你们躺在那里还不满足么？还是想走出你们长长的家，再去参加圣战？还是你们抱怨：痛苦不再来访，疾病已使尽了他的手段，你们已把欠自然（Nature）的最后一笔债还清；再也听不到敌人越聚越密的方阵，听不到贵妇人的爱日渐冷淡；当这颗地球滚着它永恒的圆周时，再没有一丝声响会穿透进来，搅扰你们长久的安息——像你们墓上的大理石一样纹丝不动，像收留你们的坟墓一样气息全无！还有你，啊，你！我的心转向你、只要还有知觉就永远转向你的你，你爱了一场空，你的第一声叹息也就是你最后一声叹息的你——当那颗悲苦的心不再悲苦，当那份只为你降生人世来承受的哀伤已经死去，你不也安息了么（还是你要从你冰冷的黄土床上向我喊冤诉苦）！
可以断言，前世的想法里，没有任何东西能像身后的前景那样激起我们的渴慕。我们对在何时开始这一生感到满意；我们没有更早上路的野心；并且觉得，从那时一路厮杀过来，已经够我们受的了。我们不能说——

> “尼努斯王的战事我们记得真切，

> 还有古老的阿萨拉库斯与神圣的伊那科斯。”

===Original===

Neither have we any wish: we are contented to read of them in story, and to stand and gaze at the vast sea of time that separates us from them. It was early days then: the world was not *well-aired* enough for us: we have no inclination to have been up and stirring. We do not consider the six thousand years of the world before we were born as so much time lost to us: we are perfectly indifferent about the matter. We do not grieve and lament that we did not happen to be in time to see the grand mask and pageant of human life going on in all that period; though we are mortified at being obliged to quit our stand before the rest of the procession passes.
It may be suggested in explanation of this difference, that we know from various records and traditions what happened in the time of Queen Anne, or even in the reigns of the Assyrian monarchs, but that we have no means of ascertaining what is to happen hereafter but by awaiting the event, and that our eagerness and curiosity are sharpened in proportion as we are in the dark about it. This is not at all the case; for at that rate we should be constantly wishing to make a voyage of discovery to Greenland or to the Moon, neither of which we have, in general, the least desire to do. Neither, in truth, have we any particular solicitude to pry into the secrets of futurity, but as a pretext for prolonging our own existence. It is not so much that we care to be alive a hundred or a thousand years hence, any more than to have been alive a hundred or a thousand years ago: but the thing lies here, that we would all of us wish the present moment to last forever. We would be as we are, and would have the world remain just as it is, to please us.

> “The present eye catches the present object﻿—”

to have and to hold while it may; and abhors, on any terms, to have it torn from us, and nothing left in its room. It is the pang of parting, the unloosing our grasp, the breaking asunder some strong tie, the leaving some cherished purpose unfulfilled, that creates the repugnance to go, and “makes calamity of so long life,” as it often is.

> “O! thou strong heart!

There’s such a covenant ’twixt the world and thee

They’re loth to break!”

===Chinese===

我们也并无这份愿望：在史册里读到他们，我们就满足了；站在那里凝望把我们同他们隔开的那片汪洋时间，我们就满足了。那时是太初的日子：世界还没有为我们“晾透”；我们全无起来奔忙的意思。世界诞生以来、我们出生以前的六千年，我们并不看作白白损失的时间：我们对这事全无所谓。我们没有赶上亲眼看那整段时期里人生那场盛大的假面戏与巡游，也并不悲伤叹惜；虽然巡游尚未过完便不得不撤下我们的位置，倒是叫我们懊恼。
或许可以这样解释这层差别：凭借种种记载与传闻，我们知道安妮女王时代、甚至亚述诸王治下发生过什么；而今后将发生什么，除了坐等事到临头，我们无从查考，于是越是在黑暗里，我们的急切与好奇便磨得越尖。这全然不是实情；因为照那个道理，我们便该时时刻刻盼着去格陵兰或月亮作一趟发现之旅，而这两处，我们通常都丝毫没有去的欲望。其实，我们也并无特别的热心去窥探未来的秘密，除非把它当作延长我们自身存在的一个由头。要说我们当真在乎一百年后、一千年后活着，同在乎一百年前、一千年前活过一样，倒也未必：症结在这里：我们个个都愿眼下这一刻永远持续下去。我们愿意照现在这样，愿意世界照现在这样待着，好取悦我们。

> “现在的眼睛，抓住现在的对象——”

趁还在手里时握住不放；无论什么条件，也厌恶它被生生夺走，原地空空如也。是分手的剧痛，是松开我们的把握，是扯断某条坚韧的纽带，是撇下某桩心爱的志愿未成，才造出对离去的抗拒，也才常常“使如此长久的一生成为一场灾难”。

> “啊！你坚强的心！

> 这世界与你之间立着一纸盟约，

> 他们都不肯撕毁！”

===Original===

The love of life, then, is an habitual attachment, not an abstract principle. Simply *to be* does not “content man’s natural desire”: we long to be in a certain time, place, and circumstance. We would much rather be now, “on this bank and shoal of time,” than have our choice of any future period, than take a slice of fifty or sixty years out of the Millennium, for instance. This shows that our attachment is not confined either to *being* or to *well-being*; but that we have an inveterate prejudice in favour of our immediate existence, such as it is. The mountaineer will not leave his rock, nor the savage his hut; neither are we willing to give up our present mode of life, with all its advantages and disadvantages, for any other that could be substituted for it. No man would, I think, exchange his existence with any other man, however fortunate. We had as lief *not be*, as *not be ourselves*. There are some persons of that reach of soul that they would like to live two hundred and fifty years hence, to see to what height of empire America will have grown up in that period, or whether the English constitution will last so long. These are points beyond me. But I confess I should like to live to see the downfall of the Bourbons. That is a vital question with me; and I shall like it the better, the sooner it happens!
No young man ever thinks he shall die. He may believe that others will, or assent to the doctrine that “all men are mortal” as an abstract proposition, but he is far enough from bringing it home to himself individually.92 Youth, buoyant activity, and animal spirits, hold absolute antipathy with old age as well as with death; nor have we, in the heyday of life, any more than in the thoughtlessness of childhood, the remotest conception how

> “This sensible warm motion can become

A kneaded clod﻿—”

===Chinese===

可见，对生命的爱是一种习惯的眷恋，不是一条抽象的原理。单是*存在*并不“满足人自然的欲望”：我们渴望在某个特定的时间、地点与境遇里存在。我们宁可就待在现在，“在时间的这方岸与洲上”，也不愿听凭挑选任何一个未来时期——比如，也不愿从千年至福王国里切出五六十年来过。这表明，我们的眷恋既不系于*存在*，也不系于*幸福*；而是我们对眼下的存在——不管它是什么样子——怀有一种根深蒂固的偏爱。山里人不肯离开他的山岩，野人不肯离开他的草棚；我们也不肯放弃现在这种过法——连同它全部的好处与坏处——去换任何可以替换的另一种。我想，谁也不肯同任何别人交换存在，哪怕对方再幸运。我们宁可*不存在*，也*不肯不做自己*。也有那么一些襟怀的人，想活在二百五十年后，看看美利坚在那段时期里将长成多高的一座帝国，或者看看英国的宪政撑不撑得了那么久。这些题目超出了我。但我承认，我倒愿意活着看到波旁王朝的倾覆。那于我是一件性命交关的事；而且它来得越早，我越喜欢！
没有哪个年轻人想过自己也会死。他可以相信别人会死，或者把“人皆有死”当作一条抽象命题点头认账；但要他把这话收到自己头上，他还差得远。92 青春、轻扬的活力与血气，同老年、同死亡都势不两立；我们在生命的盛年，也同在童年的无忧里一样，对下面这件事没有一丝一毫的概念——

> “这有知觉的温暖的活动，怎么会变成

> 一块揉掷的土坯——”

===Original===

nor how sanguine, florid health and vigour, shall “turn to withered, weak, and grey.” Or if in a moment of idle speculation we indulge in this notion of the close of life as a theory, it is amazing at what a distance it seems; what a long, leisurely interval there is between; what a contrast its slow and solemn approach affords to our present gay dreams of existence! We eye the farthest verge of the horizon, and think what a way we shall have to look back upon, ere we arrive at our journey’s end; and without our in the least suspecting it, the mists are at our feet, and the shadows of age encompass us. The two divisions of our lives have melted into each other: the extreme points close and meet with none of that romantic interval stretching out between them that we had reckoned upon; and for the rich, melancholy, solemn hues of age, “the sear, the yellow leaf,” the deepening shadows of an autumnal evening, we only feel a dank, cold mist, encircling all objects, after the spirit of youth is fled. There is no inducement to look forward; and what is worse, little interest in looking back to what has become so trite and common. The pleasures of our existence have worn themselves out, are “gone into the wastes of time,” or have turned their indifferent side to us: the pains by their repeated blows have worn us out, and have left us neither spirit nor inclination to encounter them again in retrospect. We do not want to rip up old grievances, nor to renew our youth like the phoenix, nor to live our lives twice over. Once is enough. As the tree falls, so let it lie. Shut up the book and close the account once for all!
It has been thought by some that life is like the exploring of a passage that grows narrower and darker the farther we advance, without a possibility of ever turning back, and where we are stifled for want of breath at last. For myself, I do not complain of the greater thickness of the atmosphere as I approach the narrow house. I felt it more formerly,93 when the idea alone seemed to suppress a thousand rising hopes, and weighed upon the pulses of the blood. At present I rather feel a thinness and want of support, I stretch out my hand to some object and find none, I am too much in a world of abstraction; the naked map of life is spread out before me, and in the emptiness and desolation I see Death coming to meet me.

也想不出红润健康的血色与精力，会如何“变成枯槁、羸弱与灰白”。即便闲想之际，我们把生命的终点当作一个理论来自我消遣，它显得那样遥远，也够令人惊异；中间隔着多么漫长、多么从容的一段；它缓慢而庄严的临近，同我们眼前对生存的欢快梦想，构成怎样的对照！我们望着地平线最远的那一道边，想着到达旅程终点之前，我们将有多少来路可以回望；殊不知，毫没提防之间，雾已到了脚边，老年的暗影已四面围拢。生命的两段早已彼此融化：两端合拢、相遇，我们原先指望横亘其间的那段罗曼蒂克的间隔，根本无影无踪；至于老年的那些丰饶、忧郁、庄严的色调，“枯黄的日子、黄叶”，秋日黄昏渐深的阴影——在青春的精灵飞走之后，我们只觉一团湿冷的雾，把万物团团裹住。向前看已无可引诱；更糟的是，向后看那些变得如此陈腐、寻常的往事，也提不起兴致。生存的种种欢愉已经磨尽了自己，“消逝进时间的荒原”，或者把冷漠的一面对准了我们；种种苦痛则凭它们再三的打击磨尽了我们，使我们既无心力、也无意愿在回顾中再同它们照一次面。我们不想重翻旧怨，不想学凤凰返老还童，也不想把一生再过一遍。一遍尽够了。树倒了，就让它躺着罢。合上账簿，把账一次结清！
有人认为，人生仿佛探索一条甬道：越往前越窄、越暗，绝无回头的可能，末了我们喘不上气，闷死在里头。至于我自己，临近那所窄屋，我并不抱怨空气越来越稠。从前我倒更觉得它稠，93那时单是那个念头，仿佛就压灭了一千个升起的希望，压在血脉的搏动上。如今我反而觉得稀薄、无所依傍：我伸手去够一件什么东西，却什么也没够着；我太深地陷在一个抽象的世界里；人生那幅赤裸的地图摊在我面前，在空旷与荒凉中，我看见死亡迎面走来。

In my youth I could not behold him for the crowd of objects and feelings, and Hope stood always between us, saying, “Never mind that old fellow!” If I had lived indeed, I should not care to die. But I do not like a contract of pleasure broken off unfulfilled, a marriage with joy unconsummated, a promise of happiness rescinded. My public and private hopes have been left a ruin, or remain only to mock me. I would wish them to be re-edified. I should like to see some prospect of good to mankind, such as my life began with. I should like to leave some sterling work behind me. I should like to have some friendly hand to consign me to the grave. On these conditions I am ready, if not willing, to depart. I shall then write on my tomb﻿—**Grateful and Contented**! But I have thought and suffered too much to be willing to have thought and suffered in vain.﻿—In looking back, it sometimes appears to me as if I had in a manner slept out my life in a dream or shadow on the side of the hill of knowledge, where I have fed on books, on thoughts, on pictures, and only heard in half-murmurs the trampling of busy feet, or the noises of the throng below. Waked out of this dim, twilight existence, and startled with the passing scene, I have felt a wish to descend to the world of realities, and join in the chase. But I fear too late, and that I had better return to my bookish chimeras and indolence once more! *Zanetto, lascia le donne, et studia la matematica.* I will think of it.
It is not wonderful that the contemplation and fear of death become more familiar to us as we approach nearer to it: that life seems to ebb with the decay of blood and youthful spirits; and that as we find everything about us subject to chance and change, as our strength and beauty die, as our hopes and passions, our friends and our affections leave us, we begin by degrees to feel ourselves mortal!
I have never seen death but once, and that was in an infant. It is years ago. The look was calm and placid, and the face was fair and firm. It was as if a waxen image had been laid out in the coffin, and strewed with innocent flowers. It was not like death, but more like an image of life! No breath moved the lips, no pulse stirred, no sight or sound would enter those eyes or ears more.

我只见过一次死，死在一个婴儿身上。那是多年前了。那神色安详平静，面容白哲而沉静。仿佛棺中安放的是一尊蜡像，撒着无辜的花朵。它不像死，倒更像一幅生命的图像！没有一丝气息掠动嘴唇，没有一次脉搏跳动，那双眼睛、那对耳朵再不会纳入任何光影与声响了。
